title: The Mortification of Sin
author: John Owen
description: John Owen’s classic on putting sin to death, built on Romans 8:13: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Owen shows why every believer must fight the sin that remains in them, what true mortification is and is not, and how it is done — by the Spirit, through faith in Christ. First published in 1656; this text follows the 1658 second edition.

paragraphs.original: Christian Reader,
paragraphs.modern: To the Christian reader,

paragraphs.original: I shall in a few words acquaint thee with the reasons that obtained my consent to the publishing of the ensuing discourse. The consideration of the present state and condition of the generality of professors, the visible evidences of the frame of their hearts and spirits, manifesting a great disability of dealing with the temptations wherewith, from the peace they have in the world and the divisions that they have among themselves, they are encompassed, holds the chief place amongst them. This I am assured is of so great importance, that if hereby I only occasion others to press more effectually on the consciences of men the work of considering their ways, and to give more clear direction for the compassing of the end proposed, I shall well esteem of my lot in this undertaking.
paragraphs.modern: Let me briefly explain why I agreed to publish this book. My chief reason is the present condition of most people who profess to be Christians. Their lives reveal the state of their hearts: they seem largely unable to deal with the temptations surrounding them. Their comfortable position in the world exposes them to some temptations, while their divisions among themselves expose them to others. I am convinced that this matter is so important that my effort will have been worthwhile even if it merely prompts other people to do the work better—to urge their hearers more effectively to examine their lives, and to give them clearer guidance toward the goal I have in view.

paragraphs.original: This was seconded by an observation of some men’s dangerous mistakes, who of late days have taken upon them to give directions for the mortification of sin, who, being unacquainted with the mystery of the gospel and the efficacy of the death of Christ, have anew imposed the yoke of a self-wrought-out mortification on the necks of their disciples, which neither they nor their forefathers were ever able to bear. A mortification they cry up and press, suitable to that of the gospel neither in respect of nature, subject, causes, means, nor effects; which constantly produces the deplorable issues of superstition, self-righteousness, and anxiety of conscience in them who take up the burden which is so bound for them.
paragraphs.modern: A second reason is that I have noticed dangerous mistakes among some recent teachers who offer instructions for putting sin to death. They do not understand the gospel’s revealed mystery or the power of Christ’s death. Consequently, they have once again placed on their followers the burden of trying to conquer sin entirely by their own efforts—a burden neither these teachers nor their predecessors could bear. They strongly promote a kind of mortification that differs from the gospel’s in every respect: what it is, who can practice it, what causes it, what means accomplish it, and what results it produces. The unhappy consequences for those who accept this burden are consistently superstition, self-righteousness, and an anxious conscience.

paragraphs.original: What is here proposed in weakness, I humbly hope will answer the spirit and letter of the gospel, with the experiences of them who know what it is to walk with God, according to the tenor of the covenant of grace. So that if not this, yet certainly something of this kind, is very necessary at this season for the promotion and furtherance of this work of gospel mortification in the hearts of believers, and their direction in paths safe, and wherein they may find rest to their souls.
paragraphs.modern: I offer this book conscious of my weakness. Yet I humbly hope that it agrees with both the meaning and the wording of the gospel, and with the experience of those who know what it is to walk with God under the covenant of grace. This book may not meet the need, but something of this kind is certainly very necessary now. Believers need help in carrying forward the gospel’s work of putting sin to death in their hearts. They need guidance along safe paths where their souls can find rest.

paragraphs.original: Something I have to add as to what in particular relates unto myself. Having preached on this subject unto some comfortable success, through the grace of Him that administereth seed to the sower, I was pressed by sundry persons, in whose hearts are the ways of God, thus to publish what I had delivered, with such additions and alterations as I should judge necessary.
paragraphs.modern: I should add something about my own circumstances. By the grace of the God who supplies seed to the sower, my preaching on this subject had encouraging results. Several people whose hearts are set on God’s ways therefore urged me to publish what I had preached, making whatever additions and changes I thought necessary.

paragraphs.original: Under the inducement of their desires, I called to remembrance the debt, wherein I have now for some years stood engaged unto sundry noble and worthy Christian friends, as to a treatise of Communion with God, some while since promised to them;[1] and thereon apprehended, that if I could not hereby compound for the greater debt, yet I might possibly tender them this discourse of variance with themselves, as interest for their forbearance of that of peace and communion with God. Besides, I considered that I had been providentially engaged in the public debate of sundry controversies in religion, which might seem to claim something in another kind of more general use, as a fruit of choice, not necessity. On these and the like accounts is this short discourse brought forth to public view, and now presented unto thee.
paragraphs.modern: Their request reminded me of another obligation. For several years, I had owed a number of valued Christian friends a promised book on Communion with God.[1] This smaller book could not discharge that larger debt. But perhaps a book about being at war with the sin within themselves could serve as interest, in return for their patience while awaiting the book about peace and communion with God. I also reflected that God’s providence had drawn me into public debates about several religious controversies. It seemed appropriate to offer something different and more generally useful—something I chose to write, rather than something controversy compelled me to write. For these and similar reasons, this short book is now published and placed before you.

paragraphs.original: I hope I may own in sincerity, that my heart’s desire unto God, and the chief design of my life in the station wherein the good providence of God hath placed me, are, that mortification and universal holiness may be promoted in my own and in the hearts and ways of others, to the glory of God; that so the gospel of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ may be adorned in all things: for the compassing of which end, if this little discourse (of the publishing whereof this is the sum of the account I shall give) may in any thing be useful to the least of the saints, it will be looked on as a return of the weak prayers wherewith it is attended by its unworthy author,
paragraphs.modern: I hope I can sincerely say that my prayer to God, and the chief aim of my life in the position his good providence has given me, is this: that sin may increasingly be put to death, and holiness may grow in every part of life, both in my own heart and conduct and in those of others, to God’s glory. In this way, the gospel of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be honored in everything. That is why I have published this little book. If it contributes anything toward that goal, even for the least of God’s people, I will receive it as an answer to the weak prayers offered with it by its unworthy author,

paragraphs.original: John Owen.
paragraphs.modern: John Owen.

paragraphs.original: [1] Since the first edition of this treatise; that other also is published.
paragraphs.modern: [1] Since the first edition of this book appeared, Communion with God has also been published.

chapters.title: Chapter I: The foundation in Romans 8:13

paragraphs.original: The foundation of the whole ensuing discourse laid in Rom. viii. 13 — The words of the apostle opened — The certain connection between true mortification and salvation — Mortification the work of believers — The Spirit the principal efficient cause of it — What meant by “the body” in the words of the apostle — What by “the deeds of the body” — Life, in what sense promised to this duty.
paragraphs.modern: The book’s foundation in Romans 8:13 — An explanation of Paul’s words — The certain connection between truly putting sin to death and salvation — This is the work of believers — The Spirit is the chief power who accomplishes it — The meaning of “the body” and “the deeds of the body” — The kind of life promised to those who do this work.

paragraphs.original: That what I have of direction to contribute to the carrying on of the work of mortification in believers may receive order and perspicuity, I shall lay the foundation of it in those words of the apostle, Rom. viii. 13, “If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body ye shall live;” and reduce the whole to an improvement of the great evangelical truth and mystery contained in them.
paragraphs.modern: To make my guidance about putting sin to death in believers orderly and clear, I will build it on Paul’s words in Romans 8:13: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Everything that follows will develop and apply the great gospel truth revealed in these words.

paragraphs.original: The apostle having made a recapitulation of his doctrine of justification by faith, and the blessed estate and condition of them who are made by grace partakers thereof, verses 1–3 of this chapter, proceeds to improve it to the holiness and consolation of believers. Among his arguments and motives unto holiness, the verse mentioned containeth one from the contrary events and effects of holiness and sin: “If ye live after the flesh, ye shall die.” What it is to “live after the flesh,” and what it is to “die,” that being not my present aim and business, I shall no otherwise explain than as they will fall in with the sense of the latter words of the verse, as before proposed.
paragraphs.modern: In Romans 8:1–3, Paul has briefly restated his teaching about justification by faith and the blessed condition of those who share in it by grace. He then applies that teaching to believers’ holiness and encouragement. One of his arguments for holiness is the contrast between the outcomes of holiness and sin: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die.” A full explanation of “living according to the flesh” and “dying” is not my present purpose. I will explain them only as necessary to understand the second half of the verse, which is our subject.

paragraphs.original: In the words peculiarly designed for the foundation of the ensuing discourse, there is, — First, A duty prescribed: “Mortify the deeds of the body.” Secondly, The persons are denoted to whom it is prescribed: “Ye,” — “if ye mortify.” Thirdly, There is in them a promise annexed to that duty: “Ye shall live.” Fourthly, The cause or means of the performance of this duty, — the Spirit: “If ye through the Spirit.” Fifthly, The conditionality of the whole proposition, wherein duty, means, and promise are contained: “If ye,” etc.
paragraphs.modern: The words on which this book is based contain five things. First, a commanded duty: “Put to death the deeds of the body.” Second, the people to whom the command is addressed: “You”—“if you put to death.” Third, a promise attached to the duty: “You will live.” Fourth, the power or means by which the duty is carried out: “by the Spirit.” Fifth, the conditional form of the whole statement, which joins the duty, the means, and the promise: “If you,” and so on.

paragraphs.original: 1. The first thing occurring in the words as they lie in the entire proposition is the conditional note, Εἰ δὲ, “But if.” Conditionals in such propositions may denote two things:—
paragraphs.modern: 1. The first feature of the sentence is its conditional expression, Ei de: “But if.” In statements like this, a condition can indicate either of two things.

paragraphs.original: (1.) The uncertainty of the event or thing promised, in respect of them to whom the duty is prescribed. And this takes place where the condition is absolutely necessary unto the issue, and depends not itself on any determinate cause known to him to whom it is prescribed. So we say, “If we live, we will do such a thing.” This cannot be the intendment of the conditional expression in this place. Of the persons to whom these words are spoken, it is said, verse 1 of the same chapter, “There is no condemnation to them.”
paragraphs.modern: (1.) It can express uncertainty about whether the stated outcome will happen to the people being addressed. This is so when the condition is essential to that outcome, but the people addressed know of nothing that guarantees the condition will be fulfilled. We use this kind of condition when we say, “If we are still alive, we will do this.” But that cannot be the intended meaning here. Of the very people addressed, verse 1 of this chapter says, “There is no condemnation for them.”

paragraphs.original: (2.) The certainty of the coherence and connection that is between the things spoken of; as we say to a sick man, “If you will take such a potion, or use such a remedy, you will be well.” The thing we solely intend to express is the certainty of the connection that is between the potion or remedy and health. And this is the use of it here. The certain connection that is between the mortifying of the deeds of the body and living is intimated in this conditional particle.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) A condition can instead express the certainty of the connection between two things. We might tell a sick person, “If you take this medicine or use this remedy, you will recover.” Our point is to affirm the connection between the remedy and recovery. That is how the condition functions here. “If” points to the certain connection between putting the deeds of the body to death and living.

paragraphs.original: Now, the connection and coherence of things being manifold, as of cause and effect, of way and means and the end, this between mortification and life is not of cause and effect properly and strictly, — for “eternal life is the gift of God through Jesus Christ,” Rom. vi. 23, — but of means and end. God hath appointed this means for the attaining that end, which he hath freely promised. Means, though necessary, have a fair subordination to an end of free promise. A gift, and procuring cause in him to whom it is given, are inconsistent. The intendment, then, of this proposition as conditional is, that there is a certain infallible connection and coherence between true mortification and eternal life: if you use this means, you shall obtain that end; if you do mortify, you shall live. And herein lies the main motive unto and enforcement of the duty prescribed.
paragraphs.modern: Things can be connected in different ways: as cause and effect, for example, or as a means and the goal it leads to. Strictly speaking, putting sin to death does not cause or earn eternal life, because “eternal life is God’s gift through Jesus Christ” (Romans 6:23). Rather, the relationship is one of means and goal. God has freely promised the goal, and he has appointed this means of reaching it. A necessary means can serve a freely promised outcome without turning that outcome into something earned. What the recipient earns cannot, in that same respect, be a gift. The conditional statement therefore means that there is an unfailing connection between genuinely putting sin to death and eternal life: use this appointed means, and you will reach that goal; put sin to death, and you will live. This connection supplies the chief reason for obeying the command.

paragraphs.original: 2. The next thing we meet withal in the words is the persons to whom this duty is prescribed, and that is expressed in the word “Ye,” in the original included in the verb, θανατοῦτε “if ye mortify;” — that is, ye believers; ye to whom “there is no condemnation,” verse 1; ye that are “not in the flesh, but in the Spirit,” verse 9; who are “quickened by the Spirit of Christ,” verses 10, 11; to you is this duty prescribed. The pressing of this duty immediately on any other is a notable fruit of that superstition and self-righteousness that the world is full of, — the great work and design of devout men ignorant of the gospel, Rom. x. 3, 4; John xv. 5. Now, this description of the persons, in conjunction with the prescription of the duty, is the main foundation of the ensuing discourse, as it lies in this thesis or proposition:—
paragraphs.modern: 2. Next consider the people to whom the duty is addressed. They are identified by “you,” which in Greek is contained within the verb thanatoute: “you put to death.” Paul means you who believe; you for whom “there is no condemnation” (verse 1); you who are “not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (verse 9); you who are made alive by Christ’s Spirit (verses 10–11). This is a command to you. To impose this work directly on anyone else, without first directing that person to Christ, is a characteristic expression of the superstition and self-righteousness so widespread in the world. It is the great project of religious people who do not understand the gospel (Romans 10:3–4; John 15:5). This identification of the people, together with the command itself, gives us the central proposition on which the rest of the book rests:

paragraphs.original: The choicest believers, who are assuredly freed from the condemning power of sin, ought yet to make it their business all their days to mortify the indwelling power of sin.
paragraphs.modern: Even the most mature believers, who have certainly been freed from sin’s power to condemn them, must make it their lifelong work to put to death the power of sin that still lives within them.

paragraphs.original: 3. The principal efficient cause of the performance of this duty is the Spirit: Εἰ δὲ Πνεύματι, — “ If by the Spirit.” The Spirit here is the Spirit mentioned verse 11, the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit of God, that “dwells in us,” verse 9, that “quickens us,” verse 11; “the Holy Ghost,” verse 14;[2] the “Spirit of adoption,” verse 15; the Spirit “that maketh intercession for us,” verse 26. All other ways of mortification are vain, all helps leave us helpless; it must be done by the Spirit. Men, as the apostle intimates, Rom. ix. 30–32, may attempt this work on other principles, by means and advantages administered on other accounts, as they always have done, and do: but, saith he, “This is the work of the Spirit; by him alone is it to be wrought, and by no other power is it to be brought about.” Mortification from a self-strength, carried on by ways of self-invention, unto the end of a self-righteousness, is the soul and substance of all false religion in the world. And this is a second principle of my ensuing discourse.
paragraphs.modern: 3. The Spirit is the chief power who actually accomplishes this duty: Ei de Pneumati, “But if by the Spirit.” This is the same Spirit named throughout the chapter: the Spirit of Christ; God’s Spirit who “dwells in us” (verse 9), makes us alive (verse 11), is the Holy Spirit referred to in verse 14,[2] gives us adoption (verse 15), and intercedes for us (verse 26). Every other method of putting sin to death is futile. Every other supposed help leaves us helpless. This work must be done by the Spirit. As Paul indicates in Romans 9:30–32, people may try to do it on other grounds and with resources drawn from elsewhere. They always have, and still do. But Paul’s point is that this is the Spirit’s work: he alone accomplishes it, and no other power can bring it about. Trying to put sin to death by our own strength, through methods of our own invention, in order to establish our own righteousness, is the very heart and substance of false religion throughout the world. This is the second principle of the argument that follows.

paragraphs.original: 4. The duty itself, “Mortify the deeds of the body,” is nextly to be remarked. Three things are here to be inquired into:— (1.) What is meant by the body; (2.) What by the deeds of the body; (3.) What by mortifying of them.
paragraphs.modern: 4. Next consider the duty itself: “Put to death the deeds of the body.” We need to ask three questions. What does “the body” mean? What are “the deeds of the body”? And what does it mean to put them to death?

paragraphs.original: (1.) The body in the close of the verse is the same with the flesh in the beginning: “If ye live after the flesh ye shall die; but if ye … mortify the deeds of the body,” — that is, of the flesh. It is that which the apostle hath all along discoursed of under the name of the flesh; which is evident from the prosecution of the antithesis between the Spirit and the flesh, before and after. The body, then, here is taken for that corruption and depravity of our natures whereof the body, in a great part, is the seat and instrument, the very members of the body being made servants unto unrighteousness thereby, Rom. vi. 19. It is indwelling sin, the corrupted flesh or lust, that is intended. Many reasons might be given of this metonymical expression, that I shall not now insist on. The “body” here is the same with παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος, and σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας, the “old man,” and the “body of sin,” Rom. vi. 6; or it may synecdochically express the whole person considered as corrupted, and the seat of lusts and distempered affections.
paragraphs.modern: (1.) “The body” in the second half of the verse refers to the same thing as “the flesh” in the first half: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if you … put to death the deeds of the body”—that is, the deeds of the flesh. Paul has been discussing this all along under the name “the flesh.” The continuing contrast between flesh and Spirit, both before and after this verse, makes that clear. Here, then, “the body” stands for the corruption of our nature, which largely finds its location and means of expression in the body. Sin makes the very parts of our bodies servants of unrighteousness (Romans 6:19). Paul means indwelling sin: the corrupted flesh and its sinful desires. I will not stop to explain all the reasons for this figure of speech. “The body” here corresponds to the Greek expressions “the old person” and “the body of sin” in Romans 6:6. Alternatively, “body” can stand for the whole person considered as corrupted and as the home of sinful desires and disordered affections.

paragraphs.original: (2.) The deeds of the body. The word is πράξεις, which, indeed, denoteth the outward actions chiefly, “the works of the flesh,” as they are called, τὰ ἔργα τῆς σαρκός, Gal. v. 19; which are there said to be “manifest,” and are enumerated. Now, though the outward deeds are here only expressed, yet the inward and next causes are chiefly intended; the “axe is to be laid to the root of the tree,” — the deeds of the flesh are to be mortified in their causes, from whence they spring. The apostle calls them deeds, as that which every lust tends unto; though it do but conceive and prove abortive, it aims to bring forth a perfect sin.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) “The deeds of the body.” The Greek word praxeis mainly refers to outward actions—the “works of the flesh,” as Galatians 5:19 calls them before saying that they are obvious and listing them. Yet although Paul names outward deeds, he chiefly intends the inward causes immediately producing them. The axe must be laid to the tree’s root: the deeds of the flesh must be put to death by attacking the causes from which they spring. Paul calls them “deeds” because every sinful desire aims at action. Even when a desire only conceives a sin that never reaches birth, its aim is a fully developed sinful act.

paragraphs.original: Having, both in the seventh and the beginning of this chapter, treated of indwelling lust and sin as the fountain and principle of all sinful actions, he here mentions its destruction under the name of the effects which it doth produce. Πράξεις τοῦ σώματος are, as much as φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός, Rom. viii. 6, the “wisdom of the flesh,” by a metonymy of the same nature with the former; or as the παθήματα and ἐπιθυμίαι, the “passions and lusts of the flesh,” Gal. v. 24, whence the deeds and fruits of it do arise; and in this sense is the body used, Rom. viii. 10: “The body is dead because of sin.”
paragraphs.modern: In Romans 7 and the beginning of Romans 8, Paul has treated indwelling desire and sin as the source and active principle of every sinful action. Here, he speaks of destroying that source by naming the effects it produces. “The deeds of the body” therefore stands for the same underlying reality as “the mindset of the flesh” in Romans 8:6. This is another instance of naming one closely connected thing in place of another. It also corresponds to “the passions” and “the desires” of the flesh in Galatians 5:24, from which its actions and results arise. “Body” is used in this sense in Romans 8:10 as well: “The body is dead because of sin.”

paragraphs.original: (3.) To mortify. Εἰ θανατοῦτε, — “If ye put to death;” a metaphorical expression, taken from the putting of any living thing to death. To kill a man, or any other living thing, is to take away the principle of all his strength, vigour, and power, so that he cannot act or exert, or put forth any proper actings of his own; so it is in this case. Indwelling sin is compared to a person, a living person, called “the old man,” with his faculties, and properties, his wisdom, craft, subtlety, strength; this, says the apostle, must be killed, put to death, mortified, — that is, have its power, life, vigour, and strength, to produce its effects, taken away by the Spirit. It is, indeed, meritoriously, and by way of example, utterly mortified and slain by the cross of Christ; and the “old man” is thence said to be “crucified with Christ,” Rom. vi. 6, and ourselves to be “dead” with him, verse 8, and really initially in regeneration, Rom. vi. 3–5, when a principle contrary to it, and destructive of it, Gal. v. 17, is planted in our hearts; but the whole work is by degrees to be carried on towards perfection all our days. Of this more in the process of our discourse.
paragraphs.modern: (3.) “To mortify.” Ei thanatoute means “if you put to death.” This is a metaphor drawn from killing a living thing. To kill a person or another living creature is to remove the source of its strength and power so that it can no longer act. The same idea applies here. Indwelling sin is pictured as a living person, “the old person,” with abilities and characteristics of its own: intelligence, cunning, subtlety, and strength. Paul says this person must be killed. That means the Spirit must take away sin’s power and vitality to produce its effects. In terms of what Christ has secured for us, and of the pattern his death supplies, sin has already been completely put to death through Christ’s cross. Therefore, the old person is said to have been “crucified with Christ” (Romans 6:6), and we are said to have “died with him” (verse 8). This death also begins to become an actual reality in our regeneration, or new birth (Romans 6:3–5). At that point, God plants in our hearts a new principle that opposes sin and works toward its destruction (Galatians 5:17). Nevertheless, this work must advance gradually toward completion throughout our lives. I will explain this further as we proceed.

paragraphs.original: The intendment of the apostle in this prescription of the duty mentioned is, — that the mortification of indwelling sin remaining in our mortal bodies, that it may not have life and power to bring forth the works or deeds of the flesh is the constant duty of believers.
paragraphs.modern: Paul’s meaning in this command is therefore this: believers must continually put to death the indwelling sin that remains in their mortal bodies, so that it will not have the vitality and power to produce the actions of the flesh.

paragraphs.original: 5. The promise unto this duty is life: “Ye shall live.” The life promised is opposed to the death threatened in the clause foregoing, “If ye live after the flesh, ye shall die;” which the same apostle expresseth, “Ye shall of the flesh reap corruption,” Gal. vi. 8, or destruction from God. Now, perhaps the word may not only intend eternal life, but also the spiritual life in Christ, which here we have; not as to the essence and being of it, which is already enjoyed by believers, but as to the joy, comfort, and vigour of it: as the apostle says in another case, “Now I live, if ye stand fast,” 1 Thess. iii. 8; — “Now my life will do me good; I shall have joy and comfort with my life;” — “Ye shall live, lead a good, vigorous, comfortable, spiritual life whilst you are here, and obtain eternal life hereafter.”
paragraphs.modern: 5. The promise attached to this duty is life: “You will live.” This life is the opposite of the death threatened in the preceding clause: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die.” Paul expresses that same warning elsewhere as reaping corruption from the flesh (Galatians 6:8)—that is, destruction from God. But perhaps “life” includes not only eternal life but also the spiritual life in Christ that we experience now. It would not mean receiving spiritual life for the first time, since believers already possess it. It would mean enjoying its joy, comfort, and strength. Compare Paul’s words in another setting: “Now we live, if you stand firm” (1 Thessalonians 3:8). His meaning is, “Now life will be a blessing to me; I will experience its joy and comfort.” In that sense the promise here is, “You will enjoy a healthy, strong, comforting spiritual life now, and you will receive eternal life afterward.”

paragraphs.original: Supposing what was said before of the connection between mortification and eternal life, as of means and end, I shall add only, as a second motive to the duty prescribed, that, — The vigour, and power, and comfort of our spiritual life depends on the mortification of the deeds of the flesh.
paragraphs.modern: Keeping in mind the relationship already explained between putting sin to death and eternal life—the relationship of means to goal—I will add only this second motive for the duty: the strength, power, and comfort of our spiritual life depend on putting the deeds of the flesh to death.

paragraphs.original: [2] There seems to be an oversight here, as the expression “Holy Ghost” does not occur in the verse cited. — Ed.
paragraphs.modern: [2] This appears to be a slip: the actual expression “Holy Ghost” does not occur in Romans 8:14. — Historical editor.

chapters.title: Chapter II: A lifelong duty for every believer

paragraphs.original: The principal assertion concerning the necessity of mortification proposed to confirmation — Mortification the duty of the best believers, Col. iii. 5; 1 Cor. ix. 27 — Indwelling sin always abides; no perfection in this life, Phil. iii. 12; 1 Cor. xiii. 12; 2 Pet. iii. 18; Gal. v. 17, etc. — The activity of abiding sin in believers, Rom. vii. 23; James iv. 5; Heb. xii. 1 — Its fruitfulness and tendency — Every lust aims at the height in its kind — The Spirit and new nature given to contend against indwelling sin, Gal. v. 17; 2 Pet. i. 4, 5; Rom. vii. 23 — The fearful issue of the neglect of mortification, Rev. iii. 2; Heb. iii. 13 — The first general principle of the whole discourse hence confirmed — Want of this duty lamented.
paragraphs.modern: Why putting sin to death is necessary — A duty even for the strongest believers (Colossians 3:5; 1 Corinthians 9:27) — Indwelling sin remains throughout life; perfection is not reached here (Philippians 3:12; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 2 Peter 3:18; Galatians 5:17) — Sin remains active in believers (Romans 7:23; James 4:5; Hebrews 12:1) — Its products and direction: every sinful desire aims at the furthest extreme of its kind — The Spirit and the new nature are given to fight it (Galatians 5:17; 2 Peter 1:4–5; Romans 7:23) — The frightening results of neglect (Revelation 3:2; Hebrews 3:13) — The book’s first principle established — Grief over the neglect of this duty.

paragraphs.original: Having laid this foundation, a brief confirmation of the fore-mentioned principal deductions will lead me to what I chiefly intend, — I. That the choicest believers, who are assuredly freed from the condemning power of sin, ought yet to make it their business all their days to mortify the indwelling power of sin.
paragraphs.modern: Now that this foundation is in place, I will briefly establish the main conclusions already drawn from it. This will lead us into my chief subject. I. Even the most mature believers, who have certainly been freed from sin’s condemning power, must make it their lifelong work to put to death the power of sin that remains within them.

paragraphs.original: So the apostle, Col. iii. 5, “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.” Whom speaks he to? Such as were “risen with Christ,” verse 1; such as were “dead” with him, verse 3; such as whose life Christ was, and who should “appear with him in glory,” verse 4. Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin or it will be killing you. Your being dead with Christ virtually, your being quickened with him, will not excuse you from this work. And our Saviour tells us how his Father deals with every branch in him that beareth fruit, every true and living branch. “He purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit,” John xv. 2. He prunes it, and that not for a day or two, but whilst it is a branch in this world. And the apostle tells you what was his practice, 1 Cor. ix. 27, “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection.” “I do it,” saith he, “daily; it is the work of my life: I omit it not; this is my business.” And if this were the work and business of Paul, who was so incomparably exalted in grace, revelations, enjoyments, privileges, consolations, above the ordinary measure of believers, where may we possibly bottom an exemption from this work and duty whilst we are in this world? Some brief account of the reasons hereof may be given:—
paragraphs.modern: Paul says in Colossians 3:5, “Therefore put to death what is earthly in you.” Who is he addressing? People who have been “raised with Christ” (verse 1), who have “died” with him (verse 3), whose life is Christ, and who will “appear with him in glory” (verse 4). Put sin to death. Make this your daily work. Keep at it as long as you live; do not take a day off. Be killing sin, or sin will be killing you. Having died with Christ by virtue of your union with him, and having been made alive with him, does not exempt you from this work. Our Savior also tells us how his Father treats every genuine, living, fruitful branch in him: “He prunes it, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). That pruning does not last only a day or two; it continues as long as the branch remains in this world. Paul describes his own practice in 1 Corinthians 9:27: “I discipline my body and bring it under control.” In other words, “I do this daily. It is my lifelong work. I do not neglect it.” Paul received grace, revelations, spiritual joys, privileges, and encouragement far beyond the ordinary experience of believers. If this was his lifelong business, on what possible grounds could we claim exemption while we remain in this world? Here are several reasons for the duty.

paragraphs.original: 1. Indwelling sin always abides whilst we are in this world; therefore it is always to be mortified. The vain, foolish, and ignorant disputes of men about perfect keeping the commands of God, of perfection in this life, of being wholly and perfectly dead to sin, I meddle not now with. It is more than probable that the men of those abominations never knew what belonged to the keeping of any one of God’s commands, and are so much below perfection of degrees, that they never attained to a perfection of parts in obedience or universal obedience in sincerity. And, therefore, many in our days who have talked of perfection have been wiser, and have affirmed it to consist in knowing no difference between good and evil. Not that they are perfect in the things we call good, but that all is alike to them, and the height of wickedness is their perfection.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Indwelling sin remains with us as long as we live in this world. Therefore, we must keep putting it to death. I will not enter into the empty, foolish, and ignorant disputes about perfectly keeping God’s commands, reaching perfection in this life, or becoming completely dead to sin. Those who advance these dreadful claims probably have never understood what obeying even one of God’s commands involves. They are not merely short of perfect degrees of obedience; they may never have reached sincere obedience that extends to every part of life. Some contemporary advocates of perfection have therefore found a more convenient approach: they say perfection consists in no longer recognizing any difference between good and evil. They do not mean they have become perfect at what we call good. They mean everything is alike to them, so that extreme wickedness itself becomes their “perfection.”

paragraphs.original: Others who have found out a new way to it, by denying original, indwelling sin, and attempering the spirituality of the law of God unto men’s carnal hearts, as they have sufficiently discovered themselves to be ignorant of the life of Christ and the power of it in believers, so they have invented a new righteousness that the gospel knows not of, being vainly puffed up by their fleshly minds.
paragraphs.modern: Others have invented another route to perfection. They deny original, indwelling sin and lower the spiritual demands of God’s law until those demands fit unspiritual human hearts. In doing so, they reveal their ignorance of Christ’s life and its power in believers. Inflated by their own fleshly thinking, they have invented a kind of righteousness the gospel does not recognize.

paragraphs.original: For us, who dare not be wise above what is written, nor boast by other men’s lives of what God hath not done for us, we say that indwelling sin lives in us, in some measure and degree, whilst we are in this world. We dare not speak as “though we had already attained, or were already perfect,” Phil. iii. 12. Our “inward man is to be renewed day by day” whilst here we live, 2 Cor. iv. 16; and according to the renovations of the new are the breaches and decays of the old. Whilst we are here we “know but in part,” 1 Cor. xiii. 12, having a remaining darkness to be gradually removed by our “growth in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ,” 2 Pet. iii. 18; and “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, so that we cannot do the things that we would,” Gal. v. 17: and are therefore defective in our obedience as well as in our light, 1 John i. 8. We have a “body of death,” Rom. vii. 24; from whence we are not delivered but by the death of our bodies, Phil. iii. 21. Now, it being our duty to mortify, to be killing of sin whilst it is in us, we must be at work. He that is appointed to kill an enemy, if he leave striking before the other ceases living, doth but half his work, Gal. vi. 9; Heb. xii. 1; 2 Cor. vii. 1.
paragraphs.modern: We, however, dare not claim a wisdom beyond Scripture or boast, on the strength of other people’s reported experience, about something God has not done in us. We acknowledge that indwelling sin remains in us to some degree throughout this life. We dare not speak as though we had already arrived or were already perfect (Philippians 3:12). Our inward person must be renewed day by day while we live here (2 Corinthians 4:16). As the new person is renewed, the old person is correspondingly weakened. Here we “know only in part” (1 Corinthians 13:12); some darkness remains, to be gradually removed as we grow in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 3:18). The flesh also desires what opposes the Spirit, preventing us from doing what we would wish (Galatians 5:17). Our obedience is therefore incomplete, just as our understanding is incomplete (1 John 1:8). We carry a “body of death” (Romans 7:24), from which we are not finally freed before bodily death and transformation (Philippians 3:21). Since our duty is to keep killing sin while it remains in us, we must keep working. A person assigned to kill an enemy has done only half the job if he stops striking while the enemy is still alive (Galatians 6:9; Hebrews 12:1; 2 Corinthians 7:1).

paragraphs.original: 2. Sin doth not only still abide in us, but is still acting, still labouring to bring forth the deeds of the flesh. When sin lets us alone we may let sin alone; but as sin is never less quiet than when it seems to be most quiet, and its waters are for the most part deep when they are still, so ought our contrivances against it to be vigorous at all times and in all conditions, even where there is least suspicion. Sin doth not only abide in us, but “the law of the members is still rebelling against the law of the mind,” Rom. vii. 23; and “the spirit that dwells in us lusteth to envy,” James iv. 5. It is always in continual work; “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit,” Gal. v. 17; lust is still tempting and conceiving sin, James i. 14; in every moral action it is always either inclining to evil, or hindering from that which is good, or disframing the spirit from communion with God.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Sin does not merely remain in us; it remains active, constantly trying to produce the deeds of the flesh. When sin leaves us alone, we may leave it alone. But it is often most active when it seems quietest; its still waters usually run deep. We must therefore oppose it energetically at all times and in every situation, even when we have least reason to suspect it. Sin is not merely present: “the law in our members” continually rebels against “the law of our mind” (Romans 7:23), and the spirit dwelling in us desires enviously (James 4:5). It never stops working. The flesh desires what opposes the Spirit (Galatians 5:17), and sinful desire keeps tempting us and conceiving sin (James 1:14). In every morally significant action, it is doing one of three things: inclining us toward evil, holding us back from good, or disturbing our readiness for communion with God.

paragraphs.original: It inclines to evil. “The evil which I would not, that I do,” saith the apostle, Rom. vii. 19. Whence is that? Why, “Because in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing.” And it hinders from good: “The good that I would do, that I do not,” verse 19; — “Upon the same account, either I do it not, or not as I should; all my holy things being defiled by this sin.” “The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would,” Gal. v. 17. And it unframes our spirit, and thence is called “The sin that so easily besets us,” Heb. xii. 1; on which account are those grievous complaints that the apostle makes of it, Rom. vii. So that sin is always acting, always conceiving, always seducing and tempting. Who can say that he had ever any thing to do with God or for God, that indwelling sin had not a hand in the corrupting of what he did? And this trade will it drive more or less all our days.
paragraphs.modern: Sin inclines us toward evil. “I do the evil I do not want to do,” Paul says in Romans 7:19. Why? Because nothing good dwells in him—that is, in his flesh. Sin also holds us back from good: “I do not do the good I want to do” (verse 19). For the same reason, either I fail to do it or I fail to do it as I should; even my holy actions are polluted by sin. “The flesh desires what opposes the Spirit, so that you cannot do what you would wish” (Galatians 5:17). Sin also unsettles our inner life, which is why Hebrews 12:1 calls it the sin that so readily entangles us. This explains Paul’s anguished complaints in Romans 7. Sin is always acting, always conceiving, always enticing and tempting. Who can say that they have ever done anything with God or for God without indwelling sin contributing some corruption to it? To a greater or lesser degree, sin will continue this business throughout our lives.

paragraphs.original: If, then, sin will be always acting, if we be not always mortifying, we are lost creatures. He that stands still and suffers his enemies to double blows upon him without resistance, will undoubtedly be conquered in the issue. If sin be subtle, watchful, strong, and always at work in the business of killing our souls, and we be slothful, negligent, foolish, in proceeding to the ruin thereof, can we expect a comfortable event? There is not a day but sin foils or is foiled, prevails or is prevailed on; and it will be so whilst we live in this world. I shall discharge him from this duty who can bring sin to a composition, to a cessation of arms in this warfare; if it will spare him any one day, in any one duty (provided he be a person that is acquainted with the spirituality of obedience and the subtlety of sin), let him say to his soul, as to this duty, “Soul, take thy rest.” The saints, whose souls breathe after deliverance from its perplexing rebellion, know there is no safety against it but in a constant warfare.
paragraphs.modern: Since sin never stops acting, we are lost if we stop putting it to death. Someone who stands still while enemies strike him again and again, without resisting, will certainly be defeated. Sin is cunning, alert, strong, and constantly working to destroy our souls. If we oppose it lazily, carelessly, and foolishly, what good outcome can we expect? Not a day passes without sin either defeating us or being defeated, gaining ground or losing it. That will continue throughout our life here. I will release anyone from this duty who can negotiate a treaty with sin and secure a ceasefire. Let someone who really understands spiritual obedience and sin’s subtlety show that sin spares him for one day, in even one duty. Then he may tell his soul, “Rest from this work.” But believers who long to be free from sin’s distressing rebellion know that the only safety lies in continual warfare.

paragraphs.original: 3. Sin will not only be striving, acting, rebelling, troubling, disquieting, but if let alone, if not continually mortified, it will bring forth great, cursed, scandalous, soul-destroying sins. The apostle tells us what the works and fruits of it are, Gal. v. 19–21, “The works of the flesh are manifest, which are, adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like.” You know what it did in David and sundry others. Sin aims always at the utmost; every time it rises up to tempt or entice, might it have its own course, it would go out to the utmost sin in that kind. Every unclean thought or glance would be adultery if it could; every covetous desire would be oppression, every thought of unbelief would be atheism, might it grow to its head. Men may come to that, that sin may not be heard speaking a scandalous word in their hearts, — that is, provoking to any great sin with scandal in its mouth; but yet every rise of lust, might it have its course, would come to the height of villany: it is like the grave, that is never satisfied.
paragraphs.modern: 3. Sin will not merely struggle, act, rebel, trouble, and disturb. Left alone instead of continually being put to death, it will produce dreadful, scandalous sins that destroy the soul. Paul lists its actions and results in Galatians 5:19–21: “The works of the flesh are obvious: adultery, sexual immorality, impurity, shameless sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalry, divisions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, wild drinking parties, and things like these.” You know what sin did in David and others. Sin always aims at the furthest extreme. Whenever it tempts or entices us, it would, if allowed its own way, develop into the most extreme sin of its kind. Every impure thought or glance would become adultery if it could. Every greedy desire would become oppression. Every unbelieving thought would become atheism if allowed to mature. A person may reach a point where sin no longer openly proposes some shocking outward offense. Nevertheless, every rising sinful desire would, if allowed its full course, reach the height of wickedness. Like the grave, it is never satisfied.

paragraphs.original: And herein lies no small share of the deceitfulness of sin, by which it prevails to the hardening of men, and so to their ruin, Heb. iii. 13, — it is modest, as it were, in its first motions and proposals, but having once got footing in the heart by them, it constantly makes good its ground, and presseth on to some farther degrees in the same kind. This new acting and pressing forward makes the soul take little notice of what an entrance to a falling off from God is already made; it thinks all is indifferent well if there be no farther progress; and so far as the soul is made insensible of any sin, — that is, as to such a sense as the gospel requireth, — so far it is hardened: but sin is still pressing forward, and that because it hath no bounds but utter relinquishment of God and opposition to him; that it proceeds towards its height by degrees, making good the ground it hath got by hardness, is not from its nature, but its deceitfulness. Now nothing can prevent this but mortification; that withers the root and strikes at the head of sin every hour, so that whatever it aims at it is crossed in. There is not the best saint in the world but, if he should give over this duty, would fall into as many cursed sins as ever any did of his kind.
paragraphs.modern: This is a major part of sin’s deceitfulness, by which it hardens people and brings them to ruin (Hebrews 3:13). Its first suggestions seem almost modest. But once they gain a foothold in the heart, sin secures that ground and presses toward further degrees of the same evil. Its newest advance distracts the soul from noticing how far it has already begun to move away from God. The person thinks things are reasonably well as long as sin does not advance any further. Yet to whatever extent someone loses the awareness of sin that the gospel requires, that person has become hardened. Meanwhile, sin keeps advancing, because its only ultimate limit is complete abandonment of God and opposition to him. Its gradual progress does not mean its nature is moderate. Gradual progress is its deceptive strategy: it uses hardening to secure each gain. Only putting sin to death prevents this. That work dries up the root and strikes sin at its head continually, frustrating whatever it attempts. Even the finest believer in the world, if he abandoned this duty, would fall into sins as dreadful as those committed by anyone with the same inclinations.

paragraphs.original: 4. This is one main reason why the Spirit and the new nature is given unto us, — that we may have a principle within whereby to oppose sin and lust. “The flesh lusteth against the Spirit.” Well! and what then? Why, “The Spirit also lusteth against the flesh,” Gal. v. 17. There is a propensity in the Spirit, or spiritual new nature, to be acting against the flesh, as well as in the flesh to be acting against the Spirit: so 2 Pet. i. 4, 5. It is our participation of the divine nature that gives us an escape from the pollutions that are in the world through lust; and, Rom. vii. 23, there is a law of the mind, as well as a law of the members.
paragraphs.modern: 4. One chief reason God gives us the Spirit and a new nature is to supply an inward power with which to oppose sin and sinful desire. “The flesh desires what opposes the Spirit.” But that is not the whole story: “the Spirit also desires what opposes the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). The Spirit, and the new spiritual nature he gives, has an inclination to act against the flesh, just as the flesh inclines to act against the Spirit. Second Peter 1:4–5 likewise teaches that sharing in the divine nature enables us to escape the world’s corruption through sinful desire. And Romans 7:23 speaks of a law of the mind as well as a law in the bodily members.

paragraphs.original: Now this is, first, the most unjust and unreasonable thing in the world, when two combatants are engaged, to bind one and keep him up from doing his utmost, and to leave the other at liberty to wound him at his pleasure; and, secondly, the foolishest thing in the world to bind him who fights for our eternal condition, [salvation?] and to let him alone who seeks and violently attempts our everlasting ruin. The contest is for our lives and souls. Not to be daily employing the Spirit and new nature for the mortifying of sin, is to neglect that excellent succour which God hath given us against our greatest enemy. If we neglect to make use of what we have received, God may justly hold his hand from giving us more. His graces, as well as his gifts, are bestowed on us to use, exercise, and trade with. Not to be daily mortifying sin, is to sin against the goodness, kindness, wisdom, grace, and love of God, who hath furnished us with a principle of doing it.
paragraphs.modern: When two opponents are fighting, it is utterly unjust and unreasonable to tie one up, preventing him from doing his best, while leaving the other free to wound him at will. It is also supremely foolish to tie up the one fighting for our eternal welfare—our salvation—and leave free the one violently seeking our everlasting ruin. Our lives and souls are at stake. If we do not daily depend on the Spirit and exercise the new nature to put sin to death, we neglect the excellent help God has supplied against our greatest enemy. If we fail to use what we have received, God may justly withhold further supplies. He gives us graces, as well as gifts, to put to work and develop. Failure to put sin to death daily therefore sins against the goodness, kindness, wisdom, grace, and love of the God who has given us the power to do it.

paragraphs.original: 5. Negligence in this duty casts the soul into a perfect contrary condition to that which the apostle affirms was his, 2 Cor. iv. 16, “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.” In these the inward man perisheth, and the outward man is renewed day by day. Sin is as the house of David, and grace as the house of Saul. Exercise and success are the two main cherishers of grace in the heart; when it is suffered to lie still, it withers and decays: the things of it are ready to die, Rev. iii. 2; and sin gets ground towards the hardening of the heart, Heb. iii. 13. This is that which I intend: by the omission of this duty grace withers, lust flourisheth, and the frame of the heart grows worse and worse; and the Lord knows what desperate and fearful issues it hath had with many.
paragraphs.modern: 5. Neglecting this duty puts the soul in the opposite condition from the one Paul describes in 2 Corinthians 4:16: “Though our outward person is wasting away, our inward person is being renewed day by day.” In negligent people, the inward person deteriorates while the outward, fleshly life gains fresh strength each day. Sin becomes like David’s house, growing stronger, while grace becomes like Saul’s house, growing weaker. Exercising grace and gaining victories are two chief ways grace is nourished in the heart. Left unused, it withers and declines; what remains is ready to die (Revelation 3:2), while sin gains ground and hardens the heart (Hebrews 3:13). My point is this: neglect this duty, and grace withers, sinful desire flourishes, and the heart’s condition steadily worsens. God knows the desperate and frightening outcomes this has produced in many people.

paragraphs.original: Where sin, through the neglect of mortification, gets a considerable victory, it breaks the bones of the soul, Ps. xxxi. 10, li. 8, and makes a man weak, sick, and ready to die, Ps. xxxviii. 3–5, so that he cannot look up, Ps. xl. 12, Isa. xxxiii. 24; and when poor creatures will take blow after blow, wound after wound, foil after foil, and never rouse up themselves to a vigorous opposition, can they expect any thing but to be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, and that their souls should bleed to death? 2 John 8. Indeed, it is a sad thing to consider the fearful issues of this neglect, which lie under our eyes every day.
paragraphs.modern: When neglected sin wins a major victory, it breaks the soul’s bones, as the Psalms picture it (Psalm 31:10; 51:8). It leaves a person spiritually weak, sick, and near death (Psalm 38:3–5), unable even to look up (Psalm 40:12; Isaiah 33:24). If people accept blow after blow, wound after wound, and defeat after defeat without rousing themselves to resist vigorously, what can they expect? Sin’s deceitfulness will harden them, and their souls will, figuratively, bleed to death. Consider the warning in 2 John 8. The frightening consequences of this neglect, which we see around us daily, are deeply saddening.

paragraphs.original: See we not those, whom we knew humble, melting, broken-hearted Christians, tender and fearful to offend, zealous for God and all his ways, his Sabbaths and ordinances, grown, through a neglect of watching unto this duty, earthly, carnal, cold, wrathful, complying with the men of the world and things of the world, to the scandal of religion and the fearful temptation of them that know them? The truth is, what between placing mortification in a rigid, stubborn frame of spirit, which is for the most part earthly, legal, censorious, partial, consistent with wrath, envy, malice, pride, on the one hand, and pretences of liberty, grace, and I know not what, on the other, true evangelical mortification is almost lost amongst us: of which afterward.
paragraphs.modern: Have we not known Christians who were humble, tender, and brokenhearted over sin? They feared offending God and were zealous for him, his ways, his Sabbaths, and the practices he appointed. Yet through neglecting watchfulness in this duty, they became worldly, fleshly, cold, and angry, accommodating themselves to worldly people and pursuits. They brought disgrace on religion and placed severe temptations before those who knew them. The truth is that genuinely gospel-based mortification has almost disappeared among us. On one side, people mistake it for a rigid, stubborn disposition that is often worldly, legalistic, judgmental, and selective—and entirely compatible with anger, envy, malice, and pride. On the other side, people excuse themselves with talk about liberty, grace, and whatever else. I will return to this later.

paragraphs.original: 6. It is our duty to be “perfecting holiness in the fear of God,” 2 Cor. vii. 1; to be “growing in grace” every day, 1 Pet. ii. 2, 2 Pet. iii. 18; to be “renewing our inward man day by day,” 2 Cor. iv. 16. Now, this cannot be done without the daily mortifying of sin. Sin sets its strength against every act of holiness, and against every degree we grow to. Let not that man think he makes any progress in holiness who walks not over the bellies of his lusts. He who doth not kill sin in this way takes no steps towards his journey’s end. He who finds not opposition from it, and who sets not himself in every particular to its mortification, is at peace with it, not dying to it.
paragraphs.modern: 6. Our duty is to bring holiness toward completion in the fear of God (2 Corinthians 7:1), to grow in grace daily (1 Peter 2:2; 2 Peter 3:18), and to be renewed inwardly day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16). None of this can happen without daily putting sin to death. Sin throws its strength against every holy action and every degree of growth. No one should imagine that he is advancing in holiness unless he is trampling down his sinful desires. Whoever does not kill sin in this way takes no steps toward the end of the journey. Someone who experiences no opposition from sin, and does not deliberately oppose it in each particular form, is at peace with sin—not dying to it.

paragraphs.original: This, then, is the first general principle of our ensuing discourse: Notwithstanding the meritorious mortification, if I may so speak, of all and every sin in the cross of Christ; notwithstanding the real foundation of universal mortification laid in our first conversion, by conviction of sin, humiliation for sin, and the implantation of a new principle opposite to it and destructive of it; — yet sin doth so remain, so act and work in the best of believers, whilst they live in this world, that the constant daily mortification of it is all their days incumbent on them.
paragraphs.modern: This, then, is the first general principle of the book. Christ’s cross has secured the death of every sin, if I may put it that way. And at our conversion, God truly laid the foundation for putting all sin to death: he convicted us of sin, humbled us over it, and planted in us a new principle that opposes and destroys it. Nevertheless, sin remains and works so actively even in the strongest believers throughout this life that continually putting it to death remains their daily, lifelong duty.

paragraphs.original: Before I proceed to the consideration of the next principle, I cannot but by the way complain of many professors of these days, who, instead of bringing forth such great and evident fruits of mortification as are expected, scarce bear any leaves of it. There is, indeed, a broad light fallen upon the men of this generation, and together therewith many spiritual gifts communicated, which, with some other considerations, have wonderfully enlarged the bounds of professors and profession; both they and it are exceedingly multiplied and increased. Hence there is a noise of religion and religious duties in every corner, preaching in abundance, — and that not in an empty, light, trivial, and vain manner, as formerly, but to a good proportion of a spiritual gift, — so that if you will measure the number of believers by light, gifts, and profession, the church may have cause to say, “Who hath born me all these?” But now if you will take the measure of them by this great discriminating grace of Christians, perhaps you will find their number not so multiplied.
paragraphs.modern: Before moving to the next principle, I must pause to lament the condition of many people who profess Christianity today. Instead of producing the abundant and unmistakable fruit of mortification we should expect, they scarcely show its leaves. Great spiritual light has certainly reached this generation, accompanied by many spiritual gifts. These and other factors have greatly increased the number of people professing Christianity and the public visibility of their profession. Everywhere there is talk of religion and religious duties. Preaching abounds—and much of it displays a real measure of spiritual gifting rather than the emptiness, shallowness, and triviality too often found before. If we count believers by their knowledge, gifts, and profession, the church might well ask in amazement, “Who has borne me all these children?” But if we measure by this grace that so distinctively marks Christians—the putting to death of sin—we may find that their number has not increased nearly so much.

paragraphs.original: Where almost is that professor who owes his conversion to these days of light, and so talks and professes at such a rate of spirituality as few in former days were, in any measure, acquainted with (I will not judge them, but perhaps boasting what the Lord hath done in them), that doth not give evidence of a miserably unmortified heart? If vain spending of time, idleness, unprofitableness in men’s places, envy, strife, variance, emulations, wrath, pride, worldliness, selfishness, 1 Cor. i., be badges of Christians, we have them on us and amongst us in abundance.
paragraphs.modern: Where can we find many people converted in these days of abundant teaching who do not still show a sadly unmortified heart? They speak and profess a level of spirituality hardly familiar to earlier generations. I will not pronounce judgment on them, but perhaps they are boasting about what the Lord has done in them. If wasting time, laziness, failing to serve usefully in one’s calling, envy, rivalry, quarrels, jealousy, anger, pride, worldliness, and selfishness were Christian badges, we would possess them in abundance. Compare 1 Corinthians 1.

paragraphs.original: And if it be so with them who have much light, and which, we hope, is saving, what shall we say of some who would be accounted religious and yet despise gospel light, and for the duty we have in hand, know no more of it but what consists in men’s denying themselves sometimes in outward enjoyments, which is one of the outmost branches of it, which yet they will seldom practise? The good Lord send out a spirit of mortification to cure our distempers, or we are in a sad condition!
paragraphs.modern: If this is true of people who possess much spiritual understanding—understanding we hope is saving—what should we say of those who want to be considered religious while despising the light of the gospel? They know nothing of this duty beyond occasionally denying themselves some outward pleasure. That is only one of its most external branches, and even that they seldom practice. May the good Lord send a spirit of mortification to heal our spiritual disorders; otherwise, our condition is sad indeed!

paragraphs.original: There are two evils which certainly attend every unmortified professor; — the first, in himself; the other, in respect of others:—
paragraphs.modern: Two evils inevitably accompany every person who professes Christianity without putting sin to death: one concerns the person himself, and the other concerns his effect on other people.

paragraphs.original: 1. In himself. Let him pretend what he will, he hath slight thoughts of sin; at least, of sins of daily infirmity. The root of an unmortified course is the digestion of sin without bitterness in the heart. When a man hath confirmed his imagination to such an apprehension of grace and mercy as to be able, without bitterness, to swallow and digest daily sins, that man is at the very brink of turning the grace of God into lasciviousness, and being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Neither is there a greater evidence of a false and rotten heart in the world than to drive such a trade. To use the blood of Christ, which is given to cleanse us, 1 John i. 7, Tit. ii. 14; the exaltation of Christ, which is to give us repentance, Acts v. 31; the doctrine of grace, which teaches us to deny all ungodliness, Tit. ii. 11, 12, to countenance sin, is a rebellion that in the issue will break the bones.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Within himself. Whatever he claims, he takes sin lightly—at least the sins he regards as ordinary daily weaknesses. An unmortified way of life grows from being able to swallow sin without tasting bitterness in the heart. When someone settles into a view of grace and mercy that lets him absorb daily sins without distress, he stands on the very edge of turning God’s grace into permission for immorality and becoming hardened by sin’s deceitfulness. Few things give stronger evidence of a false and corrupt heart than making this one’s regular practice. Christ’s blood was given to cleanse us (1 John 1:7; Titus 2:14). Christ was exalted to give repentance (Acts 5:31). The teaching of grace trains us to reject ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). To use these very things to justify sin is a rebellion that will eventually crush us.

paragraphs.original: At this door have gone out from us most of the professors that have apostatized in the days wherein we live. For a while they were most of them under convictions; these kept them unto duties, and brought them to profession; so they “escaped the pollutions that are in the world, through the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ,” 2 Pet. ii. 20: but having got an acquaintance with the doctrine of the gospel, and being weary of duty, for which they had no principle, they began to countenance themselves in manifold neglects from the doctrine of grace. Now, when once this evil had laid hold of them, they speedily tumbled into perdition.
paragraphs.modern: This is the doorway through which most of those who have abandoned their Christian profession in our time have left us. For a while, most felt conviction of sin. Those convictions kept them performing religious duties and led them to profess faith. In that sense, they escaped the world’s defilements through knowing our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Peter 2:20). But after becoming familiar with gospel teaching, they grew tired of duties for which they had no inward spiritual power. They began using the doctrine of grace to excuse all sorts of neglect. Once this evil took hold, they quickly fell toward destruction.

paragraphs.original: 2. To others. It hath an evil influence on them on a twofold account:— (1.) It hardens them, by begetting in them a persuasion that they are in as good condition as the best professors. Whatever they see in them is so stained for want of this mortification that it is of no value with them. They have a zeal for religion; but it is accompanied with want of forbearance and universal righteousness. They deny prodigality, but with worldliness; they separate from the world, but live wholly to themselves, taking no care to exercise loving-kindness in the earth; or they talk spiritually, and live vainly; mention communion with God, and are every way conformed to the world; boasting of forgiveness of sin, and never forgiving others. And with such considerations do poor creatures harden their hearts in their unregeneracy.
paragraphs.modern: 2. In relation to others. Their influence is harmful in two ways. (1.) They harden others by convincing them that they are doing as well as even the most prominent professing Christians. The good these observers see is so stained by unmortified sin that it loses its value in their eyes. Such Christians show religious zeal but lack patience with others and righteousness across the whole of life. They reject extravagance but remain worldly. They separate themselves from the world but live entirely for themselves, making no effort to show loving kindness in it. Or they speak spiritually while living frivolously, talk about communion with God while conforming to the world in everything, and boast that their sins are forgiven while never forgiving others. Observing these things, unconverted people harden their hearts in their unconverted state.

paragraphs.original: (2.) They deceive them, in making them believe that if they can come up to their condition it shall be well with them; and so it grows an easy thing to have the great temptation of repute in religion to wrestle withal, when they may go far beyond them as to what appears in them, and yet come short of eternal life. But of these things and all the evils of unmortified walking, afterward.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) They also deceive others into believing that everything will be well if they can reach the same condition. A respectable religious reputation thus becomes dangerously easy to acquire—and becomes a powerful temptation. People may far surpass these Christians in everything outwardly visible and still fall short of eternal life. I will return later to these matters and the other evils of living without putting sin to death.

chapters.title: Chapter III: The Spirit’s power in mortification

paragraphs.original: The second general principle of the means of mortification proposed to confirmation — The Spirit the only author of this work — Vanity of popish mortification discovered — Many means of it used by them not appointed of God — Those appointed by him abused — The mistakes of others in this business — The Spirit is promised believers for this work, Ezek. xi. 19, xxxvi. 26 — All that we receive from Christ is by the Spirit — How the Spirit mortifies sin — Gal. v. 19–23 — The several ways of his operation to this end proposed — How his work and our duty.
paragraphs.modern: The second general principle: how sin is put to death — Only the Spirit can accomplish it — The futility Owen sees in Roman Catholic methods — Many practices are not appointed by God; those he does appoint are misused — Similar mistakes among others — God promises the Spirit to believers for this work (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26) — Everything we receive from Christ comes through the Spirit — How the Spirit puts sin to death (Galatians 5:19–23) — The ways he works — How this can be both his work and our duty.

paragraphs.original: The next principle relates to the great sovereign cause of the mortification treated of; which, in the words laid for the foundation of this discourse, is said to be the Spirit, — that is, the Holy Ghost, as was evinced. II. He only is sufficient for this work; all ways and means without him are as a thing of nought; and he is the great efficient of it, — he works in us as he pleases.
paragraphs.modern: The next principle concerns the supreme power who brings about the mortification we are discussing. In the words on which this book rests, that power is the Spirit—the Holy Spirit, as we have already established. II. He alone is sufficient for this work. Without him, every method and means amounts to nothing. He is the great agent who actually accomplishes it, working in us as he pleases.

paragraphs.original: 1. In vain do men seek other remedies; they shall not be healed by them. What several ways have been prescribed for this, to have sin mortified, is known. The greatest part of popish religion, of that which looks most like religion in their profession, consists in mistaken ways and means of mortification. This is the pretence of their rough garments, whereby they deceive. Their vows, orders, fastings, penances, are all built on this ground; they are all for the mortifying of sin. Their preachings, sermons, and books of devotion, they look all this way. Hence, those who interpret the locusts that came out of the bottomless pit, Rev. ix. 3, to be the friars of the Romish church, who are said to torment men, so “that they should seek death and not find it,” verse 6, think that they did it by their stinging sermons, whereby they convinced them of sin, but being not able to discover the remedy for the healing and mortifying of it, they kept them in such perpetual anguish and terror, and such trouble in their consciences, that they desired to die.
paragraphs.modern: 1. People seek other remedies in vain; those remedies will not heal them. The various methods prescribed for putting sin to death are well known. Much of Roman Catholic religion—particularly the practices that look most religious—consists of mistaken methods of mortification. This is the claimed purpose of the rough clothing that gives a misleading appearance of holiness. Religious vows, orders, fasts, and penances all rest on this basis: they are intended to put sin to death. The preaching and devotional books point in the same direction. This explains one interpretation of Revelation 9:3–6. Some identify the locusts from the bottomless pit with Roman Catholic friars, who torment people until they seek death but cannot find it. Those interpreters think the friars inflicted this torment through piercing sermons that convicted people of sin without revealing the remedy that could heal them and put sin to death. The result was continual anguish, terror, and troubled consciences, until the hearers wished to die.

paragraphs.original: This, I say, is the substance and glory of their religion; but what with their labouring to mortify dead creatures, ignorant of the nature and end of the work, — what with the poison they mixed with it, in their persuasion of its merit, yea, supererogation (as they style their unnecessary merit, with a proud, barbarous title), — their glory is their shame: but of them and their mortification more afterward, chap. vii.
paragraphs.modern: This, I say, is the substance of their religion and what they glory in. Yet they try to make spiritually dead people put sin to death, without understanding the work’s nature or purpose. They also poison it with the idea that it earns merit—even “supererogation,” their proud and uncouth term for supposedly earning more merit than God requires. Their supposed glory is therefore their shame. I will say more about them and their methods in chapter 7.

paragraphs.original: That the ways and means to be used for the mortification of sin invented by them are still insisted on and prescribed, for the same end, by some who should have more light and knowledge of the gospel, is known. Such directions to this purpose have of late been given by some, and are greedily catched at by others professing themselves Protestants, as might have become popish devotionists three or four hundred years ago. Such outside endeavours, such bodily exercises, such self-performances, such merely legal duties, without the least mention of Christ or his Spirit, are varnished over with swelling words of vanity, for the only means and expedients for the mortification of sin, as discover a deep-rooted unacquaintedness with the power of God and mystery of the gospel. The consideration hereof was one motive to the publishing of this plain discourse.
paragraphs.modern: It is also well known that methods invented in that tradition are still prescribed for putting sin to death by people who should understand the gospel better. Recently, some teachers have given instructions eagerly embraced by professing Protestants that would have suited Catholic devotional writers three or four centuries ago. Outward efforts, bodily exercises, self-generated achievements, and duties based merely on law are dressed up in grand but empty language and presented as the only ways to overcome sin. Christ and his Spirit are not even mentioned. This reveals a deeply rooted ignorance of God’s power and the gospel’s mystery. Concern about this was one reason I published this straightforward book.

paragraphs.original: Now, the reasons why the Papists can never, with all their endeavours, truly mortify any one sin, amongst others, are, — (1.) Because many of the ways and means they use and insist upon for this end were never appointed of God for that purpose. (Now, there is nothing in religion that hath any efficacy for compassing an end, but it hath it from God’s appointment of it to that purpose.) Such as these are their rough garments, their vows, penances, disciplines, their course of monastical life, and the like; concerning all which God will say, “Who hath required these things at your hand?” and, “In vain do ye worship me, teaching for doctrines the traditions of men.” Of the same nature are sundry self-vexations insisted on by others.
