paragraphs.modern: Among the reasons these Roman Catholics cannot truly put even one sin to death through all their efforts are the following. (1.) Many of the methods they use were never appointed by God for that purpose. In religion, a practice has power to accomplish a particular end only because God has appointed it to that end. Rough clothing, religious vows, penances, bodily disciplines, monastic life, and similar practices fall into this category. Concerning them God will say, “Who required these things from you?” and, “You worship me in vain, teaching human traditions as doctrines.” Various forms of self-inflicted hardship promoted by other people belong to the same class.

paragraphs.original: (2.) Because those things that are appointed of God as means are not used by them in their due place and order, — such as are praying, fasting, watching, meditation, and the like. These have their use in the business in hand; but whereas they are all to be looked on as streams, they look on them as the fountain. Whereas they effect and accomplish the end as means only, subordinate to the Spirit and faith, they look on them to do it by virtue of the work wrought. If they fast so much, and pray so much, and keep their hours and times, the work is done. As the apostle says of some in another case, “They are always learning, never coming to the knowledge of the truth;” so they are always mortifying, but never come to any sound mortification. In a word, they have sundry means to mortify the natural man, as to the natural life here we lead; none to mortify lust or corruption.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) Even the means God has appointed—prayer, fasting, watchfulness, meditation, and the like—are not used in their proper place and order. These practices do have a role in putting sin to death. But they are streams, not the spring that supplies them; these people treat them as the spring itself. Such practices serve their purpose only as means subordinate to the Spirit and faith. Instead, they are treated as though the performance of the action itself accomplished the result. Fast a certain amount, pray a certain amount, observe the prescribed hours, and the work is supposedly done. Paul says of some people in another context that they are always learning but never reach a knowledge of the truth. Similarly, these people are always practicing mortification but never arrive at genuine mortification. In short, they have many ways to weaken the natural person’s earthly life, but none that can kill sinful desire or corruption.

paragraphs.original: This is the general mistake of men ignorant of the gospel about this thing; and it lies at the bottom of very much of that superstition and will-worship that hath been brought into the world. What horrible self-macerations were practised by some of the ancient authors of monastical devotion! what violence did they offer to nature! what extremity of sufferings did they put themselves upon! Search their ways and principles to the bottom, and you will find that it had no other root but this mistake, namely, that attempting rigid mortification, they fell upon the natural man instead of the corrupt old man, — upon the body wherein we live instead of the body of death.
paragraphs.modern: This is the general error made by people who do not understand the gospel, and it underlies much of the superstition and self-invented worship introduced into the world. Some early founders of monastic devotion inflicted dreadful punishments on themselves. What violence they did to their own nature! What extreme sufferings they imposed on themselves! Examine their methods and principles thoroughly, and you will find this mistake at the root: in trying to practice rigorous mortification, they attacked the natural human person instead of the corrupt old person. They attacked the physical body in which we live instead of the “body of death”—the sin within us.

paragraphs.original: Neither will the natural Popery that is in others do it. Men are galled with the guilt of a sin that hath prevailed over them; they instantly promise to themselves and God that they will do so no more; they watch over themselves, and pray for a season, until this heat waxes cold, and the sense of sin is worn off: and so mortification goes also, and sin returns to its former dominion. Duties are excellent food for an unhealthy soul; they are no physic for a sick soul. He that turns his meat into his medicine must expect no great operation. Spiritually sick men cannot sweat out their distemper with working. But this is the way of men who deceive their own souls; as we shall see afterward.
paragraphs.modern: Nor will the same naturally self-reliant religion succeed when it appears in others outside that church. People feel painfully guilty about a sin that has overcome them. They immediately promise themselves and God that they will never do it again. They watch themselves and pray for a while. Then their initial heat cools, their awareness of sin fades, their effort to put it to death disappears, and sin regains its former rule. Religious duties are excellent nourishment for an unhealthy soul, but they are not, in themselves, medicine that cures it. Someone who turns food into a substitute for medicine should not expect a great cure. Spiritually sick people cannot sweat out their disease through hard work. Yet this is how people deceive their own souls, as we will see later.

paragraphs.original: That none of these ways are sufficient is evident from the nature of the work itself that is to be done; it is a work that requires so many concurrent actings in it as no self-endeavour can reach unto, and is of that kind that an almighty energy is necessary for its accomplishment; as shall be afterward manifested.
paragraphs.modern: The nature of the work itself shows that none of these methods is sufficient. Putting sin to death requires so many things to operate together that unaided human effort cannot supply them. It is the kind of work that requires almighty power to accomplish it, as I will explain later.

paragraphs.original: 2. It is, then, the work of the Spirit. For, — (1.) He is promised of God to be given unto us to do this work. The taking away of the stony heart, — that is, the stubborn, proud, rebellious, unbelieving heart, — is in general the work of mortification that we treat of. Now this is still promised to be done by the Spirit, Ezek. xi. 19, xxxvi. 26, “I will give my Spirit, and take away the stony heart;” and by the Spirit of God is this work wrought when all means fail, Isa. lvii. 17, 18.
paragraphs.modern: 2. This is, then, the Spirit’s work. (1.) God promises to give us the Spirit for precisely this purpose. Broadly speaking, removing the heart of stone—the stubborn, proud, rebellious, unbelieving heart—is the work of mortification we are discussing. God consistently promises to accomplish it through the Spirit: “I will give my Spirit and take away the heart of stone” (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26). God’s Spirit accomplishes this work when all other means have failed (Isaiah 57:17–18).

paragraphs.original: (2.) We have all our mortification from the gift of Christ, and all the gifts of Christ are communicated to us and given us by the Spirit of Christ: “Without Christ we can do nothing,” John xv. 5. All communications of supplies and relief, in the beginnings, increasings, actings of any grace whatever, from him, are by the Spirit, by whom he alone works in and upon believers. From him we have our mortification: “He is exalted and made a Prince and a Saviour, to give repentance unto us,” Acts v. 31; and of our repentance our mortification is no small portion. How doth he do it? Having “received the promise of the Holy Ghost,” he sends him abroad for that end, Acts ii. 33. You know the manifold promises he made of sending the Spirit, as Tertullian speaks, “Vicariam navare operam,” to do the works that he had to accomplish in us.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) Every measure of mortification we possess is Christ’s gift, and every gift from Christ reaches us through Christ’s Spirit. “Without Christ we can do nothing” (John 15:5). Whenever he supplies help—whether beginning a grace in us, increasing it, or enabling us to exercise it—he does so through the Spirit. It is by the Spirit that Christ works in and upon believers. Our putting sin to death comes from Christ: he has been exalted as Prince and Savior to give us repentance (Acts 5:31), and mortification is a substantial part of repentance. How does he give it? Having received the promised Holy Spirit, he sends the Spirit for this purpose (Acts 2:33). You know his many promises to send the Spirit to carry out, as Tertullian puts it, the work entrusted to him on Christ’s behalf—the work Christ intends to accomplish in us.

paragraphs.original: The resolution of one or two questions will now lead me nearer to what I principally intend. The first is, How doth the Spirit mortify sin? I answer, in general, three ways:—
paragraphs.modern: Answering two questions will bring us closer to my main purpose. The first is: How does the Spirit put sin to death? In general, he does so in three ways.

paragraphs.original: [1.] By causing our hearts to abound in grace and the fruits that are contrary to the flesh, and the fruits thereof and principles of them. So the apostle opposes the fruits of the flesh and of the Spirit: “The fruits of the flesh,” says he, “are so and so,” Gal. v. 19–21; “but,” says he, “the fruits of the Spirit are quite contrary, quite of another sort,” verses 22, 23. Yea; but what if these are in us and do abound, may not the other abound also? No, says he, verse 24, “They that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.” But how? Why, verse 25, “By living in the Spirit and walking after the Spirit;” — that is, by the abounding of these graces of the Spirit in us, and walking according to them. For, saith the apostle, “These are contrary one to another,” verse 17; so that they cannot both be in the same subject, in any intense or high degree. This “renewing of us by the Holy Ghost,” as it is called, Tit. iii. 5, is one great way of mortification; he causes us to grow, thrive, flourish, and abound in those graces which are contrary, opposite, and destructive to all the fruits of the flesh, and to the quiet or thriving of indwelling sin itself.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] He makes our hearts abound in graces and their fruits that oppose the flesh, its fruits, and the principles producing them. Paul contrasts these in Galatians 5. He lists the works of the flesh in verses 19–21, then gives a completely different kind of fruit—the Spirit’s—in verses 22–23. Could both flourish in us at the same time? No, he says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (verse 24). How? By living in the Spirit and walking according to the Spirit (verse 25). That means allowing the Spirit’s graces to abound in us and conducting ourselves accordingly. These two are opposed to each other (verse 17), so they cannot both be present in the same person in full strength. This “renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5) is one great way sin is put to death. The Spirit makes us grow and flourish in graces that oppose and destroy the works of the flesh, and that prevent indwelling sin itself from settling comfortably or thriving.

paragraphs.original: [2.] By a real physical efficiency on the root and habit of sin, for the weakening, destroying, and taking it away. Hence he is called a “Spirit of judgment and burning,” Isa. iv. 4, really consuming and destroying our lusts. He takes away the stony heart by an almighty efficiency; for as he begins the work as to its kind, so he carries it on as to its degrees. He is the fire which burns up the very root of lust.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] He directly and effectively acts upon sin’s root and settled disposition, weakening, destroying, and removing it. By “physical efficiency” I mean real, effective action upon sin itself—not merely persuasion, and not physical injury to the body. For this reason, the Spirit is called a “Spirit of judgment and burning” (Isaiah 4:4): he actually consumes and destroys our sinful desires. He removes the heart of stone through almighty power. The same power that begins this new kind of work carries it forward through every degree of progress. He is the fire that burns up sinful desire at its very root.

paragraphs.original: [3.] He brings the cross of Christ into the heart of a sinner by faith, and gives us communion with Christ in his death, and fellowship in his sufferings: of the manner whereof more afterward.
paragraphs.modern: [3.] Through faith, he brings Christ’s cross into the sinner’s heart. He gives us a real participation in Christ’s death and fellowship in his sufferings. I will explain how this happens later.

paragraphs.original: Secondly. If this be the work of the Spirit alone, how is it that we are exhorted to it? — seeing the Spirit of God only can do it, let the work be left wholly to him.
paragraphs.modern: The second question is this: If only the Spirit can accomplish the work, why are we commanded to do it? Since God’s Spirit alone can do it, should we not simply leave the whole matter to him?

paragraphs.original: [1.] It is no otherwise the work of the Spirit but as all graces and good works which are in us are his. He “works in us to will and to do of his own good pleasure,” Phil. ii. 13; he works “all our works in us,” Isa. xxvi. 12, — “the work of faith with power,” 2 Thess. i. 11, Col. ii. 12; he causes us to pray, and is a “Spirit of supplication,” Rom. viii. 26, Zech. xii 10; and yet we are exhorted, and are to be exhorted, to all these.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] Mortification is the Spirit’s work in the same way that every grace and good work within us is his work. He works in us both the desire and the action that fulfill his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). He accomplishes all our works in us (Isaiah 26:12), including the powerful work of faith (2 Thessalonians 1:11; Colossians 2:12). He enables us to pray and is the Spirit of supplication (Romans 8:26; Zechariah 12:10). Yet Scripture commands us to do all these things, and rightly continues to command us.

paragraphs.original: [2.] He doth not so work our mortification in us as not to keep it still an act of our obedience. The Holy Ghost works in us and upon us, as we are fit to be wrought in and upon; that is, so as to preserve our own liberty and free obedience. He works upon our understandings, wills, consciences, and affections, agreeably to their own natures; he works in us and with us, not against us or without us; so that his assistance is an encouragement as to the facilitating of the work, and no occasion of neglect as to the work itself.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] The Spirit does not put sin to death in us in a way that stops it from being our act of obedience. He works within and upon us in a way suited to the kind of beings we are, preserving our freedom and willing obedience. He works on our understanding, will, conscience, and affections in ways appropriate to each. He works in us and with us, not against us or without us. His help therefore encourages us because it makes the work possible and easier; it gives us no excuse to neglect the work itself.

paragraphs.original: And, indeed, I might here bewail the endless, foolish labour of poor souls, who, being convinced of sin, and not able to stand against the power of their convictions, do set themselves, by innumerable perplexing ways and duties, to keep down sin, but, being strangers to the Spirit of God, all in vain. They combat without victory, have war without peace, and are in slavery all their days. They spend their strength for that which is not bread, and their labour for that which profiteth not. This is the saddest warfare that any poor creature can be engaged in. A soul under the power of conviction from the law is pressed to fight against sin, but hath no strength for the combat. They cannot but fight, and they can never conquer; they are like men thrust on the sword of enemies on purpose to be slain. The law drives them on, and sin beats them back.
paragraphs.modern: Here I could grieve over the endless and mistaken labor of people convicted of sin. Unable to escape their convictions, they try countless distressing methods and duties to suppress sin. But because they do not know God’s Spirit, their effort is futile. They fight without victory, wage war without reaching peace, and remain enslaved all their lives. They spend their strength on what cannot feed them and their labor on what brings no benefit. This is the saddest warfare anyone can experience. The law’s conviction forces a person to fight sin, but supplies no strength for the battle. Such people feel they must fight, yet they cannot win. They resemble people driven onto their enemies’ swords to be killed: the law drives them forward, and sin beats them back.

paragraphs.original: Sometimes they think, indeed, that they have foiled sin, when they have only raised a dust that they see it not; that is, they distemper their natural affections of fear, sorrow, and anguish, which makes them believe that sin is conquered when it is not touched. By that time they are cold, they must to the battle again; and the lust which they thought to be slain appears to have had no wound.
paragraphs.modern: Sometimes they think they have defeated sin when all they have done is raise a cloud of dust that hides it from view. They stir their natural feelings of fear, sorrow, and anguish into such turmoil that they imagine sin has been conquered, though it has not actually been touched. As soon as their emotions cool, the battle starts again. The desire they thought they had killed proves not to have been wounded at all.

paragraphs.original: And if the case be so sad with them who do labour and strive, and yet enter not into the kingdom, what is their condition who despise all this; who are perpetually under the power and dominion of sin, and love to have it so; and are troubled at nothing, but that they cannot make sufficient provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof?
paragraphs.modern: If this is such a sad condition for those who labor and struggle yet do not enter the kingdom, what is the condition of those who despise the whole struggle? They live continually under sin’s power and rule, are happy to do so, and are troubled only that they cannot provide enough opportunities and resources to satisfy the flesh’s desires.

chapters.title: Chapter IV: Spiritual strength and comfort

paragraphs.original: The last principle; of the usefulness of mortification — The vigour and comfort of our spiritual lives depend on our mortification — In what sense — Not absolutely and necessarily; Ps. lxxxviii., Heman’s condition — Not as on the next and immediate cause — As a means; by removing of the contrary — The desperate effects of any unmortified lust; it weakens the soul, Ps. xxxviii. 3, 8, sundry ways, and darkens it — All graces improved by the mortification of sin — The best evidence of sincerity.
paragraphs.modern: The final principle: the benefits of putting sin to death — How our spiritual strength and comfort depend on it — Not as an absolute guarantee: Heman’s experience in Psalm 88 — Not as their direct and immediate source — Rather, as a means that removes what opposes them — The damaging effects of unchecked sinful desire: it weakens the soul in several ways (Psalm 38:3, 8) and darkens it — Putting sin to death strengthens every grace — Its evidence of sincerity.

paragraphs.original: The last principle I shall insist on (omitting, first, the necessity of mortification unto life, and, secondly, the certainty of life upon mortification) is, — III. That the life, vigour, and comfort of our spiritual life depend much on our mortification of sin.
paragraphs.modern: I will now address one final principle, setting aside for the moment both the necessity of mortification for life and the certainty of life where mortification is present. III. The vitality, strength, and comfort of our spiritual life depend greatly on our putting sin to death.

paragraphs.original: Strength and comfort, and power and peace, in our walking with God, are the things of our desires. Were any of us asked seriously, what it is that troubles us, we must refer it to one of these heads:— either we want strength or power, vigour and life, in our obedience, in our walking with God; or we want peace, comfort, and consolation therein. Whatever it is that may befall a believer that doth not belong to one of these two heads, doth not deserve to be mentioned in the days of our complaints. Now, all these do much depend on a constant course of mortification, concerning which observe, —
paragraphs.modern: We long for strength and comfort, power and peace, in our life with God. Asked seriously what troubles us most, we would have to place it under one of two headings. Either we lack strength, energy, and vitality in obeying and walking with God, or we lack peace, comfort, and encouragement in doing so. Whatever else may happen to a believer hardly deserves mention beside these concerns when we are speaking of our deepest troubles. All these things depend greatly on a steady practice of putting sin to death. But notice the following qualifications.

paragraphs.original: 1. I do not say they proceed from it, as though they were necessarily tied to it. A man may be carried on in a constant course of mortification all his days; and yet perhaps never enjoy a good day of peace and consolation. So it was with Heman, Ps. lxxxviii.; his life was a life of perpetual mortification and walking with God, yet terrors and wounds were his portion all his days. But God singled out Heman, a choice friend, to make him an example to them that afterward should be in distress. Canst thou complain if it be no otherwise with thee than it was with Heman, that eminent servant of God? and this shall be his praise to the end of the world. God makes it his prerogative to speak peace and consolation, Isa. lvii. 18, 19. “I will do that work,” says God, “I will comfort him,” verse 18. But how? By an immediate work of the new creation: “I create it,” says God. The use of means for the obtaining of peace is ours; the bestowing of it is God’s prerogative.
paragraphs.modern: 1. I do not mean that these blessings follow automatically from mortification, as though the connection admitted no exceptions. Someone may faithfully put sin to death throughout life and yet perhaps never enjoy a full day of settled peace and comfort. Heman’s experience in Psalm 88 was like this. He continually walked with God and opposed sin, yet terrors and wounds accompanied him throughout his life. God chose this dearly loved friend as an example for people who would later experience distress. Can you regard your condition as uniquely wrong if it is no worse than Heman’s, that distinguished servant of God? His example will honor him to the end of the world. God reserves to himself the right to speak peace and comfort (Isaiah 57:18–19). “I will do this work,” he says; “I will comfort him” (verse 18). How? By a direct act of his new-creating power: “I create it,” God says. Our responsibility is to use the appointed means of seeking peace. Giving that peace remains God’s prerogative.

paragraphs.original: 2. In the ways instituted by God for to give us life, vigour, courage, and consolation, mortification is not one of the immediate causes of it. They are the privileges of our adoption made known to our souls that give us immediately these things. “The Spirit bearing witness with our spirits that we are the children of God,” giving us a new name and a white stone, adoption and justification, — that is, as to the sense and knowledge of them, — are the immediate causes (in the hand of the Spirit) of these things. But this I say, —
paragraphs.modern: 2. Within God’s appointed way of giving us spiritual life, strength, courage, and comfort, mortification is not their direct source. Their immediate source is our awareness of the privileges of adoption. The Spirit bears witness with our spirits that we are God’s children, assuring us of acceptance—pictured as a new name and a white stone. Adoption and justification, as the Spirit makes us conscious of them, directly produce these blessings. Nevertheless, I do say this:

paragraphs.original: 3. In our ordinary walking with God, and in an ordinary course of his dealing with us, the vigour and comfort of our spiritual lives depend much on our mortification, not only as a “causa sine qua non,” but as a thing that hath an effectual influence thereinto. For, — (1.) This alone keeps sin from depriving us of the one and the other. Every unmortified sin will certainly do two things:— [1.] It will weaken the soul, and deprive it of its vigour. [2.] It will darken the soul, and deprive it of its comfort and peace.
paragraphs.modern: 3. In our ordinary life with God, and in his usual dealings with us, the strength and comfort of our spiritual lives depend greatly on putting sin to death. Mortification is not merely a necessary condition—a causa sine qua non, something without which the result will not ordinarily occur. It also makes a real, effective contribution. (1.) It alone prevents sin from robbing us of both spiritual strength and spiritual comfort. Every sin we leave unmortified will certainly do two things: weaken the soul and drain its energy, and darken the soul and deprive it of comfort and peace.

paragraphs.original: [1.] It weakens the soul, and deprives it of its strength. When David had for a while harboured an unmortified lust in his heart, it broke all his bones, and left him no spiritual strength; hence he complained that he was sick, weak, wounded, faint. “There is,” saith he, “no soundness in me,” Ps. xxxviii. 3; “I am feeble and sore broken,” verse 8; “yea, I cannot so much as look up,” Ps. xl. 12. An unmortified lust will drink up the spirit, and all the vigour of the soul, and weaken it for all duties. For, —
paragraphs.modern: [1.] Sin weakens the soul and takes away its strength. When David sheltered an unmortified desire in his heart for a time, it broke his bones, as he describes it, and left him without spiritual strength. He complained of sickness, weakness, wounds, and exhaustion. “There is no soundness in me” (Psalm 38:3); “I am feeble and badly broken” (verse 8); “I cannot even look up” (Psalm 40:12). A sinful desire left alive will drain the soul’s spirit and energy and weaken it for every duty. Here is how.

paragraphs.original: 1st. It untunes and unframes the heart itself, by entangling its affections. It diverts the heart from the spiritual frame that is required for vigorous communion with God; it lays hold on the affections, rendering its object beloved and desirable, so expelling the love of the Father, 1 John. ii. 15, iii 17; so that the soul cannot say uprightly and truly to God, “Thou art my portion,” having something else that it loves. Fear, desire, hope, which are the choice affections of the soul, that should be full of God, will be one way or other entangled with it.
paragraphs.modern: First, sin throws the heart out of tune by entangling its affections. It pulls the heart away from the spiritual condition needed for lively communion with God. It seizes the affections and makes its object seem lovable and desirable, pushing out love for the Father (1 John 2:15; 3:17). Because the soul now loves something else in competition with God, it cannot sincerely tell him, “You are my portion.” Fear, desire, and hope—among our most important affections, which should be occupied with God—become entangled with this sinful attachment in one way or another.

paragraphs.original: 2dly. It fills the thoughts with contrivances about it. Thoughts are the great purveyors of the soul to bring in provision to satisfy its affections; and if sin remain unmortified in the heart, they must ever and anon be making provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof. They must glaze, adorn, and dress the objects of the flesh, and bring them home to give satisfaction; and this they are able to do, in the service of a defiled imagination, beyond all expression.
paragraphs.modern: Second, sin fills the mind with schemes for satisfying it. Our thoughts are the soul’s suppliers: they seek out what will satisfy our affections. If sin remains unmortified in the heart, our thoughts will repeatedly make provision for the flesh and its desires. They polish, decorate, and dress up sinful objects, then bring them before the heart for its enjoyment. Serving a corrupted imagination, they can do this to an extent beyond description.

paragraphs.original: 3dly. It breaks out and actually hinders duty. The ambitious man must be studying, and the worldling must be working or contriving, and the sensual, vain person providing himself for vanity, when they should be engaged in the worship of God. Were this my present business, to set forth the breaches, ruin, weakness, desolations, that one unmortified lust will bring upon a soul, this discourse must be extended much beyond my intendment.
paragraphs.modern: Third, sin breaks out into action and directly interferes with duty. The ambitious person feels compelled to study for advancement, the worldly person to work or scheme, and the pleasure-seeking person to arrange frivolous enjoyments, when they should be worshiping God. Were my purpose here to describe all the damage, ruin, weakness, and devastation that one unmortified desire can inflict on the soul, this book would have to become much longer than I intend.

paragraphs.original: [2.] As sin weakens, so it darkens the soul. It is a cloud, a thick cloud, that spreads itself over the face of the soul, and intercepts all the beams of God’s love and favour. It takes away all sense of the privilege of our adoption; and if the soul begins to gather up thoughts of consolation, sin quickly scatters them: of which afterward.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] Sin not only weakens the soul; it also darkens it. It spreads over the soul like a thick cloud and blocks the rays of God’s love and favor. It removes our felt enjoyment of the privilege of adoption. Whenever the soul begins gathering encouraging thoughts, sin quickly scatters them. I will discuss this further later.

paragraphs.original: Now, in this regard doth the vigour and power of our spiritual life depend on our mortification: It is the only means of the removal of that which will allow us neither the one nor the other. Men that are sick and wounded under the power of lust make many applications for help; they cry to God when the perplexity of their thoughts overwhelms them, even to God do they cry, but are not delivered; in vain do they use many remedies, — “ they shall not be healed.” So, Hos. v. 13, “Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound,” and attempted sundry remedies: nothing will do until they come (verse 15) to “acknowledge their offence.” Men may see their sickness and wounds, but yet, if they make not due applications, their cure will not be effected.
paragraphs.modern: This explains one way our spiritual vitality and strength depend on mortification: it is the only means of removing the sin that denies us both strength and comfort. People sick and wounded under the power of sinful desire try many ways to find help. When anxious and confused thoughts overwhelm them, they cry to God—yes, to God himself—but find no deliverance. They try one remedy after another in vain and remain unhealed. Hosea 5:13 says that Ephraim saw its sickness and Judah its wound, and they tried various remedies. Yet nothing works until they acknowledge their offense (verse 15). People may recognize their sickness and wounds, but they will not be cured unless they apply the right remedy.

paragraphs.original: (2.) Mortification prunes all the graces of God, and makes room for them in our hearts to grow. The life and vigour of our spiritual lives consists in the vigour and flourishing of the plants of grace in our hearts. Now, as you may see in a garden, let there be a precious herb planted, and let the ground be untilled, and weeds grow about it, perhaps it will live still, but be a poor, withering, unuseful thing. You must look and search for it, and sometimes can scarce find it; and when you do, you can scarce know it, whether it be the plant you look for or no; and suppose it be, you can make no use of it at all. When, let another of the same kind be set in the ground, naturally as barren and bad as the other, but let it be well weeded, and every thing that is noxious and hurtful removed from it, — it flourishes and thrives; you may see it at first look into the garden, and have it for your use when you please.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) Mortification tends all the graces God has planted and gives them room to grow in our hearts. Our spiritual vitality consists in these plants of grace growing strongly and flourishing. Think of a garden. Plant a valuable herb, leave the soil uncultivated, and let weeds surround it. It may survive, but it will become weak, withered, and useless. You may have to search hard to find it. Even when you do, you may scarcely recognize it as the plant you wanted, and it may be too feeble to use. Now plant another of the same kind in soil naturally just as poor. Weed it carefully and remove everything harmful. It will flourish. You can spot it as soon as you look into the garden and use it whenever you need it.

paragraphs.original: So it is with the graces of the Spirit that are planted in our hearts. That is true; they are still, they abide in a heart where there is some neglect of mortification; but they are ready to die, Rev. iii. 2, they are withering and decaying. The heart is like the sluggard’s field, — so overgrown with weeds that you can scarce see the good corn. Such a man may search for faith, love, and zeal, and scarce be able to find any; and if he do discover that these graces are there yet alive and sincere, yet they are so weak, so clogged with lusts, that they are of very little use; they remain, indeed, but are ready to die.
paragraphs.modern: The Spirit’s graces planted in our hearts are like those plants. They may still be present where mortification has been neglected, but they are withering, declining, and ready to die (Revelation 3:2). The heart becomes like the lazy person’s field, so overgrown with weeds that the good grain is almost invisible. Someone in that condition may search for faith, love, and zeal and scarcely find them. Even if he discovers that they are still genuine and alive, they are so weak and so choked by sinful desires that they are of little practical use. They remain, but they are close to death.

paragraphs.original: But now let the heart be cleansed by mortification, the weeds of lust constantly and daily rooted up (as they spring daily, nature being their proper soil), let room be made for grace to thrive and flourish, — how will every grace act its part, and be ready for every use and purpose!
paragraphs.modern: But let the heart be cleared through mortification. Uproot the weeds of sinful desire daily—as daily they spring up, since our corrupted nature is their natural soil. Make room for grace to grow and flourish. Then every grace will perform its proper work and be ready for every purpose for which it is needed!

paragraphs.original: (3.) As to our peace; as there is nothing that hath any evidence of sincerity without it, so I know nothing that hath such an evidence of sincerity in it; — which is no small foundation of our peace. Mortification is the soul’s vigorous opposition to self, wherein sincerity is most evident.
paragraphs.modern: (3.) Finally, consider our peace. Without mortification, nothing else supplies convincing evidence of sincerity. And I know of nothing that carries stronger evidence of sincerity within itself. Such evidence contributes greatly to peace. Mortification is the soul’s vigorous opposition to its own sinful self, and that is where sincerity becomes especially clear.

chapters.title: Chapter V: What mortification is not

paragraphs.original: The principal intendment of the whole discourse proposed — The first main case of conscience stated — What it is to mortify any sin, negatively considered — Not the utter destruction of it in this life — Not the dissimulation of it —Not the improvement of any natural principle — Not the diversion of it — Not an occasional conquest — Occasional conquests of sin, what and when; upon the eruption of sin; in time of danger or trouble.
paragraphs.modern: The book’s main practical purpose — The central question of conscience — What putting sin to death does not mean — Not its complete eradication in this life — Not concealing it — Not merely improving a natural temperament — Not redirecting it into another channel — Not an occasional victory — How apparent victories occur after a serious outbreak of sin or during danger and trouble.

paragraphs.original: These things being premised, I come to my principal intention, of handling some questions or practical cases that present themselves in this business of mortification of sin in believers. The first, which is the head of all the rest, and whereunto they are reduced, may be considered as lying under the ensuing proposal:—
paragraphs.modern: With these foundations established, I now come to my chief purpose: addressing practical questions and cases of conscience that arise when believers seek to put sin to death. The first question is the central one, to which all the others relate. It can be stated like this.

paragraphs.original: Suppose a man to be a true believer, and yet finds in himself a powerful indwelling sin, leading him captive to the law of it, consuming his heart with trouble, perplexing his thoughts, weakening his soul as to duties of communion with God, disquieting him as to peace, and perhaps defiling his conscience, and exposing him to hardening through the deceitfulness of sin, — what shall he do? what course shall he take and insist on for the mortification of this sin, lust, distemper, or corruption, to such a degree as that, though it be not utterly destroyed, yet, in his contest with it, he may be enabled to keep up power, strength, and peace in communion with God?
paragraphs.modern: Suppose someone truly believes in Christ but discovers a powerful indwelling sin within himself. It takes him captive to its demands, fills his heart with distress, confuses his thoughts, weakens him in the practices through which he enjoys communion with God, and disrupts his peace. Perhaps it also defiles his conscience and exposes him to being hardened by sin’s deceitfulness. What should he do? What course should he adopt and persist in so that this sin—this sinful desire, disorder, or corruption—is put to death enough that, even though it is not completely eradicated, he can maintain strength, spiritual power, and peace in communion with God while fighting it?

paragraphs.original: In answer to this important inquiry, I shall do these things:— I. Show what it is to mortify any sin, and that both negatively and positively, that we be not mistaken in the foundation. II. Give general directions for such things as without which it will be utterly impossible for any one to get any sin truly and spiritually mortified. III. Draw out the particulars whereby this is to be done; in the whole carrying on this consideration, that it is not of the doctrine of mortification in general, but only in reference to the particular case before proposed, that I am treating.
paragraphs.modern: To answer this important question, I will do three things. I. Explain both what putting sin to death is not and what it is, so that our foundation is not mistaken. II. Give general directions concerning things without which no one can possibly put any sin to death truly and spiritually. III. Explain the specific steps by which this is done. Throughout, remember that I am not attempting to cover the whole doctrine of mortification in general. I am addressing it as it bears on the particular case just described.

paragraphs.original: I. 1. (1.) To mortify a sin is not utterly to kill, root it out, and destroy it, that it should have no more hold at all nor residence in our hearts. It is true this is that which is aimed at; but this is not in this life to be accomplished. There is no man that truly sets himself to mortify any sin, but he aims at, intends, desires its utter destruction, that it should leave neither root nor fruit in the heart or life. He would so kill it that it should never move nor stir any more, cry or call, seduce or tempt, to eternity. Its not-being is the thing aimed at. Now, though doubtless there may, by the Spirit and grace of Christ, a wonderful success and eminency of victory against any sin be attained, so that a man may have almost constant triumph over it, yet an utter killing and destruction of it, that it should not be, is not in this life to be expected.
paragraphs.modern: I. First, consider what mortification is not. (1.) Putting a sin to death does not mean completely eradicating it so that it has no remaining foothold or presence in our hearts. That is certainly our goal, but it is not achieved in this life. Everyone who genuinely sets out to put a sin to death wants its total destruction. He wants neither root nor fruit of it left in his heart or conduct. He would kill it so thoroughly that it could never again move, cry out, entice, or tempt him for all eternity. Its complete nonexistence is the aim. Through Christ’s Spirit and grace, a person can certainly gain remarkable success and outstanding victory over a particular sin, perhaps enjoying almost continual triumph over it. But he must not expect its absolute eradication during this life.

paragraphs.original: This Paul assures us of, Phil. iii. 12, “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect.” He was a choice saint, a pattern for believers, who, in faith and love, and all the fruits of the Spirit, had not his fellow in the world, and on that account ascribes perfection to himself in comparison of others, verse 15; yet he had not “attained,” he was not “perfect,” but was “following after:” still a vile body he had, and we have, that must be changed by the great power of Christ at last, verse 21. This we would have; but God sees it best for us that we should be complete in nothing in ourselves, that in all things we must be “complete in Christ;” which is best for us, Col. ii. 10.
paragraphs.modern: Paul makes this clear in Philippians 3:12: “Not that I have already attained it or am already perfect.” He was an outstanding believer and an example to others, unequaled in his faith, love, and the Spirit’s fruits. In that relative sense, he counts himself among the mature or “perfect” in verse 15. Yet he had not arrived at absolute perfection; he was still pressing on. He still had, as we do, a lowly body that must finally be transformed by Christ’s great power (verse 21). We would welcome complete freedom from sin now. But God judges it best that we should be complete in nothing independently of him, so that in everything we must find our completeness in Christ. That truly is best for us (Colossians 2:10).

paragraphs.original: (2.) I think I need not say it is not the dissimulation of a sin. When a man on some outward respects forsakes the practice of any sin, men perhaps may look on him as a changed man. God knows that to his former iniquity he hath added cursed hypocrisy, and is got in a safer path to hell than he was in before. He hath got another heart than he had, that is more cunning; not a new heart, that is more holy.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) It should hardly need saying that mortification is not hiding a sin. Someone may stop practicing a sin for outward reasons, and others may regard him as a changed person. But God knows that he has added hypocrisy to his earlier wrongdoing and placed himself on a more deceptively secure road to hell. He has a different heart in the sense that it is more cunning, not a new heart that is more holy.

paragraphs.original: (3.) The mortification of sin consists not in the improvement of a quiet, sedate nature. Some men have an advantage by their natural constitution so far as that they are not exposed to such violence of unruly passions and tumultuous affections as many others are. Let now these men cultivate and improve their natural frame and temper by discipline, consideration, and prudence, and they may seem to themselves and others very mortified men, when, perhaps, their hearts are a standing sink of all abominations. Some man is never so much troubled all his life, perhaps, with anger and passion, nor doth trouble others, as another is almost every day; and yet the latter hath done more to the mortification of the sin than the former. Let not such persons try their mortification by such things as their natural temper gives no life or vigour to. Let them bring themselves to self-denial, unbelief, envy, or some such spiritual sin, and they will have a better view of themselves.
paragraphs.modern: (3.) Putting sin to death is not simply improving an already calm and quiet temperament. Some people naturally have an advantage: they are less exposed than others to violent, unruly passions and turbulent emotions. If they develop their temperament through discipline, reflection, and good judgment, they may appear to themselves and others to be very far advanced in mortification, while their hearts may still be reservoirs of all sorts of evil. One person may experience less anger and cause less trouble through it in his whole life than another does almost daily. Yet the second may have done much more to put that sin to death than the first. Do not measure your mortification by sins to which your natural temperament supplies little energy. Test yourself instead where self-denial is required, or against unbelief, envy, and similar inward sins. You will gain a more accurate view of yourself.

paragraphs.original: (4.) A sin is not mortified when it is only diverted. Simon Magus for a season left his sorceries; but his covetousness and ambition, that set him on work, remained still, and would have been acting another way. Therefore Peter tells him, “I perceive thou art in the gall of bitterness;” — “Notwithstanding the profession thou hast made, notwithstanding thy relinquishment of thy sorceries, thy lust is as powerful as ever in thee; the same lust, only the streams of it are diverted. It now exerts and puts forth itself another way, but it is the old gall of bitterness still.” A man may be sensible of a lust, set himself against the eruptions of it, take care that it shall not break forth as it has done, but in the meantime suffer the same corrupted habit to vent itself some other way; as he who heals and skins a running sore thinks himself cured, but in the meantime his flesh festereth by the corruption of the same humour, and breaks out in another place.
paragraphs.modern: (4.) Redirecting a sin does not put it to death. Simon the magician stopped practicing sorcery for a time, but the greed and ambition that had driven him remained and sought another outlet. Peter therefore told him, “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness.” His meaning was: “Despite your profession of faith and your abandonment of sorcery, your sinful desire is as powerful as ever. It is the same desire flowing through a different channel. It acts in a new way, but the old bitter poison remains.” Someone may recognize a sinful desire, oppose its obvious outbreaks, and make sure it no longer appears in its former form, while allowing the same corrupt disposition to express itself elsewhere. He is like someone who thinks an open sore is cured because skin has grown over it, while the underlying corruption continues to fester and breaks out in another place.

paragraphs.original: And this diversion, with the alterations that attend it, often befalls men on accounts wholly foreign unto grace: change of the course of life that a man was in, of relations, interests, designs, may effect it; yea, the very alterations in men’s constitutions, occasioned by a natural progress in the course of their lives, may produce such changes as these. Men in age do not usually persist in the pursuit of youthful lusts, although they have never mortified any one of them.
paragraphs.modern: This redirection, and the changes accompanying it, often happens for reasons entirely unrelated to grace. A change in someone’s way of life, relationships, interests, or plans may bring it about. Even the natural changes in bodily constitution that accompany growing older can produce such alterations. Older people do not usually pursue youthful desires in the same way, even when they have never truly put any of those desires to death.

paragraphs.original: And the same is the case of bartering of lusts, and leaving to serve one that a man may serve another. He that changes pride for worldliness, sensuality for Pharisaism, vanity in himself to the contempt of others, let him not think that he hath mortified the sin that he seems to have left. He hath changed his master, but is a servant still.
paragraphs.modern: The same applies to trading one sinful desire for another—leaving the service of one in order to serve another. Someone who exchanges pride for worldliness, sensual indulgence for self-righteous religion, or personal vanity for contempt toward others must not imagine that he has killed the sin he appears to have abandoned. He has changed masters, but he is still a slave.

paragraphs.original: (5.) Occasional conquests of sin do not amount to a mortifying of it. There are two occasions or seasons wherein a man who is contending with any sin may seem to himself to have mortified it:—
paragraphs.modern: (5.) Occasional victories over sin are not the same as putting it to death. There are two situations in which someone struggling with a sin may mistakenly think he has mortified it.

paragraphs.original: [1.] When it hath had some sad eruption, to the disturbance of his peace, terror of his conscience, dread of scandal, and evident provocation of God. This awakens and stirs up all that is in the man, and amazes him, fills him with abhorrency of sin, and himself for it; sends him to God, makes him cry out as for life, to abhor his lust as hell, and to set himself against it. The whole man, spiritual and natural, being now awaked, sin shrinks in its head, appears not, but lies as dead before him: as when one that hath drawn nigh to an army in the night, and hath killed a principal person, — instantly the guards awake, men are roused up, and strict inquiry is made after the enemy, who, in the meantime, until the noise and tumult be over, hides himself, or lies like one that is dead, yet with firm resolution to do the like mischief again upon the like opportunity.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] A sin may have broken out in a particularly distressing way. It destroys his peace, terrifies his conscience, makes him fear public disgrace, and plainly provokes God. This shocks him and awakens everything within him. He abhors the sin and himself for committing it. He turns to God, cries out as though his life depends on it, hates his sinful desire as he hates hell, and sets himself against it. With the whole person now awake—both spiritual graces and natural emotions—sin ducks out of sight and appears to lie dead. Picture an enemy who slips into an army camp at night and kills a leading officer. Immediately the guards wake, the soldiers are roused, and a thorough search begins. Meanwhile, the enemy hides or plays dead until the noise subsides, still fully intending to repeat the attack when the opportunity returns.

paragraphs.original: Upon the sin among the Corinthians, see how they muster up themselves for the surprisal and destruction of it, 2 Epist. chap. vii. 11. So it is in a person when a breach hath been made upon his conscience, quiet, perhaps credit, by his lust, in some eruption of actual sin; — carefulness, indignation, desire, fear, revenge, are all set on work about it and against it, and lust is quiet for a season, being run down before them; but when the hurry is over and the inquest past, the thief appears again alive, and is as busy as ever at his work.
paragraphs.modern: In 2 Corinthians 7:11, see how the Corinthians rallied to confront and destroy the sin among them. Something similar happens within a person whose sinful desire has erupted into an act that damages his conscience, peace, and perhaps reputation. Earnest concern, indignation, longing, fear, and a determination to punish the sin all become active against it. Overwhelmed by this response, the desire stays quiet for a time. But once the commotion and investigation end, the thief reappears alive and becomes as busy as ever.

paragraphs.original: [2.] In a time of some judgment, calamity, or pressing affliction; the heart is then taken up with thoughts and contrivances of flying from the present troubles, fears, and dangers. This, as a convinced person concludes, is to be done only by relinquishment of sin, which gains peace with God. It is the anger of God in every affliction that galls a convinced person. To be quit of this, men resolve at such times against their sins. Sin shall never more have any place in them; they will never again give up themselves to the service of it. Accordingly, sin is quiet, stirs not, seems to be mortified; not, indeed, that it hath received any one wound, but merely because the soul hath possessed its faculties, whereby it should exert itself, with thoughts inconsistent with the motions thereof; which, when they are laid aside, sin returns again to its former life and vigour.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] The other situation is a time of judgment, disaster, or severe affliction. The heart becomes absorbed in finding escape from its present troubles, fears, and dangers. A person under conviction concludes that escape requires abandoning sin and finding peace with God. What pains him in the affliction is his sense of God’s anger. To escape that, he resolves against his sins: sin will never again have a place in him; he will never again serve it. Accordingly, sin grows quiet and seems dead. But it has not actually received a wound. Rather, the mind and other faculties through which it normally acts are completely occupied with thoughts that leave it no room to operate. Once those thoughts are set aside, sin returns with its old vitality and strength.

paragraphs.original: So they Ps. lxxviii. 32–37, are a full instance and description of this frame of spirit whereof I speak: “For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works. Therefore their days did he consume in vanity, and their years in trouble. When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned and inquired early after God. And they remembered that God was their rock, and the high God their redeemer. Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues. For their heart was not right with him, neither were they steadfast in his covenant.”
paragraphs.modern: Psalm 78:32–37 gives a full example of the condition I mean: “Despite all this, they kept sinning and did not believe because of his wonderful works. So he brought their days to an end in emptiness and their years in terror. When he struck them down, they sought him; they turned back and eagerly sought God. They remembered that God was their rock and the Most High God their redeemer. Nevertheless, they flattered him with their mouths and lied to him with their tongues. Their hearts were not right with him, and they were not faithful to his covenant.”

paragraphs.original: I no way doubt but that when they sought, and returned, and inquired early after God, they did it with full purpose of heart as to the relinquishment of their sins; it is expressed in the word “returned.” To turn or return to the Lord is by a relinquishment of sin. This they did “early,” — with earnestness and diligence; but yet their sin was unmortified for all this, verses 36, 37. And this is the state of many humiliations in the days of affliction, and a great deceit in the hearts of believers themselves lies oftentimes herein.
paragraphs.modern: I do not doubt that when they sought God and turned back to him, they firmly intended to abandon their sins. The word “returned” expresses that intention: turning back to the Lord involves leaving sin. They did this “early”—earnestly and diligently. Yet verses 36–37 show that, despite all this, their sin remained unmortified. Many experiences of humbling during affliction are of this kind. Even believers can be seriously deceived at this point.

paragraphs.original: These and many other ways there are whereby poor souls deceive themselves, and suppose they have mortified their lusts, when they live and are mighty, and on every occasion break forth, to their disturbance and disquietness.
paragraphs.modern: In these and many other ways, people deceive themselves into thinking they have put their sinful desires to death. In reality, those desires remain alive and strong, ready to break out whenever an opportunity appears and to disturb and distress them again.

paragraphs.original: The mortification of sin in particular described — The several parts and degrees thereof — The habitual weakening of its root and principle — The power of lust to tempt — Differences of that power as to persons and times — Constant fighting against sin — The parts thereof considered — Success against it — The sum of this discourse considered.
paragraphs.modern: What putting a particular sin to death involves — Its elements and degrees — Weakening sin at its root and as a settled disposition — The power of sinful desire to tempt — How that power varies between people and circumstances — Continual resistance to sin and what that requires — Success against it — A summary of the argument.

paragraphs.original: What it is to mortify a sin in general, which will make farther way for particular directions, is nextly to be considered. 2. The mortification of a lust consists in three things:—
paragraphs.modern: We now need a positive account of what putting a sin to death means. This will prepare the way for practical directions. Second, then, putting a sinful desire to death consists of three things.

paragraphs.original: (1.) An habitual weakening of it. Every lust is a depraved habit or disposition, continually inclining the heart to evil. Thence is that description of him who hath no lust truly mortified, Gen. vi. 5, “Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart is only evil continually.” He is always under the power of a strong bent and inclination to sin. And the reason why a natural man is not always perpetually in the pursuit of some one lust, night and day, is because he hath many to serve, every one crying to be satisfied; thence he is carried on with great variety, but still in general he lies towards the satisfaction of self.
paragraphs.modern: (1.) A lasting weakening of its settled power. Every sinful desire is a corrupt disposition that continually inclines the heart toward evil. That explains the description of the person in whom no sinful desire has truly been put to death: “Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5). He remains under a strong tendency toward sin. The reason an unrenewed person does not pursue one particular sinful desire constantly, day and night, is that he has many desires to serve, each demanding satisfaction. They draw him in many directions, but the overall direction remains self-satisfaction.

paragraphs.original: We will suppose, then, the lust or distemper whose mortification is inquired after to be in itself a strong, deeply-rooted, habitual inclination and bent of will and affections unto some actual sin, as to the matter of it, though not, under that formal consideration, always stirring up imaginations, thoughts, and contrivances about the object of it. Hence, men are said to have their “hearts set upon evil,” the bent of their spirits lies towards it, to make “provision for the flesh.”[3]
paragraphs.modern: Let us therefore understand the sinful desire or disorder we want to mortify as a strong, deeply rooted disposition. It bends the will and affections toward some actual sin—toward the thing that is sinful, though not necessarily toward it consciously as sin. It continually stirs up images, thoughts, and plans concerning its object. This is why people are said to have their hearts set on evil: their inner inclination is toward it, making provision for the flesh.[3]

paragraphs.original: And a sinful, depraved habit, as in many other things, so in this, differs from all natural or moral habits whatever: for whereas they incline the soul gently and suitably to itself, sinful habits impel with violence and impetuousness; whence lusts are said to fight or wage “war against the soul,”[4] 1 Pet. ii. 11, — to rebel or rise up in war with that conduct and opposition which is usual therein,[5] Rom. vii. 23, — to lead captive, or effectually captivating upon success in battle, — all works of great violence and impetuousness. I might manifest fully, from that description we have of it, Rom. vii., how it will darken the mind, extinguish convictions, dethrone reason, interrupt the power and influence of any considerations that may be brought to hamper it, and break through all into a flame. But this is not my present business.
paragraphs.modern: A corrupt sinful disposition differs from ordinary natural or acquired moral habits in this as in other respects: ordinary habits incline us gently, in a manner fitting our nature, but sinful dispositions drive us with violence and force. Hence sinful desires are said to wage war against the soul (1 Peter 2:11).[4] Romans 7:23 describes them as rebelling, conducting a war, and taking prisoners when they win.[5] These are all pictures of forceful, aggressive action. From the description in Romans 7, I could show at length how sin darkens the mind, extinguishes convictions, overthrows reason, neutralizes considerations intended to restrain it, and breaks through every barrier into flame. But that is not my present task.

paragraphs.original: Now, the first thing in mortification is the weakening of this habit of sin or lust, that it shall not, with that violence, earnestness, frequency, rise up, conceive, tumultuate, provoke, entice, disquiet, as naturally it is apt to do, James i. 14, 15. I shall desire to give one caution or rule by the way, and it is this: Though every lust doth in its own nature equally, universally, incline and impel to sin, yet this must be granted with these two limitations:—
paragraphs.modern: The first element of mortification is weakening this settled disposition toward sin. It should no longer rise, conceive further sin, create turmoil, provoke, entice, and disturb us with its former force, urgency, and frequency (James 1:14–15). Here I should add a qualification. Every sinful desire, by its own nature, consistently inclines and drives toward sin. Nevertheless, that statement requires two qualifications when we consider how its power appears in practice.

paragraphs.original: [1.] One lust, or a lust in one man, may receive many accidental improvements, heightenings, and strengthenings, which may give it life, power, and vigour, exceedingly above what another lust hath, or the same lust (that is, of the same kind and nature) in another man. When a lust falls in with the natural constitutions and temper, with a suitable course of life, with occasions, or when Satan hath got a fit handle to it to manage it, as he hath a thousand ways so to do, that lust grows violent and impetuous above others, or more than the same lust in another man; then the steams of it darken the mind so, that though a man knows the same things as formerly, yet they have no power nor influence on the will, but corrupt affections and passions are set by it at liberty. But especially, lust gets strength by temptation. When a suitable temptation falls in with a lust, it gives it a new life, vigour, power, violence, and rage, which it seemed not before to have or to be capable of. Instances to this purpose might be multiplied; but it is the design of some part of another treatise to evince this observation.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] Circumstances can give one desire, or a desire in one person, additional strength far beyond that of another desire or the same kind of desire in another person. When a desire fits someone’s natural constitution and temperament, is favored by his way of life, or finds suitable opportunities, it can become exceptionally powerful. The same happens when Satan finds a means of exploiting it, as he can in countless ways. Its intensity may then greatly exceed that of other desires, or of the same desire in someone else. Its fumes darken the mind: although the person still knows the truths he knew before, those truths no longer influence his will effectively, and corrupt emotions and passions are set loose. Temptation especially strengthens sinful desire. When a fitting temptation joins it, the desire gains a new vitality, force, and fury that it seemed neither to possess nor even to be capable of before. Many examples could establish this, but I intend to develop that observation in another treatise.

paragraphs.original: [2.] Some lusts are far more sensible and discernible in their violent actings than others. Paul puts a difference between uncleanness and all other sins: 1 Cor. vi. 18, “Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.” Hence, the motions of that sin are more sensible, more discernible than of others; when perhaps the love of the world, or the like, is in a person no less habitually predominant than that, yet it makes not so great a combustion in the whole man. And on this account some men may go in their own thoughts and in the eyes of the world for mortified men, who yet have in them no less predominancy of lust than those who cry out with astonishment upon the account of its perplexing tumultuatings, yea, than those who have by the power of it been hurried into scandalous sins; only their lusts are in and about things which raise not such a tumult in the soul, about which they are exercised with a calmer frame of spirit, the very fabric of nature being not so nearly concerned in them as in some other.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] Some sinful desires are much more noticeable in their forceful activity than others. Paul distinguishes sexual immorality from other sins: “Flee sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18). The stirrings of this sin are therefore more directly felt and recognized than those of some others. Love of the world, for example, may be just as deeply dominant in someone while causing much less obvious turmoil throughout the person. Consequently, some people appear, both to themselves and to others, to be far advanced in mortification. Yet sinful desire may rule them just as much as it rules those who cry out in alarm over its inward turbulence—even those driven into scandalous acts. The difference is that their desires concern things that provoke less obvious disturbance. They pursue them calmly because their bodily constitution is less immediately involved.

paragraphs.original: I say, then, that the first thing in mortification is the weakening of this habit, that it shall not impel and tumultuate as formerly; that it shall not entice and draw aside; that it shall not disquiet and perplex the killing of its life, vigour, promptness, and readiness to be stirring. This is called “crucifying the flesh with the lusts thereof,” Gal. v. 24; that is, taking away its blood and spirits that give it strength and power, — the wasting of the body of death “day by day,” 2 Cor. iv. 16.
paragraphs.modern: So the first element in mortification is weakening sin’s settled disposition. It must no longer drive us and create turmoil as before, entice and draw us aside, or disturb and confuse us. Its vitality, energy, and readiness to become active must be killed. This is what Galatians 5:24 calls crucifying the flesh with its desires: figuratively draining away the lifeblood that gives it strength. It is the wasting away of the body of death day by day, corresponding to the daily renewal described in 2 Corinthians 4:16.

paragraphs.original: As a man nailed to the cross; he first struggles, and strives, and cries out with great strength and might, but, as his blood and spirits waste, his strivings are faint and seldom, his cries low and hoarse, scarce to be heard; — when a man first sets on a lust or distemper, to deal with it, it struggles with great violence to break loose; it cries with earnestness and impatience to be satisfied and relieved; but when by mortification the blood and spirits of it are let out, it moves seldom and faintly, cries sparingly, and is scarce heard in the heart; it may have sometimes a dying pang, that makes an appearance of great vigour and strength, but it is quickly over, especially if it be kept from considerable success.
paragraphs.modern: Think of a person nailed to a cross. At first he struggles and cries out strongly. As his lifeblood and strength diminish, his struggles grow weaker and less frequent, and his cries become low, hoarse, and scarcely audible. Similarly, when someone first confronts a sinful desire, it struggles violently to escape and impatiently demands satisfaction and relief. But as mortification drains away its strength, it stirs less often and more weakly; its demands become quieter and are scarcely heard in the heart. It may sometimes experience a final-looking spasm that gives an impression of great strength. But the spasm soon passes, especially if the desire is prevented from gaining a substantial victory.

paragraphs.original: This the apostle describes, as in the whole chapter, so especially, Rom. vi. 6. “Sin,” saith he, “is crucified; it is fastened to the cross.” To what end? “That the body of death may be destroyed,” the power of sin weakened and abolished by little and little, that “henceforth we should not serve sin;” that is, that sin might not incline, impel us with such efficacy as to make us servants to it, as it hath done heretofore. And this is spoken not only with respect to carnal and sensual affections, or desires of worldly things, — not only in respect of the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, — but also as to the flesh, that is, in the mind and will, in that opposition unto God which is in us by nature.
paragraphs.modern: Paul describes this throughout Romans 6, especially in verse 6. Sin is crucified, fastened to the cross. Why? So that its body may be destroyed—its power weakened and progressively done away with—and we may no longer serve sin. In other words, sin should no longer bend and drive us so effectively that it makes us its slaves as it did before. This applies not only to sensual passions and desires for worldly things—not only to the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life. It also applies to the flesh as it operates in the mind and will: our natural opposition to God.

paragraphs.original: Of what nature soever the troubling distemper be, by what ways soever it make itself out, either by impelling to evil or hindering from that which is good, the rule is the same; and unless this be done effectually, all after-contention will not compass the end aimed at. A man may beat down the bitter fruit from an evil tree until he is weary; whilst the root abides in strength and vigour, the beating down of the present fruit will not hinder it from bringing forth more. This is the folly of some men; they set themselves with all earnestness and diligence against the appearing eruption of lust, but, leaving the principle and root untouched, perhaps unsearched out, they make but little or no progress in this work of mortification.
paragraphs.modern: Whatever form the troubling disorder takes, and however it expresses itself—by driving us toward evil or holding us back from good—the rule is the same. Unless its root is effectively weakened, all our later struggles will fail to reach the goal. Someone can beat the bitter fruit off a bad tree until he is exhausted. But while the root remains vigorous, knocking down the present fruit will not prevent more from growing. This is some people’s mistake. They earnestly and diligently oppose the visible outbreaks of sinful desire while leaving its underlying root untouched, perhaps without even identifying it. Consequently, they make little or no progress in putting it to death.

paragraphs.original: (2.) In constant fighting and contending against sin. To be able always to be laying load on sin is no small degree of mortification. When sin is strong and vigorous, the soul is scarce able to make any head against it; it sighs, and groans, and mourns, and is troubled, as David speaks of himself, but seldom has sin in the pursuit. David complains that his sin had “taken fast hold upon him, that he could not look up,” Ps. xl. 12. How little, then, was he able to fight against it! Now, sundry things are required unto and comprised in this fighting against sin:—
paragraphs.modern: (2.) Continually fighting and resisting sin. The ability to keep pressing the attack against sin already represents a considerable degree of mortification. When sin is strong, the soul can scarcely stand against it. It sighs, groans, mourns, and suffers, as David describes, but seldom manages to put sin on the defensive. David complains that his sins had taken such a firm hold of him that he could not look up (Psalm 40:12). How little strength he then had to fight them! Several things are necessary for this continuing battle.

paragraphs.original: [1.] To know that a man hath such an enemy to deal withal, to take notice of it, to consider it as an enemy indeed, and one that is to be destroyed by all means possible, is required hereunto. As I said before, the contest is vigorous and hazardous, — it is about the things of eternity. When, therefore, men have slight and transient thoughts of their lusts, it is no great sign that they are mortified, or that they are in a way for their mortification. This is every man’s “knowing the plague of his own heart,” 1 Kings viii. 38, without which no other work can be done. It is to be feared that very many have little knowledge of the main enemy that they carry about with them in their bosoms. This makes them ready to justify themselves, and to be impatient of reproof or admonition, not knowing that they are in any danger, 2 Chron. xvi. 10.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] We must recognize that we have this enemy. We must notice it, regard it as a real enemy, and understand that it must be destroyed by every proper means available. As I said, this is an intense and dangerous conflict involving eternal realities. Casual, passing thoughts about our sinful desires do not suggest that they are mortified, or even that we are on the way to mortifying them. Each person must know the plague of his own heart (1 Kings 8:38). Without that knowledge, the other work cannot proceed. I fear that many people scarcely know the chief enemy they carry within themselves. Not realizing their danger, they are quick to justify themselves and resent correction or warning (2 Chronicles 16:10).

paragraphs.original: [2.] To labour to be acquainted with the ways, wiles, methods, advantages, and occasions of its success, is the beginning of this warfare. So do men deal with enemies. They inquire out their counsels and designs, ponder their ends, consider how and by what means they have formerly prevailed, that they may be prevented. In this consists the greatest skill in conduct. Take this away, and all waging of war, wherein is the greatest improvement of human wisdom and industry, would be brutish. So do they deal with lust who mortify it indeed. Not only when it is actually vexing, enticing, and seducing, but in their retirements they consider, “This is our enemy; this is his way and progress, these are his advantages, thus hath he prevailed, and thus he will do, if not prevented.” So David, “My sin is ever before me,” Ps. li. 3.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] This warfare begins by learning sin’s ways, tricks, methods, advantages, and opportunities for success. That is how people deal with enemies: they investigate their plans, consider their objectives, and study how they have won before so they can prevent a repetition. This is a major part of skilled leadership in war. Without it, warfare—an activity that calls for so much human intelligence and effort—would be merely brutish. People who genuinely mortify sinful desire treat it this way. They do not think about it only while it is actively troubling or enticing them. In quiet reflection they say, “This is our enemy. This is how it moves forward. These are its advantages. This is how it has won, and how it will win again unless stopped.” David says, “My sin is always before me” (Psalm 51:3).

paragraphs.original: And, indeed, one of the choicest and most eminent parts of practically spiritual wisdom consists in finding out the subtilties, policies, and depths of any indwelling sin; to consider and know wherein its greatest strength lies, — what advantage it uses to make of occasions, opportunities, temptations, — what are its pleas, pretences, reasonings, — what its stratagems, colours, excuses; to set the wisdom of the Spirit against the craft of the old man; to trace this serpent in all its turnings and windings; to be able to say, at its most secret and (to a common frame of heart) imperceptible actings, “This is your old way and course; I know what you aim at;” — and so to be always in readiness is a good part of our warfare.
paragraphs.modern: One of the finest expressions of practical spiritual wisdom is uncovering an indwelling sin’s subtleties, strategies, and hidden depths. Learn where its greatest strength lies, how it exploits circumstances, opportunities, and temptations, and what arguments, pretenses, reasoning, disguises, and excuses it uses. Set the Spirit’s wisdom against the old person’s cunning. Track this serpent through all its twists and turns. Learn to recognize even its most secret movements, which an ordinarily inattentive heart would miss, and say, “I know this old method. I know what you are aiming at.” Maintaining that readiness is a substantial part of our warfare.

paragraphs.original: [3.] To load it daily with all the things which shall after be mentioned, that are grievous, killing, and destructive to it, is the height of this contest. Such a one never thinks his lust dead because it is quiet, but labours still to give it new wounds, new blows every day. So the apostle, Col. iii. 5. Now, whilst the soul is in this condition, whilst it is thus dealing, it is certainly uppermost; sin is under the sword and dying.
paragraphs.modern: [3.] The fullest expression of this battle is daily bringing against sin all the things I will describe later that hurt, weaken, and destroy it. Such a person never assumes a desire is dead merely because it is quiet. He keeps striking it afresh each day, as Paul commands in Colossians 3:5.
