While the soul acts in this way, it has the upper hand: sin is under the sword and dying.

paragraphs.original: (3.) In success. Frequent success against any lust is another part and evidence of mortification. By success I understand not a mere disappointment of sin, that it be not brought forth nor accomplished, but a victory over it, and pursuit of it to a complete conquest. For instance, when the heart finds sin at any time at work, seducing, forming imaginations to make provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof, it instantly apprehends sin, and brings it to the law of God and love of Christ, condemns it, follows it with execution to the uttermost.
paragraphs.modern: (3.) Success. Frequent victories over a sinful desire are another element and evidence of mortification. By success, I do not mean merely frustrating sin so that its intended act never occurs. I mean defeating it and pursuing that victory as thoroughly as possible. For example, when the heart discovers sin enticing it and forming images or plans to provide for the flesh’s desires, it immediately arrests the sin. It brings it before God’s law and Christ’s love, condemns it, and presses the judgment against it to the fullest extent.

paragraphs.original: Now, I say, when a man comes to this state and condition, that lust is weakened in the root and principle, that its motions and actions are fewer and weaker than formerly, so that they are not able to hinder his duty nor interrupt his peace, — when he can, in a quiet, sedate frame of spirit, find out and fight against sin, and have success against it, — then sin is mortified in some considerable measure, and, notwithstanding all its opposition, a man may have peace with God all his days.
paragraphs.modern: Suppose someone reaches this condition: the desire is weakened at its root; its impulses and actions are fewer and weaker than before; it no longer prevents his obedience or disrupts his peace; and he can calmly identify it, fight it, and gain victories over it. Then that sin has been put to death to a considerable degree. Despite all its remaining opposition, he may enjoy peace with God throughout his life.

paragraphs.original: Unto these heads, then, do I refer the mortification aimed at; that is, of any one perplexing distemper, whereby the general pravity and corruption of our nature attempts to exert and put forth itself:— First, The weakening of its indwelling disposition, whereby it inclines, entices, impels to evil, rebels, opposes, fights against God, by the implanting, habitual residence, and cherishing of a principle of grace that stands in direct opposition to it and is destructive of it, is the foundation of it.
paragraphs.modern: These, then, are the main elements of the mortification I have in view: putting to death a particular troubling disorder through which the general corruption of our nature tries to express itself. First, its indwelling disposition must be weakened—the disposition that inclines, entices, and drives us toward evil, rebelling and fighting against God. The foundation of this weakening is the planting, continuing presence, and cultivation of a principle of grace that directly opposes and destroys it.

paragraphs.original: So, by the implanting and growth of humility is pride weakened, passion by patience, uncleanness by purity of mind and conscience, love of this world by heavenly-mindedness: which are graces of the Spirit, or the same habitual grace variously acting itself by the Holy Ghost, according to the variety or diversity of the objects about which it is exercised; as the other are several lusts, or the same natural corruption variously acting itself, according to the various advantages and occasions that it meets withal.
paragraphs.modern: Thus pride is weakened as humility is planted and grows; uncontrolled anger is weakened by patience; impurity by purity of mind and conscience; and love of this world by a mind set on heavenly things. These are the Spirit’s graces. Or we may say they are the same settled grace expressing itself in different ways through the Holy Spirit, according to the different objects and situations it addresses. Likewise, the opposing sins are different desires, or the same natural corruption expressing itself differently as it encounters various advantages and opportunities.

paragraphs.original: — The promptness, alacrity, vigour of the Spirit, or new man, in contending with, cheerful fighting against, the lust spoken of, by all the ways and with all the means that are appointed thereunto, constantly using the succours provided against its motions and actings, is a second thing hereunto required. — Success unto several degrees attends these two. Now this, if the distemper hath not an unconquerable advantage from its natural situation, may possibly be to such a universal conquest as the soul may never more sensibly feel its opposition, and shall, however, assuredly arise to an allowance of peace to the conscience, according to the tenor of the covenant of grace.
paragraphs.modern: Second, the Spirit-given new person must readily, eagerly, and energetically fight this desire. He must use every appointed method and continually make use of the help provided against its impulses and actions. Third, victories in varying degrees accompany these first two elements. Unless a person’s natural constitution gives this particular disorder an advantage that cannot be fully overcome here, the victory may possibly become so complete that the soul no longer noticeably feels its opposition. In any case, this work will certainly provide grounds for a peaceful conscience in accordance with the covenant of grace.

paragraphs.original: [3] Rom. xiii 14. [4] Στρατεύονται κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς. [5] Ἀντιστρατευόμενον, αἰχμαλωτίζοντα.
paragraphs.modern: [3] Romans 13:14. [4] The Greek means “they wage war against the soul.” [5] The Greek words mean “waging war against” and “taking captive.”

chapters.title: Chapter VII: First general rule: belong to Christ

paragraphs.original: General rules, without which no lust will be mortified — No mortification unless a man be a believer — Dangers of attempting mortification of sin by unregenerate persons — The duty of unconverted persons as to this business of mortification considered — The vanity of the Papists’ attempts and rules for mortification thence discovered.
paragraphs.modern: General requirements without which no sinful desire can be put to death — The necessity of being a believer — Dangers when unconverted people attempt mortification without conversion — What unconverted people should do — The resulting critique of Roman Catholic methods and instructions.

paragraphs.original: II. The ways and means whereby a soul may proceed to the mortification of any particular lust and sin, which Satan takes advantage by to disquiet and weaken him, come next under consideration. Now, there are some general considerations to be premised, concerning some principles and foundations of this work, without which no man in the world, be he never so much raised by convictions, and resolved for the mortification of any sin, can attain thereunto. General rules and principles, without which no sin will be ever mortified, are these:—
paragraphs.modern: II. We now turn to the ways a person can put to death a particular sinful desire that Satan exploits to disturb and weaken him. First, however, we must establish some general principles and foundations. Without these, no one can accomplish this work, however deeply convicted of sin or firmly resolved to destroy it. The indispensable general principles are as follows.

paragraphs.original: 1. Unless a man be a believer, — that is, one that is truly ingrafted into Christ, — he can never mortify any one sin; I do not say, unless he know himself to be so, but unless indeed he be so. Mortification is the work of believers: Rom. viii. 13, “If ye through the Spirit,” etc., — ye believers, to whom there is no condemnation, verse 1. They alone are exhorted to it: Col. iii. 5, “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.” Who should mortify? You who “are risen with Christ,” verse 1; whose “life is hid with Christ in God,” verse 3; who “shall appear with him in glory,” verse 4.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Unless someone is a believer—truly grafted into and united to Christ—he cannot put even one sin to death in this spiritual sense. I do not mean that he must be certain he is a believer; I mean that he must actually be one. Mortification is believers’ work. “If you, by the Spirit…” says Romans 8:13: you believers, for whom there is no condemnation (verse 1). The command is addressed to them: “Therefore put to death what is earthly in you” (Colossians 3:5). Who must do this? Those raised with Christ (verse 1), whose life is hidden with Christ in God (verse 3), and who will appear with him in glory (verse 4).

paragraphs.original: An unregenerate man may do something like it; but the work itself, so as it may be acceptable with God, he can never perform. You know what a picture of it is drawn in some of the philosophers, — Seneca, Tully, Epictetus; what affectionate discourses they have of contempt of the world and self, of regulating and conquering all exorbitant affections and passions! The lives of most of them manifested that their maxims differed as much from true mortification as the sun painted on a sign-post from the sun in the firmament; they had neither light nor heat. Their own Lucian sufficiently manifests what they all were.
paragraphs.modern: An unconverted person may do something resembling mortification, but cannot perform the work itself in a way acceptable to God. Some philosophers—Seneca, Cicero, and Epictetus—have painted impressive pictures of it. They speak movingly about despising worldly things and self, and governing and conquering excessive emotions and passions. Yet most of their lives showed that their maxims differed from genuine mortification as much as a sun painted on a sign differs from the sun in the sky: they supplied neither its light nor its heat. Their own writer Lucian sufficiently exposed what they were like.

paragraphs.original: There is no death of sin without the death of Christ. You know what attempts there are made after it by the Papists, in their vows, penances, and satisfactions. I dare say of them (I mean as many of them as act upon the principles of their church, as they call it) what Paul says of Israel in point of righteousness, Rom. ix. 31, 32, — They have followed after mortification, but they have not attained to it. Wherefore? “Because they seek it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law.” The same is the state and condition of all amongst ourselves who, in obedience to their convictions and awakened consciences, do attempt a relinquishment of sin; — they follow after it, but they do not attain it.
paragraphs.modern: There is no death of sin apart from Christ’s death. You know the attempts made through Roman Catholic vows, penances, and acts intended to make satisfaction for sin. Of those who act on the principles of that church, as they call it, I would say what Paul says about Israel’s pursuit of righteousness in Romans 9:31–32: they pursue mortification but do not attain it. Why? Because they seek it not by faith but as though it came through works of the law. The same is true of people among ourselves who attempt to abandon sin merely in response to conviction and an awakened conscience. They pursue it but do not attain it.

paragraphs.original: It is true, it is, it will be, required of every person whatever that hears the law or gospel preached, that he mortify sin. It is his duty, but it is not his immediate duty; it is his duty to do it, but to do it in God’s way. If you require your servant to pay so much money for you in such a place, but first to go and take it up in another, it is his duty to pay the money appointed, and you will blame him if he do it not; yet it was not his immediate duty, — he was first to take it up, according to your direction. So it is in this case: sin is to be mortified, but something is to be done in the first place to enable us thereunto.
paragraphs.modern: Certainly everyone who hears God’s law or gospel preached is required to put sin to death. It is his duty, but it is not the first thing he must do independently of everything else. He must do it in God’s way. Suppose you tell a servant to make a payment for you at one place, but first to collect the money somewhere else. Making the payment is his duty, and you would rightly blame him for failing to do it. Yet his immediate task is to collect the money as you directed. The same principle applies here: sin must be put to death, but something must first happen to enable us to do that.

paragraphs.original: I have proved that it is the Spirit alone that can mortify sin; he is promised to do it, and all other means without him are empty and vain. How shall he, then, mortify sin that hath not the Spirit? A man may easier see without eyes, speak without a tongue, than truly mortify one sin without the Spirit. Now, how is he attained? It is the Spirit of Christ: and as the apostle says, “If we have not the Spirit of Christ, we are none of his,” Rom. viii. 9; so, if we are Christ’s, have an interest in him, we have the Spirit, and so alone have power for mortification. This the apostle discourses at large, Rom. viii. 8, “So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.” It is the inference and conclusion he makes of his foregoing discourse about our natural state and condition, and the enmity we have unto God and his law therein. If we are in the flesh, if we have not the Spirit, we cannot do any thing that should please God.
paragraphs.modern: I have established that only the Spirit can put sin to death. God promises him for this purpose, and every other means is empty without him. How, then, can someone without the Spirit do this work? A person could more easily see without eyes or speak without a tongue than truly put one sin to death without the Spirit. How do we receive him? He is Christ’s Spirit. Paul says that anyone without Christ’s Spirit does not belong to Christ (Romans 8:9). Conversely, if we belong to Christ and share in him, we have the Spirit, and only in this way do we possess the power for mortification. Paul develops this in Romans 8:8: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” This concludes his preceding discussion of our natural condition and its hostility toward God and his law. If we remain in the flesh without the Spirit, we cannot do anything that pleases God.

paragraphs.original: But what is our deliverance from this condition? Verse 9, “But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you;” — “Ye believers, that have the Spirit of Christ, ye are not in the flesh.” There is no way of deliverance from the state and condition of being in the flesh but by the Spirit of Christ. And what if this Spirit of Christ be in you? Why, then, you are mortified; verse 10, “The body is dead because of sin,” or unto it; mortification is carried on; the new man is quickened to righteousness. This the apostle proves, verse 11, from the union we have with Christ by the Spirit, which will produce suitable operations in us to what it wrought in him. All attempts, then, for mortification of any lust, without an interest in Christ, are vain.
paragraphs.modern: How are we delivered from that condition? Verse 9 answers: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, provided that God’s Spirit dwells in you.” Believers who have Christ’s Spirit are no longer in the flesh. There is no other way out of that condition than through Christ’s Spirit. And if his Spirit is in you, mortification is at work. Verse 10 says that the body is dead because of sin—or, in the sense under discussion, dead to it—and the new person is made alive to righteousness. In verse 11, Paul grounds this in our union with Christ through the Spirit: the Spirit produces in us effects corresponding to his work in Christ. Therefore, every attempt to put a sinful desire to death apart from belonging to Christ is futile.

paragraphs.original: Many men that are galled with and for sin, the arrows of Christ for conviction, by the preaching of the word, or some affliction having been made sharp in their hearts, do vigorously set themselves against this or that particular lust, wherewith their consciences have been most disquieted or perplexed. But, poor creatures! they labour in the fire, and their work consumeth. When the Spirit of Christ comes to this work he will be “like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap,” and he will purge men as gold and as silver, Mal. iii. 2, 3, — take away their dross and tin, their filth and blood, as Isa. iv. 4; but men must be gold and silver in the bottom, or else refining will do them no good. The prophet gives us the sad issue of wicked men’s utmost attempts for mortification, by what means soever that God affords them: Jer. vi. 29, 30, “The bellows are burned, and the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain. Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the Lord hath rejected them.” And what is the reason hereof? Verse 28, They were “brass and iron” when they were put into the furnace. Men may refine brass and iron long enough before they will be good silver.
paragraphs.modern: Many people are pained by sin. Through preaching or affliction, Christ’s arrows of conviction pierce their hearts. They then vigorously oppose whichever particular desire most troubles their consciences. Yet their labor is like work consumed in a fire. When Christ’s Spirit undertakes this work, he is like a refiner’s fire and cleansing soap. He purifies people like gold and silver (Malachi 3:2–3), removing their impurities, filth, and bloodstains (Isaiah 4:4). But beneath the impurities they must actually be gold and silver; otherwise, refining will not help. Jeremiah 6:29–30 describes the sad outcome of wicked people’s greatest attempts, even with the means God provides: “The bellows are burned; the lead is consumed by the fire; the refiner melts in vain. They will be called rejected silver, because the Lord has rejected them.” Why? Verse 28 says they were brass and iron when they entered the furnace. You may refine brass and iron indefinitely without turning them into good silver.

paragraphs.original: I say, then, mortification is not the present business of unregenerate men. God calls them not to it as yet; conversion is their work, — the conversion of the whole soul, — not the mortification of this or that particular lust. You would laugh at a man that you should see setting up a great fabric, and never take any care for a foundation; especially if you should see him so foolish as that, having a thousand experiences that what he built one day fell down another, he would yet continue in the same course. So it is with convinced persons; though they plainly see, that what ground they get against sin one day they lose another, yet they will go on in the same road still, without inquiring where the destructive flaw in their progress lies.
paragraphs.modern: Therefore, the immediate task of unconverted people is not the mortification of particular sins. God calls them first to conversion—the turning of the whole soul to him—not merely to defeating this or that desire. You would consider someone ridiculous if he kept erecting a great building without attending to its foundation, especially if, after seeing a thousand times that yesterday’s construction collapsed today, he continued exactly as before. People under conviction can behave that way. They plainly see that the ground they gain against sin one day is lost the next. Yet they keep following the same method without asking what fundamental flaw is destroying their progress.

paragraphs.original: When the Jews, upon the conviction of their sin, were cut to the heart, Acts ii. 37, and cried out, “What shall we do?” what doth Peter direct them to do? Does he bid them go and mortify their pride, wrath, malice, cruelty, and the like? No; he knew that was not their present work, but he calls them to conversion and faith in Christ in general, verse 38. Let the soul be first thoroughly converted, and then, “looking on Him whom they had pierced,” humiliation and mortification will ensue.
paragraphs.modern: When the Jewish hearers were pierced to the heart by conviction and cried, “What should we do?” (Acts 2:37), how did Peter direct them? Did he simply tell them to go and mortify their pride, anger, malice, cruelty, and similar sins? No. He knew that was not their first task. He called them to conversion and faith in Christ (verse 38). Let the whole soul first be converted. Then, as people look upon the one they pierced, humbling and mortification will follow.

paragraphs.original: Thus, when John came to preach repentance and conversion, he said, “The axe is now laid to the root of the tree,” Matt. iii. 10. The Pharisees had been laying heavy burdens, imposing tedious duties, and rigid means of mortification, in fastings, washings, and the like, all in vain. Says John, “The doctrine of conversion is for you; the axe in my hand is laid to the root.” And our Saviour tells us what is to be done in this case; says he, “Do men gather grapes from thorns?” Matt. vii. 16. But suppose a thorn be well pruned and cut, and have pains taken with him? “Yea, but he will never bear figs,” verses 17, 18; it cannot be but every tree will bring forth fruit according to its own kind. What is then to be done, he tells us, Matt. xii. 33, “Make the tree good, and his fruit will be good.” The root must be dealt with, the nature of the tree changed, or no good fruit will be brought forth.
paragraphs.modern: Likewise, when John preached repentance and conversion, he said, “The axe is already laid at the tree’s root” (Matthew 3:10). The Pharisees had been imposing heavy burdens, exhausting duties, and harsh methods of mortification—fasts, ritual washings, and the like—all in vain. John’s message was, “You need conversion. My axe goes to the root.” Our Savior makes the same point: “Do people gather grapes from thorn bushes?” (Matthew 7:16). But what if a thorn bush is carefully pruned, trimmed, and tended? It still will not produce figs. Trees bear according to their nature (verses 17–18). What, then, is needed? “Make the tree good, and its fruit will be good” (Matthew 12:33). The root must be addressed and the tree’s nature changed, or good fruit will never appear.

paragraphs.original: This is that I aim at: unless a man be regenerate, unless he be a believer, all attempts that he can make for mortification, be they never so specious and promising, — all means he can use, let him follow them with never so much diligence, earnestness, watchfulness, and intention of mind and spirit, — are to no purpose. In vain shall he use many remedies; he shall not be healed. Yea, there are sundry desperate evils attending an endeavour in convinced persons, that are no more but so, to perform this duty:—
paragraphs.modern: This is my point: unless someone has been born again and is a believer, every attempt at mortification is ineffective, however impressive or promising it appears. He may use every available method with extraordinary diligence, earnestness, vigilance, and concentration, but he will not accomplish the intended work. He may try many remedies in vain and remain unhealed. Indeed, several grave dangers accompany attempts to perform this duty by people who have conviction of sin but nothing beyond conviction.

paragraphs.original: (1.) The mind and soul is taken up about that which is not the man’s proper business, and so he is diverted from that which is so. God lays hold by his word and judgments on some sin in him, galls his conscience, disquiets his heart, deprives him of his rest; now other diversions will not serve his turn; he must apply himself to the work before him. The business in hand being to awake the whole man unto a consideration of the state and condition wherein he is, that he might be brought home to God, instead hereof he sets himself to mortify the sin that galls him, — which is a pure issue of self-love, to be freed from his trouble, and not at all to the work he is called unto, — and so is diverted from it.
paragraphs.modern: (1.) His mind and soul become occupied with something other than his immediate task, distracting him from what he really needs to do. Through his word and judgments, God exposes a particular sin, wounds the person’s conscience, disturbs his heart, and deprives him of rest. Ordinary distractions no longer work; he must address the problem. God’s purpose is to awaken the whole person to his overall spiritual condition and bring him home to God. Instead, he merely tries to kill the sin that hurts him. His aim may arise entirely from self-love: he wants relief from trouble. In pursuing that relief, he turns aside from the very work to which God is calling him.

paragraphs.original: Thus God tells us of Ephraim, when he “spread his net upon them, and brought them down as the fowls of heaven, and chastised them,” Hos. vii. 12, caught them, entangled them, convinced them that they could not escape; saith he of them, “They return, but not to the Most High;” — they set themselves to a relinquishment of sin, but not in that manner, by universal conversion, as God called for it. Thus are men diverted from coming unto God by the most glorious ways that they can fix upon to come to him by. And this is one of the most common deceits whereby men ruin their own souls.
paragraphs.modern: God describes this in Ephraim. He spread his net over them, brought them down like birds, and disciplined them (Hosea 7:12). He caught them, entangled them, and showed them that they could not escape. Yet he says, “They return, but not to the Most High.” They tried to abandon sin, but not through the wholehearted conversion God required. Thus the very methods people regard as their most admirable way of approaching God can keep them from coming to him. This is one of the commonest deceptions through which people ruin their souls.

paragraphs.original: I wish that some whose trade it is to daub with untempered mortar in the things of God did not teach this deceit, and cause the people to err by their ignorance. What do men do, what ofttimes are they directed unto, when their consciences are galled by sin and disquietment from the Lord, who hath laid hold upon them? Is not a relinquishment of the sin, as to practice, that they are, in some fruits of it, perplexed withal, and making head against it, the sum of what they apply themselves unto? and is not the gospel end of their convictions lost thereby? Here men abide and perish.
paragraphs.modern: I wish certain teachers, whose work in God’s affairs resembles patching a wall with defective mortar, did not spread this deception and lead people astray through ignorance. When the Lord lays hold of people and their consciences are disturbed by sin, what do they do—and what are they often told to do? Is it not simply to stop practicing the particular sin whose consequences trouble them, and to resist that sin? Does this not lose sight of the gospel purpose of their conviction? People settle there and perish.

paragraphs.original: (2.) This duty being a thing good in itself, in its proper place, a duty evidencing sincerity, bringing home peace to the conscience; a man finding himself really engaged in it, his mind and heart set against this or that sin, with purpose and resolution to have no more to do with it, — he is ready to conclude that his state and condition is good, and so to delude his own soul. For, —
paragraphs.modern: (2.) In its proper place, this duty is good: it displays sincerity and brings peace to the conscience. Therefore, someone who finds himself genuinely engaged in opposing a particular sin—firmly intending to have nothing more to do with it—may conclude that his overall spiritual condition is good. In this way he deceives himself. Notice two aspects of the deception.

paragraphs.original: [1.] When his conscience hath been made sick with sin, and he could find no rest, when he should go to the great Physician of souls, and get healing in his blood, the man by this engagement against sin pacifies and quiets his conscience, and sits down without going to Christ at all. Ah! how many poor souls are thus deluded to eternity! “When Ephraim saw his sickness, he sent to king Jareb,” Hos. v. 13; which kept him off from God. The whole bundle of the popish religion is made up of designs and contrivances to pacify conscience without Christ; all described by the apostle, Rom. x. 3.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] Sin has made his conscience sick and restless. He should go to the great Physician of souls and find healing in Christ’s blood. Instead, his campaign against a particular sin soothes his conscience, and he settles down without coming to Christ at all. How many souls are deceived in this way to their eternal loss! “When Ephraim saw his sickness, he sent to King Jareb” (Hosea 5:13), and that kept him away from God. The whole system of Roman Catholic religion, as I am criticizing it here, consists of plans for quieting conscience without Christ. Paul describes the principle in Romans 10:3.

paragraphs.original: [2.] By this means men satisfy themselves that their state and condition is good, seeing they do that which is a work good in itself, and they do not do it to be seen. They know they would have the work done in sincerity, and so are hardened in a kind of self-righteousness.
paragraphs.modern: [2.] People thereby persuade themselves that their condition is good. After all, they are doing something good in itself, and not merely to impress others. They know that they sincerely want the sin overcome. This very conviction hardens them in a kind of self-righteousness.

paragraphs.original: (3.) When a man hath thus for a season been deluded, and hath deceived his own soul, and finds in a long course of life that indeed his sin is not mortified, or if he hath changed one he hath gotten another, he begins at length to think that all contending is in vain, — he shall never be able to prevail; he is making a dam against water that increaseth on him. Hereupon he gives over, as one despairing of any success, and yields up himself to the power of sin and that habit of formality that he hath gotten.
paragraphs.modern: (3.) After remaining in this self-deception for a time, perhaps through many years, he discovers that his sin is not actually mortified. Or he has merely exchanged it for another. Eventually he begins to think that all resistance is useless and that he can never win. It feels like building a dam against water that keeps rising. Despairing of success, he gives up and surrenders to sin’s power and to the outward religious routine he has acquired.

paragraphs.original: And this is the usual issue with persons attempting the mortification of sin without an interest in Christ first obtained. It deludes them, hardens them, — destroys them. And therefore we see that there are not usually more vile and desperate sinners in the world than such as, having by conviction been put on this course, have found it fruitless, and deserted it without a discovery of Christ. And this is the substance of the religion and godliness of the choicest formalists in the world, and of all those who in the Roman synagogue are drawn to mortification, as they drive Indians to baptism or cattle to water. I say, then, that mortification is the work of believers, and believers only. To kill sin is the work of living men; where men are dead (as all unbelievers, the best of them, are dead), sin is alive, and will live.
paragraphs.modern: This is the usual outcome when people attempt mortification without first belonging to Christ: the attempt deceives them, hardens them, and destroys them. We therefore often find some of the most reckless and hardened sinners among those who were driven by conviction into this course, found it fruitless, and abandoned it without discovering Christ. Such a process constitutes the religion of even the most impressive merely outward worshipers, and of those compelled into mortification within the Roman system—as Indigenous peoples were driven to baptism, or cattle driven to water. I repeat: mortification is the work of believers alone. Killing sin is the work of people who are spiritually alive. Where people are spiritually dead—as all unbelievers are, even the best of them—sin remains alive and will continue to live.

paragraphs.original: 2. It is the work of faith, the peculiar work of faith. Now, if there be a work to be done that will be effected by one only instrument, it is the greatest madness for any to attempt the doing of it that hath not that instrument. Now, it is faith that purifies the heart, Acts xv. 9; or, as Peter speaks, we “purify our souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit,” 1 Pet. i. 22; and without it, it will not be done. What hath been spoken I suppose is sufficient to make good my first general rule:— Be sure to get an interest in Christ; if you intend to mortify any sin without it, it will never be done.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Mortification is the distinctive work of faith. If a task can be accomplished through only one instrument, trying to do it without that instrument is madness. Faith is what purifies the heart (Acts 15:9). Or, as Peter puts it, we purify our souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit (1 Peter 1:22). Without faith, this work will not be done. I think this sufficiently establishes my first general rule: make sure you truly belong to Christ. Any intention to put sin to death without that union will never succeed.

paragraphs.original: Obj. You will say, “What, then, would you have unregenerate men that are convinced of the evil of sin do? Shall they cease striving against sin, live dissolutely, give their lusts their swing, and be as bad as the worst of men? This were a way to set the whole world into confusion, to bring all things into darkness, to set open the flood-gates of lust, and lay the reins upon the necks of men to rush into all sin with delight and greediness, like the horse into the battle.”
paragraphs.modern: Objection: “What, then, should unconverted people do when they are convinced that sin is evil? Should they stop resisting it, live recklessly, give their desires free rein, and become as wicked as anyone? That would throw the world into chaos and darkness. It would open the floodgates of sinful desire, letting people charge eagerly and delightedly into every kind of sin, like a horse charging into battle.”

paragraphs.original: Ans. 1. God forbid! It is to be looked on as a great issue of the wisdom, goodness, and love of God, that by manifold ways and means he is pleased to restrain the sons of men from running forth into that compass of excess and riot which the depravedness of their nature would carry them out unto with violence. By what way soever this is done, it is an issue of the care, kindness, and goodness of God, without which the whole earth would be a hell of sin and confusion.
paragraphs.modern: Answer: 1. Certainly not! God’s many ways of restraining people from the excess and disorder toward which their corrupt nature would violently carry them are a great expression of his wisdom, goodness, and love. Whatever means he uses, such restraint displays his care and kindness. Without it, the whole earth would become a hell of sin and confusion.

paragraphs.original: 2. There is a peculiar convincing power in the word, which God is oftentimes pleased to put forth, to the wounding, amazing, and, in some sort, humbling of sinners, though they are never converted. And the word is to be preached though it hath this end, yet not with this end. Let, then, the word be preached, and the sins of men [will be] rebuked, lust will be restrained, and some oppositions will be made against sin; though that be not the effect aimed at.
paragraphs.modern: 2. God’s word has a distinctive power to convict. God often uses it to wound, alarm, and in some measure humble sinners even when they are never converted. The word must still be preached, although it sometimes produces only this result; but that must not be the preacher’s final goal. Let the word be preached, then. People’s sins will be rebuked, desires restrained, and some resistance to sin produced, even where the intended saving result has not yet occurred.

paragraphs.original: 3. Though this be the work of the word and Spirit, and it be good in itself, yet it is not profitable nor available as to the main end in them in whom it is wrought; they are still in the gall of bitterness, and under the power of darkness.
paragraphs.modern: 3. Although this restraining work comes through the word and Spirit and is good in itself, it does not by itself accomplish the chief goal for those who experience it. Without conversion, they remain in bitter bondage and under the power of darkness.

paragraphs.original: 4. Let men know it is their duty, but in its proper place; I take not men from mortification, but put them upon conversion. He that shall call a man from mending a hole in the wall of his house, to quench a fire that is consuming the whole building, is not his enemy. Poor soul! it is not thy sore finger but thy hectic fever that thou art to apply thyself to the consideration of. Thou settest thyself against a particular sin, and dost not consider that thou art nothing but sin.
paragraphs.modern: 4. Tell people that mortification is their duty, but put it in its proper order. I am not turning people away from mortification; I am directing them toward conversion. Someone who calls you away from patching a hole in your wall to extinguish the fire consuming your whole house is not your enemy. Troubled soul, your main concern is not a sore finger but a fever affecting your whole person. You are concentrating on a particular sin without recognizing that your whole unrenewed condition is sinful.

paragraphs.original: Let me add this to them who are preachers of the word, or intend, through the good hand of God, that employment: It is their duty to plead with men about their sins, to lay load on particular sins, but always remember that it be done with that which is the proper end of law and gospel; — that is, that they make use of the sin they speak against to the discovery of the state and condition wherein the sinner is; otherwise, haply, they may work men to formality and hypocrisy, but little of the true end of preaching the gospel will be brought about. It will not avail to beat a man off from his drunkenness into a sober formality. A skilful master of the assemblies lays his axe at the root, drives still at the heart.
paragraphs.modern: Let me add a word for those who preach Scripture, or hope by God’s kindness to enter that work. You must plead with people about their sins and press home the seriousness of particular sins. But always do so with the proper purpose of both law and gospel in view: use the particular sin to expose the sinner’s overall spiritual condition. Otherwise, you may merely produce outward religion and hypocrisy, accomplishing little of the true purpose of gospel preaching. Driving someone from drunkenness into sober religious formalism will not achieve that purpose. A skilled teacher lays the axe at the root and keeps aiming at the heart.

paragraphs.original: To inveigh against particular sins of ignorant, unregenerate persons, such as the land is full of, is a good work; but yet, though it may be done with great efficacy, vigour, and success, if this be all the effect of it, that they are set upon the most sedulous endeavours of mortifying their sins preached down, all that is done is but like the beating of an enemy in an open field, and driving him into an impregnable castle, not to be prevailed against. Get you at any time a sinner at the advantage, on the account of any one sin whatever? have you any thing to take hold of him by? — bring it to his state and condition, drive it up to the head, and there deal with him. To break men off particular sins, and not to break their hearts, is to deprive ourselves of advantages of dealing with them.
paragraphs.modern: It is good to speak forcefully against the particular sins of the ignorant, unconverted people who fill the land. But even effective, energetic preaching can leave them only diligently trying to defeat the sins named. If that is its entire effect, it resembles defeating an enemy in an open field only to drive him into a fortress you cannot capture. Whenever a particular sin gives you an opening to address a sinner, use it to expose his overall condition. Follow the issue to its source and deal with him there. To detach people from particular sins without bringing their hearts to repentance is to surrender the very opportunity those sins gave us to help them.

paragraphs.original: And herein is the Roman mortification grievously peccant; they drive all sorts of persons to it, without the least consideration whether they have a principle for it or no. Yea, they are so far from calling on men to believe, that they may be able to mortify their lusts, that they call men to mortification instead of believing. The truth is, they neither know what it is to believe nor what mortification itself intends. Faith with them is but a general assent to the doctrine taught in their church; and mortification the betaking of a man by a vow to some certain course of life, wherein he denies himself something of the use of the things of this world, not without a considerable compensation. Such men know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Their boasting of their mortification is but their glorying in their shame.
paragraphs.modern: This is where Roman Catholic mortification goes seriously wrong. It presses every sort of person into the work without considering whether the person possesses the inward spiritual power to perform it. Instead of calling people to believe so that they can mortify sinful desires, it calls them to mortification in place of believing. The truth is that these teachers understand neither what believing means nor what mortification intends. They treat faith as general agreement with their church’s teaching, and mortification as a vow to follow a particular way of life in which a person gives up some worldly uses or pleasures—usually with substantial compensations. Such people understand neither Scripture nor God’s power. Boasting about this mortification is boasting about their shame.

paragraphs.original: Some casuists among ourselves, who, overlooking the necessity of regeneration, do avowedly give this for a direction to all sorts of persons that complain of any sin or lust, that they should vow against it, at least for a season, a month or so, seem to have a scantling of light in the mystery of the gospel, much like that of Nicodemus when he came first to Christ. They bid men vow to abstain from their sin for a season. This commonly makes their lust more impetuous. Perhaps with great perplexity they keep their word; perhaps not, which increases their guilt and torment.
paragraphs.modern: Some advisers on cases of conscience among ourselves also overlook the necessity of new birth. They openly tell anyone troubled by a sin to make a vow against it, at least for a period such as a month. Their understanding of the gospel’s mystery seems as limited as Nicodemus’s when he first came to Christ. They tell people to vow temporary abstinence from the sin. This often makes the desire more violent. Perhaps the person keeps the vow with great distress; perhaps he breaks it, increasing his guilt and torment.

paragraphs.original: Is their sin at all mortified hereby? Do they find a conquest over it? Is their condition changed, though they attain a relinquishment of it? Are they not still in the gall of bitterness? Is not this to put men to make brick, if not without straw, yet, which is worse, without strength? What promise hath any unregenerate man to countenance him in this work? what assistance for the performance of it? Can sin be killed without an interest in the death of Christ, or mortified without the Spirit? If such directions should prevail to change men’s lives, as seldom they do, yet they never reach to the change of their hearts or conditions.
paragraphs.modern: Has the sin actually been put to death by this? Have they conquered it? Even if they stop practicing it, has their underlying condition changed? Do they not remain in bitter bondage? Is this not like ordering people to make bricks—if not without straw, then, even worse, without strength? What promise authorizes an unconverted person to expect success in this work apart from Christ? What help enables him to perform it? Can sin be killed without sharing in Christ’s death, or mortified without the Spirit? Even if such advice changes people’s outward lives, which it seldom does, it cannot of itself change their hearts or spiritual condition.

paragraphs.original: They may make men self-justiciaries or hypocrites, not Christians. It grieves me ofttimes to see poor souls, that have a zeal for God and a desire of eternal welfare, kept by such directors and directions under a hard, burdensome, outside worship and service of God, with many specious endeavours for mortification, in an utter ignorance of the righteousness of Christ, and unacquaintedness with his Spirit, all their days. Persons and things of this kind I know too many. If ever God shine into their hearts, to give them the knowledge of his glory in the face of his Son Jesus Christ, they will see the folly of their present way.
paragraphs.modern: Such methods may produce self-righteous people or hypocrites, but not Christians. It often grieves me to see people who are zealous for God and desire eternal well-being kept by these advisers and their advice in a harsh, burdensome, merely outward service of God. They make many impressive-looking efforts to mortify sin while remaining entirely ignorant of Christ’s righteousness and unfamiliar with his Spirit throughout their lives. I know too many such people and situations. If God shines into their hearts and gives them the knowledge of his glory in the face of his Son Jesus Christ, they will recognize the folly of their present course.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII: Second general rule: seek obedience in everything

paragraphs.original: The second general rule proposed — Without universal sincerity for the mortifying of every lust, no lust will be mortified — Partial mortification always from a corrupt principle — Perplexity of temptation from a lust oftentimes a chastening for other negligences.
paragraphs.modern: The second general rule — No sinful desire is truly put to death without a sincere commitment to oppose them all — Selective mortification springs from a corrupt motive — A troubling temptation may expose or discipline other areas of neglect.

paragraphs.original: 2. The second principle which to this purpose I shall propose is this:— Without sincerity and diligence in a universality of obedience, there is no mortification of any one perplexing lust to be obtained. The other was to the person; this to the thing itself. I shall a little explain this position.
paragraphs.modern: 2. My second general principle is this: without sincere and diligent obedience across the whole of life, no particular troubling desire can truly be put to death. The first principle concerned who can do this work; this one concerns how the work itself must be approached. Let me explain.

paragraphs.original: A man finds any lust to bring him into the condition formerly described; it is powerful, strong, tumultuating, leads captive, vexes, disquiets, takes away peace; he is not able to bear it; wherefore he sets himself against it, prays against it, groans under it, sighs to be delivered: but in the meantime, perhaps, in other duties, — in constant communion with God, — in reading, prayer, and meditation, — in other ways that are not of the same kind with the lust wherewith he is troubled, — he is loose and negligent. Let not that man think that ever he shall arrive to the mortification of the lust he is perplexed withal.
paragraphs.modern: Someone discovers a desire that brings him into the condition already described. It is powerful and turbulent; it takes him captive, troubles him, and robs him of peace. Unable to bear it, he opposes it, prays against it, groans under it, and longs for deliverance. Yet meanwhile he may be careless in other duties: regular communion with God, reading Scripture, prayer, meditation, or other aspects of conduct unrelated to this particular desire. Such a person must not imagine that he will succeed in putting the troubling desire to death while continuing that neglect.

paragraphs.original: This is a condition that not seldom befalls men in their pilgrimage. The Israelites, under a sense of their sin, drew nigh to God with much diligence and earnestness, with fasting and prayer, Isa. lviii.: many expressions are made of their earnestness in the work, verse 2 “They seek me daily, and delight to know my ways; they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God.” But God rejects all. Their fast is a remedy that will not heal them, and the reason given of it, verses 5–7, is, because they were particular in this duty. They attended diligently to that, but in others were negligent and careless.
paragraphs.modern: This condition is not uncommon on the Christian journey. In Isaiah 58, the Israelites, conscious of sin, approached God earnestly through fasting and prayer. Verse 2 repeatedly describes their diligence: “They seek me daily and delight to know my ways. They ask me for righteous judgments and delight in approaching God.” Yet God rejects their effort. Their fast is a remedy that will not heal them. Verses 5–7 explain why: their obedience was selective. They attended diligently to this one duty while neglecting others.

paragraphs.original: He that hath a “running sore” (it is the Scripture expression) upon him, arising from an ill habit of body, contracted by intemperance and ill diet, let him apply himself with what diligence and skill he can to the cure of his sore, if he leave the general habit of his body under distempers, his labour and travail will be in vain. So will his attempts be that shall endeavour to stop a bloody issue of sin and filth in his soul, and is not equally careful of his universal spiritual temperature and constitution. For, —
paragraphs.modern: Imagine someone with a “running sore,” to use Scripture’s expression, arising from a generally unhealthy bodily condition caused by excess and poor nourishment. However skillfully and diligently he treats the sore, his efforts will fail if he leaves the underlying condition untreated. The same applies to someone who tries to stop a particular outflow of sin and defilement from his soul without being equally attentive to his overall spiritual health. Here are the reasons.

paragraphs.original: (1.) This kind of endeavour for mortification proceeds from a corrupt principle, ground, and foundation; so that it will never proceed to a good issue. The true and acceptable principles of mortification shall be afterward insisted on. Hatred of sin as sin, not only as galling or disquieting, a sense of the love of Christ in the cross, lie at the bottom of all true spiritual mortification. Now, it is certain that that which I speak of proceeds from self-love.
paragraphs.modern: (1.) This kind of effort rests on a corrupt motive and foundation, so it cannot produce the right result. I will discuss the true and acceptable motives for mortification later. All genuine spiritual mortification rests on hatred of sin because it is sin—not merely because it hurts or disturbs us—and on an awareness of Christ’s love displayed at the cross. The selective effort I am describing, however, proceeds from self-love.

paragraphs.original: Thou settest thyself with all diligence and earnestness to mortify such a lust or sin; what is the reason of it? It disquiets thee, it hath taken away thy peace, it fills thy heart with sorrow, and trouble, and fear; thou hast no rest because of it. Yea; but, friend, thou hast neglected prayer or reading; thou hast been vain and loose in thy conversation in other things, that have not been of the same nature with that lust wherewith thou art perplexed. These are no less sins and evils than those under which thou groanest. Jesus Christ bled for them also. Why dost thou not set thyself against them also? If thou hatest sin as sin, every evil way, thou wouldst be no less watchful against every thing that grieves and disquiets the Spirit of God, than against that which grieves and disquiets thine own soul. It is evident that thou contendest against sin merely because of thy own trouble by it. Would thy conscience be quiet under it, thou wouldst let it alone. Did it not disquiet thee, it should not be disquieted by thee.
paragraphs.modern: You are earnestly and diligently trying to kill a particular desire. Why? Because it disturbs you, takes away your peace, fills you with sorrow and fear, and gives you no rest. But, my friend, you have also neglected prayer or Scripture reading. You have been frivolous or careless in other areas of conduct, even though those failures differ from the desire that troubles you. They are no less truly sins than the one you groan over. Jesus Christ shed his blood for them too. Why are you not opposing them as well? If you hated sin as sin—every evil way—you would be as watchful against what grieves God’s Spirit as against what grieves your own soul. Your selectiveness shows that you are fighting this sin merely because of the trouble it causes you. If your conscience remained quiet under it, you would leave it alone. If it did not disturb you, you would not disturb it.

paragraphs.original: Now, canst thou think that God will set in with such hypocritical endeavours, — that ever his Spirit will bear witness to the treachery and falsehood of thy spirit? Dost thou think he will ease thee of that which perplexeth thee, that thou mayst be at liberty to that which no less grieves him? No. Says God, “Here is one, if he could be rid of this lust I should never hear of him more; let him wrestle with this, or he is lost.” Let not any man think to do his own work that will not do God’s. God’s work consists in universal obedience; to be freed of the present perplexity is their own only. Hence is that of the apostle, 2 Cor. vii. 1, “Cleanse yourselves from all pollution of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.” If we will do any thing, we must do all things. So, then, it is not only an intense opposition to this or that peculiar lust, but a universal humble frame and temper of heart, with watchfulness over every evil and for the performance of every duty, that is accepted.
paragraphs.modern: Can you expect God to support such hypocritical efforts? Will his Spirit endorse the dishonesty of your heart? Do you think he will relieve the sin that troubles you so that you can freely continue in other things that grieve him just as much? No. God might say, “If this person were rid of this desire, I would never hear from him again. He must keep wrestling here, or he will be lost.” Do not expect to accomplish your own purpose while refusing God’s. God’s purpose is obedience throughout life; your merely self-interested purpose is relief from this immediate distress. Therefore Paul says, “Cleanse yourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1). To undertake this work rightly, we must embrace the whole range of obedience. What God accepts is not merely intense opposition to one particular desire, but a humble heart attentive to every evil and committed to every duty.

paragraphs.original: (2.) How knowest thou but that God hath suffered the lust wherewith thou hast been perplexed to get strength in thee, and power over thee, to chasten thee for thy other negligences and common lukewarmness in walking before him; at least to awaken thee to the consideration of thy ways, that thou mayst make a thorough work and change in thy course of walking with him? The rage and predominancy of a particular lust is commonly the fruit and issue of a careless, negligent course in general, and that upon a double account:—
paragraphs.modern: (2.) How do you know that God has not allowed this troubling desire to gain strength in order to discipline your other neglects and your general lukewarmness toward him? At least it may be intended to wake you up to examine your whole life and make a thorough change in how you walk with him. The intense power of one particular desire commonly results from general carelessness in two ways.

paragraphs.original: [1.] As its natural effect, if I may so say. Lust, as I showed in general, lies in the heart of every one, even the best, whilst he lives; and think not that the Scripture speaks in vain, that it is subtle, cunning, crafty, — that it seduces, entices, fights, rebels. Whilst a man keeps a diligent watch over his heart, its root and fountain, — whilst above all keepings he keeps his heart, whence are the issues of life and death, — lust withers and dies in it. But if, through negligence, it makes an eruption any particular way, gets a passage to the thoughts by the affections, and from them and by them perhaps breaks out into open sin in the conversation, the strength of it bears that way it hath found out, and that way mainly it urgeth, until, having got a passage, it then vexes and disquiets, and is not easily to be restrained: thus, perhaps, a man may be put to wrestle all his days in sorrow with that which, by a strict and universal watch, might easily have been prevented.
paragraphs.modern: [1.] It is a natural consequence, so to speak. As already explained, sinful desire remains in everyone’s heart throughout life, even in the best believer. Scripture does not speak idly when it calls sin subtle and cunning and says that it entices, deceives, fights, and rebels. While a person carefully guards his heart—the root and source from which life’s directions flow—sinful desire withers. But negligence may give it an opening. Through the affections it gains access to the thoughts, and through those it may break into outward sinful conduct. Its force then concentrates along the channel it has discovered. Once that passage is established, it repeatedly troubles and disturbs the person and becomes difficult to restrain. Someone may therefore spend the rest of life painfully struggling with a problem that careful watchfulness across the whole of life might have prevented.

paragraphs.original: [2.] As I said, God oftentimes suffers it to chasten our other negligences: for as with wicked men, he gives them up to one sin as the judgment of another, a greater for the punishment of a less, or one that will hold them more firmly and securely for that which they might have possibly obtained a deliverance from;[6] so even with his own, he may, he doth, leave them sometimes to some vexatious distempers, either to prevent or cure some other evil. So was the messenger of Satan let loose on Paul, that he “might not be lifted up through the abundance of spiritual revelations.”[7] Was it not a correction to Peter’s vain confidence, that he was left to deny his Master?
paragraphs.modern: [2.] As I said, God often allows such trouble to discipline other areas of neglect. With the wicked, he may hand them over to one sin as judgment for another—a greater sin for a lesser one, or a more firmly enslaving sin for one from which they might otherwise have escaped.[6] Even with his own people, he sometimes allows distressing disorders to remain in order to prevent or correct another evil. A messenger of Satan was allowed to afflict Paul so that the abundance of his revelations would not make him proud.[7] And was Peter’s being left to deny his Master not a correction of his empty self-confidence?

paragraphs.original: Now, if this be the state and condition of lust in its prevalency, that God oftentimes suffers it so to prevail, at least to admonish us, and to humble us, perhaps to chasten and correct us for our general loose and careless walking, is it possible that the effect should be removed and the cause continued, — that the particular lust should be mortified and the general course be unreformed? He, then, that would really, thoroughly, and acceptably mortify any disquieting lust, let him take care to be equally diligent in all parts of obedience, and know that every lust, every omission of duty, is burdensome to God, though but one is so to him.[8]
paragraphs.modern: If God sometimes allows a desire to gain power in order to warn and humble us—or to discipline our generally careless way of life—can we expect the effect to be removed while the cause continues? Can we expect this particular desire to be mortified while the rest of our conduct remains unreformed? Anyone who wants truly, thoroughly, and acceptably to put a troubling desire to death must therefore be equally diligent in every part of obedience. He must recognize that every sinful desire and every neglected duty burdens God, even when only one of them burdens him.[8]

paragraphs.original: Whilst there abides a treachery in the heart to indulge to any negligence in not pressing universally to all perfection in obedience, the soul is weak, as not giving faith its whole work; and selfish, as considering more the trouble of sin than the filth and guilt of it; and lives under a constant provocation of God: so that it may not expect any comfortable issue in any spiritual duty that it doth undertake, much less in this under consideration, which requires another principle and frame of spirit for its accomplishment.
paragraphs.modern: As long as the heart dishonestly permits some chosen negligence and refuses to pursue fuller obedience in every area, the soul remains weak because it does not allow faith to do its whole work. It remains selfish because it cares more about the trouble sin causes than about sin’s defilement and guilt. It also continually provokes God. In that condition, it cannot expect an encouraging outcome from any spiritual duty it undertakes, least of all this one. Putting sin to death requires a different motive and disposition of heart.

paragraphs.original: [6] Rom. i. 26. [7] 2 Cor. xii. 7. [8] Isa. xliii. 24.
paragraphs.modern: [6] Romans 1:26. [7] 2 Corinthians 12:7. [8] Isaiah 43:24.

chapters.title: Chapter IX: First direction: recognize dangerous symptoms

paragraphs.original: Particular directions in relation to the foregoing case proposed — First. Consider the dangerous symptoms of any lust — 1. Inveterateness — 2. Peace obtained under it; the several ways whereby that is done — 3. Frequency of success in its seductions — 4. The soul’s fighting against it with arguments only taken from the event — 5. Its being attended with judiciary hardness — 6. Its withstanding particular dealings from God — The state of persons in whom these things are found.
paragraphs.modern: Practical directions for the case already described — First: examine a sinful desire for dangerous signs — 1. Long-established power — 2. Finding peace while keeping it, and how that happens — 3. Frequent success in winning consent — 4. Fighting it only because of its consequences — 5. Hardening or discipline from God — 6. Resistance to God’s particular warnings — What these signs do and do not reveal about a person.

paragraphs.original: III. The foregoing general rules being supposed, particular directions to the soul for its guidance under the sense of a disquieting lust or distemper, being the main thing I aim at, come next to be proposed. Now, of these some are previous and preparatory, and in some of them the work itself is contained. Of the first sort are these ensuing:—
paragraphs.modern: III. Assuming the general principles just established, I now offer specific guidance to someone distressed by a sinful desire or disorder. This is my main purpose. Some directions prepare the heart for the work; others describe the work itself. The following belong to the preparatory kind.

paragraphs.original: First. Consider what dangerous symptoms thy lust hath attending or accompanying it, — whether it hath any deadly mark on it or no; if it hath, extraordinary remedies are to be used; an ordinary course of mortification will not do it. You will say, “What are these dangerous marks and symptoms, the desperate attendancies of an indwelling lust, that you intend?” Some of them I shall name:—
paragraphs.modern: First: examine the dangerous signs accompanying your sinful desire. Does it show any indications of a potentially deadly condition? If so, exceptional remedies are required; an ordinary approach to mortification will not suffice. You may ask what dangerous signs I mean. Here are some of them.

paragraphs.original: 1. Inveterateness. — If it hath lain long corrupting in thy heart, if thou hast suffered it to abide in power and prevalency, without attempting vigorously the killing of it, and the healing of the wounds thou hast received by it, for some long season, thy distemper is dangerous. Hast thou permitted worldliness, ambition, greediness of study, to eat up other duties, the duties wherein thou oughtest to hold constant communion with God, for some long season? or uncleanness to defile thy heart with vain, and foolish, and wicked imaginations for many days? Thy lust hath a dangerous symptom. So was the case with David: Ps. xxxviii. 5, “My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness.” When a lust hath lain long in the heart, corrupting, festering, cankering, it brings the soul to a woful condition.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Long-established power. If the desire has been corrupting your heart for a long time, remaining strong and dominant while you have made no vigorous effort to kill it or heal the wounds it has caused, the condition is dangerous. Have you long allowed worldliness, ambition, or an excessive appetite for study to consume the duties through which you should maintain communion with God? Have you allowed impurity to fill your heart with empty, foolish, and wicked images for many days? That is a dangerous sign. David described such a condition: “My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness” (Psalm 38:5). A sinful desire left long in the heart, corrupting and festering, brings the soul into a miserable state.

paragraphs.original: In such a case an ordinary course of humiliation will not do the work: whatever it be, it will by this means insinuate itself more or less into all the faculties of the soul, and habituate the affections to its company and society; it grows familiar to the mind and conscience, that they do not startle at it as a strange thing, but are bold with it as that which they are wonted unto; yea, it will get such advantage by this means as oftentimes to exert and put forth itself without having any notice taken of it at all, as it seems to have been with Joseph in his swearing by the life of Pharaoh. Unless some extraordinary course be taken, such a person hath no ground in the world to expect that his latter end shall be peace.
paragraphs.modern: An ordinary degree of humbling will not deal with this. Whatever the desire is, its long residence lets it insinuate itself into every faculty of the soul to some extent. The affections become accustomed to its company. The mind and conscience grow familiar with it and no longer start back as though encountering something alien. They treat it comfortably as an old acquaintance. Indeed, it may gain such an advantage that it acts without being noticed at all, as seems to have happened when Joseph swore by Pharaoh’s life. Unless an exceptional course of action is taken, a person in this condition has no basis for confidently expecting a peaceful end.

paragraphs.original: For, first, How will he be able to distinguish between the long abode of an unmortified lust and the dominion of sin, which cannot befall a regenerate person? Secondly, How can he promise himself that it shall ever be otherwise with him, or that his lust will cease tumultuating and seducing, when he sees it fixed and abiding, and hath done so for many days, and hath gone through a variety of conditions with him? It may be it hath tried mercies and afflictions, and those possibly so remarkable that the soul could not avoid the taking special notice of them; it may be it hath weathered out many a storm, and passed under much variety of gifts in the administration of the word; and will it prove an easy thing to dislodge an inmate pleading a title by prescription? Old neglected wounds are often mortal, always dangerous.
paragraphs.modern: First, how will he distinguish the long residence of an unmortified desire from sin’s ruling dominion, which a regenerate person cannot remain under? Second, what grounds has he for expecting things to change or the desire to stop troubling and enticing him? He sees that it has remained entrenched for a long time and survived many changes in his circumstances. It may have persisted through mercies and afflictions so striking that he could not miss them. It may have weathered many storms and sat under many different gifted ministries of the word. Will it be easy to evict a tenant who claims ownership through long possession? Old neglected wounds are often fatal and always dangerous.

paragraphs.original: Indwelling distempers grow rusty and stubborn by continuance in ease and quiet. Lust is such an inmate as, if it can plead time and some prescription, will not easily be ejected. As it never dies of itself, so if it be not daily killed it will always gather strength.
paragraphs.modern: Inward disorders become entrenched and stubborn when left undisturbed. Sinful desire is a tenant that will not leave easily once it can appeal to years of tolerated residence. It never dies naturally. Unless it is put to death daily, it continues to gain strength.

paragraphs.original: 2. Secret pleas of the heart for the countenancing of itself, and keeping up its peace, notwithstanding the abiding of a lust, without a vigorous gospel attempt for its mortification, is another dangerous symptom of a deadly distemper in the heart. Now, there be several ways whereby this may be done. I shall name some of them; as, —
paragraphs.modern: 2. Secret excuses that let the heart reassure itself and retain peace while the desire remains, without a vigorous gospel-based effort to kill it. This is another dangerous sign of a potentially deadly inward disorder. The heart can do this in several ways. Here are some examples.

paragraphs.original: (1.) When upon thoughts, perplexing thoughts about sin, instead of applying himself to the destruction of it, a man searches his heart to see what evidences he can find of a good condition, notwithstanding that sin and lust, so that it may go well with him. For a man to gather up his experiences of God, to call them to mind, to collect them, consider, try, improve them, is an excellent thing, — a duty practised by all the saints, commended in the Old Testament and the New. This was David’s work when he “communed with his own heart,” and called to remembrance the former loving-kindness of the Lord.[9] This is the duty that Paul sets us to practise, 2 Cor. xiii. 5. And as it is in itself excellent, so it hath beauty added to it by a proper season, a time of trial or temptation, or disquietness of the heart about sin, — is a picture of silver to set off this golden apple, as Solomon speaks. But now to do it for this end, to satisfy conscience, which cries and calls for another purpose, is a desperate device of a heart in love with sin.
paragraphs.modern: (1.) Troubled by thoughts about sin, a person searches his heart for evidence that his overall condition is good despite the sin, rather than setting about its destruction. Now, recalling and gathering our experiences of God, examining them, and making good use of them is excellent. It is a duty practiced by the saints and commended in both Testaments. David did this when he communed with his own heart and remembered God’s earlier loving kindness.[9] Paul directs us to self-examination in 2 Corinthians 13:5. This good duty becomes especially fitting during trial, temptation, or distress about sin—like Solomon’s golden apple in a silver setting. But doing it merely to silence a conscience that is calling for something else is a desperate trick of a heart in love with sin.

paragraphs.original: When a man’s conscience shall deal with him, when God shall rebuke him for the sinful distemper of his heart, if he, instead of applying himself to get that sin pardoned in the blood of Christ and mortified by his Spirit, shall relieve himself by any such other evidences as he hath, or thinks himself to have, and so disentangle himself from under the yoke that God was putting on his neck, his condition is very dangerous, his wound hardly curable. Thus the Jews, under the gallings of their own consciences and the convincing preaching of our Saviour, supported themselves with this, that they were “Abraham’s children,” and on that account accepted with God; and so countenanced themselves in all abominable wickedness, to their utter ruin.
paragraphs.modern: When conscience confronts a person and God rebukes the sinful condition of his heart, he should seek pardon for that sin through Christ’s blood and its death through Christ’s Spirit. If instead he comforts himself with other evidences of grace—real or imagined—and uses them to escape the yoke God is placing upon him, his condition is dangerous and his wound difficult to heal. So some of the Jews, troubled by conscience and convicted by our Savior’s preaching, reassured themselves that they were Abraham’s children and therefore accepted by God. On that basis they excused themselves in dreadful wickedness, to their ruin.

paragraphs.original: This is, in some degree, a blessing of a man’s self, and saying that upon one account or other he shall have peace, “although he adds drunkenness to thirst.” Love of sin, undervaluation of peace and of all tastes of love from God, are inwrapped in such a frame. Such a one plainly shows, that if he can but keep up hope of escaping the “wrath to come,” he can be well content to be unfruitful in the world, at any distance from God that is not final separation. What is to be expected from such a heart?
paragraphs.modern: This amounts, at least in some degree, to blessing oneself and insisting that all will be well on some ground or other, even while adding drunkenness to thirst—continuing to indulge sin. Such a disposition contains love of sin and a low regard for genuine peace and every experience of God’s love. The person shows that, as long as he can preserve hope of escaping coming wrath, he is content to remain unfruitful and as distant from God as possible without being finally separated from him. What can we expect from a heart like that?

paragraphs.original: (2.) By applying grace and mercy to an unmortified sin, or one not sincerely endeavoured to be mortified, is this deceit carried on. This is a sign of a heart greatly entangled with the love of sin. When a man hath secret thoughts in his heart, not unlike those of Naaman about his worshipping in the house of Rimmon,[10] “In all other things I will walk with God, but in this thing, God be merciful unto me,” his condition is sad.
paragraphs.modern: (2.) The deception also operates when someone appeals to grace and mercy to excuse an unmortified sin—one he is not sincerely trying to put to death. This reveals a heart deeply entangled in love for sin. He secretly reasons in a way resembling Naaman’s words about worship in Rimmon’s temple:[10] “I will walk with God in everything else, but in this one matter may God be merciful to me.” That is a sad condition.

paragraphs.original: It is true, indeed, a resolution to this purpose, to indulge a man’s self in any sin on the account of mercy, seems to be, and doubtless in any course is, altogether inconsistent with Christian sincerity, and is a badge of a hypocrite, and is the “turning of the grace of God into wantonness;”[11] yet I doubt not but, through the craft of Satan and their own remaining unbelief, the children of God may themselves sometimes be ensnared with this deceit of sin, or else Paul would never have so cautioned them against it as he doth, Rom. vi. 1, 2. Yea, indeed, there is nothing more natural than for fleshly reasonings to grow high and strong upon this account. The flesh would fain be indulged unto upon the account of grace, and every word that is spoken of mercy, it stands ready to catch at and to pervert it, to its own corrupt aims and purposes. To apply mercy, then, to a sin not vigorously mortified is to fulfil the end of the flesh upon the gospel.
paragraphs.modern: A settled decision to indulge sin because mercy is available is, certainly as a continuing way of life, entirely inconsistent with Christian sincerity. It marks a hypocrite and turns God’s grace into permission for immorality.[11] Nevertheless, I do not doubt that Satan’s cunning and believers’ remaining unbelief can sometimes trap even God’s children in this deception. Otherwise Paul would not have warned them as he does in Romans 6:1–2. Indeed, fleshly reasoning readily becomes bold and strong on this point. The flesh wants grace to provide permission for indulgence. It stands ready to seize every word about mercy and twist it toward corrupt purposes. Appealing to mercy while refusing vigorously to mortify a sin therefore turns the gospel into an instrument of the flesh’s aims.

paragraphs.original: These and many other ways and wiles a deceitful heart will sometimes make use of, to countenance itself in its abominations. Now, when a man with his sin is in this condition, that there is a secret liking of the sin prevalent in his heart, and though his will be not wholly set upon it, yet he hath an imperfect velleity towards it, he would practise it were it not for such and such considerations, and hereupon relieves himself other ways than by the mortification and pardon of it in the blood of Christ; that man’s “wounds stink and are corrupt,” and he will, without speedy deliverance, be at the door of death.
paragraphs.modern: A deceitful heart sometimes uses these and many other tricks to excuse its own wrongdoing. Suppose a secret fondness for a sin has the upper hand in someone’s heart. His will may not be fully committed to it, but he retains a half-formed wish for it: he would practice it were it not for certain restraining considerations. If he then seeks relief in ways other than the sin’s mortification and pardon through Christ’s blood, his wounds are foul and festering. Without prompt deliverance, he is approaching death’s door.

paragraphs.original: 3. Frequency of success in sin’s seduction, in obtaining the prevailing consent of the will unto it, is another dangerous symptom. This is that I mean: When the sin spoken of gets the consent of the will with some delight, though it be not actually outwardly perpetrated, yet it hath success. A man may not be able, upon outward considerations, to go along with sin to that which James calls the “finishing” of it,[12] as to the outward acts of sin, when yet the will of sinning may be actually obtained; then hath it, I say, success.
