Now, if any lust be able thus far to prevail in the soul of any man, as his condition may possibly be very bad and himself be unregenerate, so it cannot possibly be very good, but dangerous; and it is all one upon the matter whether this be done by the choice of the will or by inadvertency, for that inadvertency itself is in a manner chosen.
paragraphs.modern: 3. Frequent success in winning the will’s consent is another dangerous sign. I mean that when a sin gains the will’s consent with some pleasure, it has succeeded even if no outward act follows. External considerations may prevent a person from carrying the sin through to what James calls its completion,[12] while his inward willingness to commit it has already been secured. That is a victory for sin. If a desire repeatedly gains this much control, the person’s condition may be very bad indeed; he may be unconverted. At the least, the condition cannot be regarded as healthy: it is dangerous. In substance, it makes little difference whether the consent comes by deliberate choice or through carelessness, because that carelessness is itself, in a sense, chosen.

paragraphs.original: When we are inadvertent and negligent, where we are bound to watchfulness and carefulness, that inadvertency doth not take off from the voluntariness of what we do thereupon; for although men do not choose and resolve to be negligent and inadvertent, yet if they choose the things that will make them so, they choose inadvertency itself as a thing may be chosen in its cause. And let not men think that the evil of their hearts is in any measure extenuated because they seem, for the most part, to be surprised into that consent which they seem to give unto it; for it is negligence of their duty in watching over their hearts that betrays them into that surprisal.
paragraphs.modern: When we are careless where we are required to be watchful, that carelessness does not remove our responsibility for what follows. We may not explicitly decide to be negligent. But if we choose the things that make us negligent, we choose negligence through choosing its cause. Do not imagine that the evil of your heart is excused because you usually seem to be caught by surprise when you consent to sin. Neglect of the duty to guard your heart is what exposes you to that surprise.

paragraphs.original: 4. When a man fighteth against his sin only with arguments from the issue or the punishment due unto it, this is a sign that sin hath taken great possession of the will, and that in the heart there is a superfluity of naughtiness. Such a man as opposes nothing to the seduction of sin and lust in his heart but fear of shame among men or hell from God, is sufficiently resolved to do the sin if there were no punishment attending it; which, what it differs from living in the practice of sin, I know not.
paragraphs.modern: 4. Fighting sin only because of its consequences or deserved punishment shows that sin has gained a strong hold on the will and that much evil remains in the heart. Someone whose only answer to temptation is fear of human disgrace or God’s punishment in hell is, in effect, willing to commit the sin if there were no penalty. I do not see how that willingness differs morally from living in the practice of it.

paragraphs.original: Those who are Christ’s, and are acted in their obedience upon gospel principles, have the death of Christ, the love of God, the detestable nature of sin, the preciousness of communion with God, a deep-grounded abhorrency of sin as sin, to oppose to any seduction of sin, to all the workings, strivings, fightings of lust in their hearts. So did Joseph. “How shall I do this great evil,” saith he, “and sin against the Lord?” my good and gracious God.[13] And Paul, “The love of Christ constraineth us;”[14] and, “Having received these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from all pollution of the flesh and spirit,” 2 Cor. vii. 1.
paragraphs.modern: Those who belong to Christ and obey on gospel principles have other weapons against temptation and the inward battles of sinful desire: Christ’s death, God’s love, the hateful nature of sin, the preciousness of communion with God, and a deep hatred of sin simply because it is sin. Joseph reasoned this way: “How could I do this great evil and sin against God?”—my good and gracious God.[13] Paul likewise says, “Christ’s love compels us,”[14] and, “Since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (2 Corinthians 7:1).

paragraphs.original: But now if a man be so under the power of his lust that he hath nothing but law to oppose it withal, if he cannot fight against it with gospel weapons, but deals with it altogether with hell and judgment, which are the proper arms of the law, it is most evident that sin hath possessed itself of his will and affections to a very great prevalency and conquest. Such a person hath cast off, as to the particular spoken of, the conduct of renewing grace, and is kept from ruin only by restraining grace; and so far is he fallen from grace, and returned under the power of the law. And can it be thought that this is not a great provocation to Christ, that men should cast off his easy, gentle yoke and rule, and cast themselves under the iron yoke of the law, merely out of indulgence unto their lusts?
paragraphs.modern: But if a person is so controlled by desire that only the law remains as a weapon—if he cannot use gospel motives and fights solely with thoughts of hell and judgment—sin has plainly won a major victory over his will and affections. In this particular matter, he has abandoned the guidance of renewing grace and is kept from ruin only by restraining grace. To that extent, he has turned from grace back to the law’s control. Is it not a serious provocation to Christ when people throw off his gentle, easy rule and place themselves under the law’s iron yoke merely to indulge their desires?

paragraphs.original: Try thyself by this also: When thou art by sin driven to make a stand, so that thou must either serve it and rush at the command of it into folly, like the horse into the battle, or make head against it to suppress it, what dost thou say to thy soul? what dost thou expostulate with thyself? Is this all, — “Hell will be the end of this course; vengeance will meet with me and find me out?” It is time for thee to look about thee; evil lies at the door. Paul’s main argument to evince that sin shall not have dominion over believers is, that they “are not under the law, but under grace,” Rom. vi. 14. If thy contendings against sin be all on legal accounts, from legal principles and motives, what assurance canst thou attain unto that sin shall not have dominion over thee, which will be thy ruin?
paragraphs.modern: Test yourself here. When sin forces a decision—either obey it and rush into foolishness like a horse into battle, or stand against and suppress it—what do you say to yourself? What reasons do you use? Is your whole argument, “This road ends in hell; judgment will catch up with me”? Then it is time to wake up: danger is at your door. Paul’s main reason for saying sin will not rule believers is that they are not under law but under grace (Romans 6:14). If all your resistance rests on the law’s threats and motives, what assurance can you gain that sin will not master and ruin you?

paragraphs.original: Yea, know that this reserve will not long hold out. If thy lust hath driven thee from stronger gospel forts, it will speedily prevail against this also. Do not suppose that such considerations will deliver thee, when thou hast voluntarily given up to thine enemy those helps and means of preservation which have a thousand times their strength. Rest assuredly in this, that unless thou recover thyself with speed from this condition, the thing that thou fearest will come upon thee. What gospel principles do not, legal motives cannot do.
paragraphs.modern: This last defensive position will not hold indefinitely. If sinful desire has driven you out of the stronger defenses supplied by the gospel, it will soon defeat this weaker one as well. Do not expect thoughts of punishment to save you after you have willingly surrendered helps a thousand times stronger. Be certain of this: unless you are promptly recovered from that condition, what you fear will overtake you. Motives drawn from law cannot accomplish what you refuse to pursue through gospel principles.

paragraphs.original: 5. When it is probable that there is, or may be, somewhat of judiciary hardness, or at least of chastening punishment, in thy lust as disquieting. This is another dangerous symptom. That God doth sometimes leave even those of his own under the perplexing power at least of some lust or sin, to correct them for former sins, negligence, and folly, I no way doubt. Hence was that complaint of the church, “Why hast thou hardened us from the fear of thy name?” Isa. lxiii. 17. That this is his way of dealing with unregenerate men no man questions. But how shall a man know whether there be any thing of God’s chastening hand in his being left to the disquietment of his distemper? Ans. Examine thy heart and ways.
paragraphs.modern: 5. Another dangerous sign is reason to think that the desire’s disturbing power involves some judicial hardening, or at least God’s corrective discipline. I do not doubt that God sometimes leaves even his own people under the distressing influence of a desire in order to correct earlier sin, negligence, or folly. Hence the church’s complaint, “Why have you hardened us so that we do not fear your name?” (Isaiah 63:17). No one disputes that God deals judicially in this way with the unconverted. But how can a person recognize whether God’s disciplining hand is involved in his present struggle? Examine your heart and conduct.

paragraphs.original: What was the state and condition of thy soul before thou fellest into the entanglements of that sin which now thou so complainest of? Hadst thou been negligent in duties? Hadst thou lived inordinately to thyself? Is there the guilt of any great sin lying upon thee unrepented of? A new sin may be permitted, as well as a new affliction sent, to bring an old sin to remembrance. Hast thou received any eminent mercy, protection, deliverance, which thou didst not improve in a due manner, nor wast thankful for? or hast thou been exercised with any affliction without labouring for the appointed end of it? or hast thou been wanting to the opportunities of glorifying God in thy generation, which, in his good providence, he had graciously afforded unto thee? or hast thou conformed thyself unto the world and the men of it, through the abounding of temptations in the days wherein thou livest? If thou findest this to have been thy state, awake, call upon God; thou art fast asleep in a storm of anger round about thee.
paragraphs.modern: What was your spiritual condition before you became entangled in the sin you now lament? Had you neglected duties or lived excessively for yourself? Does some serious, unrepented sin still lie on your conscience? God may permit a new sin, just as he may send a new affliction, to bring an old sin back to mind. Have you received a striking mercy, protection, or deliverance without responding rightly or giving thanks? Have you experienced affliction without seeking its intended spiritual benefit? Have you neglected opportunities God graciously gave you to glorify him in your generation? Have the temptations of your time led you to conform to the world and its people? If this describes your condition, wake up and call on God. You are sleeping through a storm of displeasure around you.

paragraphs.original: 6. When thy lust hath already withstood particular dealings from God against it. This condition is described, Isa. lvii. 17, “For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth, and smote him: I hid me, and was wroth, and he went on frowardly in the way of his heart.” God had dealt with them about their prevailing lust, and that several ways, — by affliction and desertion; but they held out against all. This is a sad condition, which nothing but mere sovereign grace (as God expresses it in the next verse) can relieve a man in, and which no man ought to promise himself or bear himself upon.
paragraphs.modern: 6. The desire has already resisted God’s particular dealings against it. Isaiah 57:17 describes this: “Because of his sinful greed I was angry and struck him. I hid myself in anger, yet he continued stubbornly in the way of his own heart.” God confronted their dominant sin in several ways, through affliction and withdrawal of his felt presence, but they resisted everything. This is a miserable condition. Only God’s sovereign grace can rescue someone from it, as the next verse explains. No one should presume on that grace or use it as an excuse to remain there.

paragraphs.original: God oftentimes, in his providential dispensations, meets with a man, and speaks particularly to the evil of his heart, as he did to Joseph’s brethren in their selling of him into Egypt. This makes the man reflect on his sin, and judge himself in particular for it. God makes it to be the voice of the danger, affliction, trouble, sickness that he is in or under. Sometimes in reading of the word God makes a man stay on something that cuts him to the heart, and shakes him as to his present condition. More frequently in the hearing of the word preached, his great ordinance for conviction, conversion, and edification, doth he meet with men. God often hews men by the sword of his word in that ordinance, strikes directly on their bosom-beloved lust, startles the sinner, makes him engage unto the mortification and relinquishment of the evil of his heart.
paragraphs.modern: God often meets a person through providence and addresses a particular evil in his heart, as he did with Joseph’s brothers concerning their sale of Joseph into Egypt. The person is made to reflect on and judge that particular sin. God gives his danger, trouble, affliction, or sickness this pointed message. Sometimes, while someone reads Scripture, God holds him at a passage that pierces his heart and shakes his confidence in his present condition. More often, God meets people through preaching, his great appointed means of conviction, conversion, and growth. The sword of his word strikes directly at a cherished desire, startling the sinner and moving him to undertake its mortification and abandonment.

paragraphs.original: Now, if his lust have taken such hold on him as to enforce him to break these bands of the Lord, and to cast these cords from him, — if it overcomes these convictions, and gets again into its old posture, — if it can cure the wounds it so receives, — that soul is in a sad condition. Unspeakable are the evils which attend such a frame of heart. Every particular warning to a man in such an estate is an inestimable mercy; how then doth he despise God in them who holds out against them! And what infinite patience is this in God, that he doth not cast off such a one, and swear in his wrath that he shall never enter into his rest!
paragraphs.modern: But suppose the desire has such a grip that it drives the person to break these restraints and throw off God’s cords. It overcomes the convictions, regains its former position, and recovers from the wounds it received. That soul is in a sad condition indeed. The evils accompanying such a heart are beyond description. Each particular warning given to someone in this state is an immeasurable mercy. How deeply, then, does he despise God by resisting those warnings! And how immense is God’s patience in not casting him off and declaring in wrath that he will never enter God’s rest!

paragraphs.original: These and many other evidences are there of a lust that is dangerous, if not mortal. As our Saviour said of the evil spirit, “This kind goes not out but by fasting and prayer,” so say I of lusts of this kind. An ordinary course of mortification will not do it; extraordinary ways must be fixed on. This is the first particular direction: Consider whether the lust or sin you are contending with hath any of these dangerous symptoms attending of it.
paragraphs.modern: These and many other signs show that a desire is dangerous, perhaps deadly. What our Savior said of an evil spirit—“This kind does not go out except through fasting and prayer”—I apply to desires of this kind. An ordinary course of mortification will not suffice; exceptional measures must be adopted. This, then, is the first practical direction: examine whether the sin you are fighting shows any of these dangerous signs.

paragraphs.original: Before I proceed I must give you one caution by the way, lest any be deceived by what hath been spoken. Whereas I say the things and evils above-mentioned may befall true believers, let not any that finds the same things in himself thence or from thence conclude that he is a true believer. These are the evils that believers may fall into and be ensnared withal, not the things that constitute a believer. A man may as well conclude that he is a believer because he is an adulterer, because David that was so fell into adultery, as conclude it from the signs foregoing; which are the evils of sin and Satan in the hearts of believers.
paragraphs.modern: Before continuing, I must add a caution so that no one misuses what I have said. I have said that true believers may experience these evils. But finding them in yourself does not prove you are a true believer. They are evils into which believers may fall, not qualities that make someone a believer. You might as well argue, “David was a believer and committed adultery; therefore, because I am an adulterer, I must be a believer.” The signs just described are the work of sin and Satan in believers’ hearts, not evidence of faith itself.

paragraphs.original: The seventh chapter of the Romans contains the description of a regenerate man. He that shall consider what is spoken of his dark side, of his unregenerate part, of the indwelling power and violence of sin remaining in him, and, because he finds the like in himself, conclude that he is a regenerate man, will be deceived in his reckoning. It is all one as if you should argue: A wise man may be sick and wounded, yea, do some things foolishly; therefore, every one who is sick and wounded and does things foolishly is a wise man. Or as if a silly, deformed creature, hearing one speak of a beautiful person, should say that he had a mark or a scar that much disfigured him, should conclude that because he hath himself scars, and moles, and warts, he also is beautiful.
paragraphs.modern: Romans 7 describes a regenerate person. But someone who focuses only on the dark side of that description—the remaining unrenewed element, and the power and violence of indwelling sin—and concludes that he is regenerate because he finds the same things in himself has reasoned falsely. It is like saying, “A wise person may be sick, wounded, and sometimes foolish; therefore, everyone who is sick, wounded, and foolish is wise.” Or imagine an unattractive person hearing that a beautiful person has a disfiguring scar, and concluding, “Since I have scars, moles, and warts, I must be beautiful too.”

paragraphs.original: If you will have evidences of your being believers, it must be from those things that constitute men believers. He that hath these things in himself may safely conclude, “If I am a believer, I am a most miserable one.” But that any man is so, he must look for other evidences if he will have peace.
paragraphs.modern: Evidence that you are a believer must come from what actually characterizes believing. Someone who finds these dangerous signs in himself may rightly conclude, “If I am a believer, I am a very distressed and unhealthy one.” But to know that he truly is a believer, and so to have peace, he must look for other evidence.

paragraphs.original: [9] Ps. lxxvii. 6–9. [10] 2 Kings v. 18. [11] Jude 4. [12] James i. 14, 15. [13] Gen xxxix. 9. [14] 2 Cor. v. 14.

chapters.title: Chapter X: Second direction: face sin’s guilt, danger, and evil

paragraphs.original: The second particular direction: Get a clear sense of, — 1. The guilt of the sin perplexing — Considerations for help therein proposed — 2. The danger manifold — (1.) Hardening — (2.) Temporal correction — (3.) Loss of peace and strength — (4.) Eternal destruction — Rules for the management of this consideration — 3. The evil of it — (1.) In grieving the Spirit — (2.) Wounding the new creature — [(3.) Taking away a man’s usefulness.]
paragraphs.modern: The second specific direction: Clearly recognize the guilt, danger, and evil of the sin troubling you. First, understand its guilt; here are considerations that will help. Second, recognize its several dangers: a hardened heart, God’s discipline in this life, loss of peace and strength, and eternal destruction. The last of these requires careful explanation. Third, recognize its present evils: grieving the Spirit, wounding the new life God has created, and diminishing your usefulness.

paragraphs.original: The second direction is this: Get a clear and abiding sense upon thy mind and conscience of the guilt, danger, and evil of that sin wherewith thou art perplexed:—
paragraphs.modern: My second direction is this: Establish in your mind and conscience a clear, lasting awareness of the guilt, danger, and evil of the sin that is troubling you.

paragraphs.original: 1. Of the guilt of it. It is one of the deceits of a prevailing lust to extenuate its own guilt. “Is it not a little one?” “When I go and bow myself in the house of Rimmon, God be merciful to me in this thing.” “Though this be bad, yet it is not so bad as such and such an evil; others of the people of God have had such a frame; yea, what dreadful actual sins have some of them fallen into!” Innumerable ways there are whereby sin diverts the mind from a right and due apprehension of its guilt.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Recognize its guilt. One of the tricks of a dominant sinful desire is to make its guilt seem smaller. “Isn’t this only a little sin?” “When I bow in the temple of Rimmon, may God pardon me in this one matter.” “This is wrong, but not as bad as that other sin. Other believers have felt this way. Some have even committed terrible sins!” Sin has countless ways of distracting us from an honest recognition of our guilt.

paragraphs.original: Its noisome exhalations darken the mind, that it cannot make a right judgment of things. Perplexing reasonings, extenuating promises, tumultuating desires, treacherous purposes of relinquishment, hopes of mercy, all have their share in disturbing the mind in its consideration of the guilt of a prevailing lust. The prophet tells us that lust will do thus wholly when it comes to the height: Hos. iv. 11, “Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart,” — the heart, that is the understanding, as it is often used in the Scripture. And as they accomplish this work to the height in unregenerate persons, so in part in regenerate also. Solomon tells you of him who was enticed by the lewd woman, that he was “among the simple ones;” he was “a young man void of understanding,” Prov. vii. 7.
paragraphs.modern: Sin rises like poisonous vapor and clouds the mind’s judgment. Confused arguments, promises used to minimize guilt, turbulent desires, insincere intentions to give the sin up, and hopes of mercy all interfere with a clear view of its guilt. The prophet describes this effect when it reaches its fullest extent: “Prostitution, wine, and new wine take away the heart” (Hosea 4:11). Here “heart” means understanding, as it often does in Scripture. These sins can completely destroy sound judgment in the unregenerate; they also impair it in believers. Solomon describes the young man enticed by the immoral woman as one of the naive, “a young man without understanding” (Proverbs 7:7).

paragraphs.original: And wherein did his folly appear? Why, says he, in the 23d verse, “He knew not that it was for his life;” he considered not the guilt of the evil that he was involved in. And the Lord, rendering a reason why his dealings with Ephraim took no better effect, gives this account: “Ephraim is like a silly dove without heart,” Hos. vii. 11; — had no understanding of his own miserable condition.
paragraphs.modern: What showed this young man’s foolishness? Verse 23 says, “He did not know that his life was at stake.” He did not consider the guilt of the evil he was entering. Similarly, God explains why his dealings with Ephraim accomplished so little: “Ephraim is like a foolish dove without understanding” (Hosea 7:11). He did not understand his own miserable condition.

paragraphs.original: Had it been possible that David should have lain so long in the guilt of that abominable sin, but that he had innumerable corrupt reasonings, hindering him from taking a clear view of its ugliness and guilt in the glass of the law? This made the prophet that was sent for his awaking, in his dealings with him, to shut up all subterfuges and pretences by his parable, that so he might fall fully under a sense of the guilt of it. This is the proper issue of lust in the heart, — it darkens the mind that it shall not judge aright of its guilt; and many other ways it hath for its own extenuation that I shall not now insist on.
paragraphs.modern: Could David have remained so long in the guilt of his terrible sin unless he had supplied himself with countless corrupt arguments? These kept him from seeing its ugliness and guilt clearly in the mirror of God’s law. That is why the prophet sent to awaken him used a parable to close off every excuse and escape route, until David fully recognized his guilt. This is what sinful desire does in the heart: it darkens the mind so that we cannot judge our guilt rightly. It has many other methods of making itself seem less serious, which I will not discuss now.

paragraphs.original: Let this, then, be the first care of him that would mortify sin, — to fix a right judgment of its guilt in his mind. To which end take these considerations to thy assistance:—
paragraphs.modern: Anyone seeking to put sin to death must therefore first establish an honest judgment of its guilt. The following considerations will help.

paragraphs.original: (1.) Though the power of sin be weakened by inherent grace in them that have it, that sin shall not have dominion over them as it hath over others, yet the guilt of sin that doth yet abide and remain is aggravated and heightened by it: Rom. vi. 1, 2, “What shall we say then? shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” — “How shall we, that are dead?” The emphasis is on the word “we.” How shall we do it, who, as he afterward describes it, have received grace from Christ to the contrary? We, doubtless, are more evil than any, if we do it. I shall not insist on the special aggravations of the sins of such persons, — how they sin against more love, mercy, grace, assistance, relief, means, and deliverances than others. But let this consideration abide in thy mind, — there is inconceivably more evil and guilt in the evil of thy heart that doth remain, than there would be in so much sin if thou hadst no grace at all. Observe, —
paragraphs.modern: (1) Grace at work within believers weakens sin’s power, so that sin does not rule them as it rules others. Yet having received that grace makes the sin still remaining in them more culpable, not less. Romans 6:1–2 asks, “Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin still live in it?” Notice the emphasis on “we.” How can we do this, when—as Paul goes on to explain—we have received grace from Christ precisely to oppose sin? Our conduct is all the more blameworthy when we do. I will not expand on all that aggravates a believer’s sins: sinning against greater love, mercy, grace, help, relief, opportunities, and deliverances. But keep this in mind: the evil remaining in your heart carries far greater guilt than the same amount of sin would carry in someone who had received no such grace. Also observe the following.

paragraphs.original: (2.) That as God sees abundance of beauty and excellency in the desires of the heart of his servants, more than in any the most glorious works of other men, yea, more than in most of their own outward performances, which have a greater mixture of sin than the desires and pantings of grace in the heart have; so God sees a great deal of evil in the working of lust in their hearts, yea, and more than in the open, notorious acts of wicked men, or in many outward sins whereinto the saints may fall, seeing against them there is more opposition made, and more humiliation generally follows them. Thus Christ, dealing with his decaying children, goes to the root with them, lays aside their profession: Rev. iii. 15, “I know thee;” — “Thou art quite another thing than thou professest; and this makes thee abominable.”
paragraphs.modern: (2) God sees great beauty and excellence in his servants’ heartfelt desires—more than in other people’s most impressive deeds, and even more than in many of his servants’ own outward actions. Those actions are often more mixed with sin than the heart’s gracious longings are. Correspondingly, God sees great evil in the sinful desires working within his servants. These can be more culpable than the notorious acts of the wicked, or than many outward sins into which believers fall, because believers usually resist those outward sins more strongly and repent of them more deeply afterward. Thus Christ, dealing with his spiritually declining people, goes beneath their profession of faith to the root: “I know you” (Revelation 3:15). In effect: “What you really are is quite different from what you claim to be, and that makes your condition hateful.”

paragraphs.original: So, then, let these things, and the like considerations, lead thee to a clear sense of the guilt of thy indwelling lust, that there may be no room in thy heart for extenuating or excusing thoughts, whereby sin insensibly will get strength and prevail.
paragraphs.modern: Let these and similar considerations bring you to a clear recognition of the guilt of your indwelling sinful desire. Leave no room in your heart for minimizing or excusing it. Those excuses allow sin to gather strength and gain control without your noticing.

paragraphs.original: 2. Consider the danger of it, which is manifold:— (1.) Of being hardened by the deceitfulness. This the apostle sorely charges on the Hebrews, chap. iii. 12, 13, “Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To-day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.” “Take heed,” saith he, “use all means, consider your temptations, watch diligently; there is a treachery, a deceit in sin, that tends to the hardening of your hearts from the fear of God.” The hardening here mentioned is to the utmost, — utter obduration; sin tends to it, and every distemper and lust will make at least some progress towards it.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Consider its many dangers. (1) Sin’s deception can harden your heart. The apostle urgently warns the Hebrews: “Take care, brothers, that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God. Encourage one another daily, while it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you is hardened by sin’s deception” (Hebrews 3:12–13). His meaning is: “Be watchful. Use every available help. Examine your temptations. Sin contains a treachery that works to harden your heart against the fear of God.” The warning looks toward complete hardness. That is sin’s destination, and every sinful inclination takes a person at least some distance toward it.

paragraphs.original: Thou that wast tender, and didst use to melt under the word, under afflictions, wilt grow as some have profanely spoken, “sermon-proof and sickness-proof.” Thou that didst tremble at the presence of God, thoughts of death, and appearance before him, when thou hadst more assurance of his love than now thou hast, shalt have a stoutness upon thy spirit not to be moved by these things. Thy soul and thy sin shall be spoken of and spoken to, and thou shalt not be at all concerned, but shalt be able to pass over duties, praying, hearing, reading, and thy heart not in the least affected. Sin will grow a light thing to thee; thou wilt pass it by as a thing of nought; this it will grow to.
paragraphs.modern: You once had a tender heart that softened under God’s word and under suffering. Now you may become what some irreverently call “sermon-proof and sickness-proof.” You once trembled at God’s presence, at the thought of death, and at appearing before him—even when you were more assured of his love than you are now. Yet you may become stubbornly unmoved by all these things. People will speak about your soul and your sin, and speak directly to you about them, without your caring. You will pray, listen, and read without your heart being touched. Sin will seem insignificant, something to brush aside as nothing. That is where this leads.

paragraphs.original: And what will be the end of such a condition? Can a sadder thing befall thee? Is it not enough to make any heart to tremble, to think of being brought into that estate wherein he should have slight thoughts of sin? Slight thoughts of grace, of mercy, of the blood of Christ, of the law, heaven, and hell, come all in at the same season. Take heed, this is that thy lust is working towards, — the hardening of the heart, searing of the conscience, blinding of the mind, stupifying of the affections, and deceiving of the whole soul.
paragraphs.modern: Where will that condition end? Could anything more tragic happen to you? Shouldn’t the prospect of becoming someone who takes sin lightly make any heart tremble? When sin becomes trivial to you, grace, mercy, Christ’s blood, God’s law, heaven, and hell become trivial too. Be warned: this is what your sinful desire is working toward—a hardened heart, a seared conscience, a blinded mind, numbed affections, and a thoroughly deceived soul.

paragraphs.original: (2.) The danger of some great temporal correction, which the Scripture calls “vengeance,” “judgment,” and “punishment.” Ps. lxxxix. 30–33, Though God should not utterly cast thee off for this abomination that lies in thy heart, yet he will visit thee with the rod; though he pardon and forgive, he will take vengeance of thy inventions. O remember David and all his troubles! look on him flying into the wilderness, and consider the hand of God upon him. Is it nothing to thee that God should kill thy child in anger, ruin thy estate in anger, break thy bones in anger, suffer thee to be a scandal and reproach in anger, kill thee, destroy thee, make thee lie down in darkness, in anger? Is it nothing that he should punish, ruin, and undo others for thy sake? Let me not be mistaken. I do not mean that God doth send all these things always on his in anger; God forbid! but this I say, that when he doth so deal with thee, and thy conscience bears witness with him what thy provocations have been, thou wilt find his dealings full of bitterness to thy soul. If thou fearest not these things, I fear thou art under hardness.
paragraphs.modern: (2) There is the danger of severe discipline in this life, which Scripture calls “vengeance,” “judgment,” and “punishment.” Psalm 89:30–33 teaches that even when God does not finally reject you, he may discipline you for the evil harbored in your heart. He may forgive your sin and still punish your sinful practices. Remember David and his troubles. See him fleeing into the wilderness, and consider God’s hand upon him. Would it mean nothing to you for God, in anger, to take your child, ruin your possessions, break your bones, expose you to scandal and disgrace, bring you to death and destruction, or make you lie in darkness? Would it mean nothing for others to suffer ruin because of you? Do not misunderstand me: I am certainly not saying that God always sends such sufferings upon his people in anger. But when he does discipline you, and your conscience confirms the sins that provoked it, that experience will be deeply bitter. If these possibilities do not concern you, I fear your heart has already grown hard.

paragraphs.original: (3.) Loss of peace and strength all a man’s days. To have peace with God, to have strength to walk before God, is the sum of the great promises of the covenant of grace. In these things is the life of our souls. Without them in some comfortable measure, to live is to die. What good will our lives do us if we see not the face of God sometimes in peace? if we have not some strength to walk with him? Now, both these will an unmortified lust certainly deprive the souls of men of.
paragraphs.modern: (3) There is the danger of losing peace and spiritual strength for the rest of your life. Peace with God and strength to walk before him sum up the great promises of the covenant of grace. They are the life of our souls. Without some comforting experience of them, living feels like dying. What comfort can life offer without sometimes knowing God’s peaceful presence, or receiving strength to walk with him? A sinful desire left unchecked certainly robs the soul of both.

paragraphs.original: This case is so evident in David, as that nothing can be more clear. How often doth he complain that his bones were broken, his soul disquieted, his wounds grievous, on this account! Take other instances: Isa. lvii. 17, “For the iniquity of his covetousness I was wroth, and hid myself.” What peace, I pray, is there to a soul while God hides himself, or strength whilst he smites? Hos. v. 15, “I will go and return to my place, till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face;” — “I will leave them, hide my face, and what will become of their peace and strength?” If ever, then, thou hast enjoyed peace with God, if ever his terrors have made thee afraid, if ever thou hast had strength to walk with him, or ever hast mourned in thy prayer, and been troubled because of thy weakness, think of this danger that hangs over thy head.
paragraphs.modern: David’s experience makes this unmistakable. How often he describes broken bones, a troubled soul, and painful wounds because of his sin! Consider other examples. “Because of his sinful greed I was angry and hid myself” (Isaiah 57:17). What peace can a soul have when God hides himself? What strength while he strikes? “I will return to my place until they acknowledge their offense and seek my face” (Hosea 5:15). In other words: “I will leave them and hide my face. What will become of their peace and strength then?” Have you ever enjoyed peace with God, feared his terrors, received strength to walk with him, or mourned in prayer over your weakness? Then consider the danger now hanging over you.

paragraphs.original: It is perhaps but a little while and thou shalt see the face of God in peace no more. Perhaps by to-morrow thou shalt not be able to pray, read, hear, or perform any duties with the least cheerfulness, life, or vigour; and possibly thou mayst never see a quiet hour whilst thou livest, — that thou mayst carry about thee broken bones, full of pain and terror, all the days of thy life.
paragraphs.modern: Before long, you may no longer experience God’s peaceful presence. Perhaps by tomorrow you will find no joy, life, or energy in praying, reading, hearing the word, or performing any other duty. You may go through the rest of your life without a peaceful hour, carrying what feels like broken bones—constant pain and terror.

paragraphs.original: Yea, perhaps God will shoot his arrows at thee, and fill thee with anguish and disquietness, with fears and perplexities; make thee a terror and an astonishment to thyself and others; show thee hell and wrath every moment; frighten and scare thee with sad apprehensions of his hatred; so that thy sore shall run in the night season, and thy soul shall refuse comfort; so that thou shalt wish death rather than life, yea, thy soul may choose strangling. Consider this a little, — though God should not utterly destroy thee, yet he might cast thee into this condition, wherein thou shalt have quick and living apprehensions of thy destruction. Wont thy heart to thoughts hereof; let it know what is like to be the issue of its state. Leave not this consideration until thou hast made thy soul to tremble within thee.
paragraphs.modern: God may let you feel pierced by his arrows, full of anguish, unrest, fear, and confusion. Your condition may horrify both you and others. You may seem to see hell and wrath constantly before you and become terrified by the thought that he hates you. Your pain may persist through the night while your soul refuses comfort. You may even reach the despair described in Scripture as preferring death to life, or strangling to continued suffering. Consider this: even without finally destroying you, God could allow you to enter a condition in which destruction feels intensely real and near. Accustom your heart to considering where its present course could lead. Do not dismiss the thought before its seriousness makes you tremble.

paragraphs.original: (4.) There is the danger of eternal destruction. For the due management of this consideration, observe, — [1.] That there is such a connection between a continuance in sin and eternal destruction, that though God does resolve to deliver some from a continuance in sin that they may not be destroyed, yet he will deliver none from destruction that continue in sin; so that whilst any one lies under an abiding power of sin, the threats of destruction and everlasting separation from God are to be held out to him. So Heb. iii. 12; to which add chap. x. 38. This is the rule of God’s proceeding: If any man “depart” from him, “draw back” through unbelief, “God’s soul hath no pleasure in him;” — “that is, his indignation shall pursue him to destruction:” so evidently, Gal. vi. 8.
paragraphs.modern: (4) There is the danger of eternal destruction. To think about this rightly, observe two things. [1] Continuing in sin is inseparably connected with eternal destruction. God does rescue some people from continuing in sin, so that they will not be destroyed. But he does not rescue from destruction those who persist in sin to the end. Therefore, while someone remains under sin’s settled dominion, the warnings of destruction and everlasting separation from God must be set before that person. See Hebrews 3:12 and 10:38. God’s stated rule is that he takes no pleasure in someone who turns away from him and draws back in unbelief; his indignation pursues that course to destruction. Galatians 6:8 makes this equally clear.

paragraphs.original: [2.] That he who is so entangled, as above described, under the power of any corruption, can have at that present no clear prevailing evidence of his interest in the covenant, by the efficacy whereof he may be delivered from fear of destruction; so that destruction from the Lord may justly be a terror to him; and he may, he ought to look upon it, as that which will be the end of his course and ways. “There is no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus,” Rom. viii. 1. True; but who shall have the comfort of this assertion? who may assume it to himself? “They that walk after the Spirit, and not after the flesh.” But you will say, “Is not this to persuade men to unbelief?” I answer, No. There is a twofold judgement that a man may make of himself, — first, of his person; and, secondly, of his ways. It is the judgement of his ways, not his person, that I speak of.
paragraphs.modern: [2] Someone entangled under a corruption’s power in the way I have described cannot, at that moment, possess clear and convincing evidence that he belongs to God’s covenant—evidence strong enough to remove the fear of destruction. The Lord’s judgment may therefore rightly terrify him. He ought to recognize destruction as the destination of the course he is following. “There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Certainly. But who may take comfort in that statement? Those who walk according to the Spirit rather than the flesh. You may object, “Doesn’t this encourage unbelief?” No. A person can make two different judgments: one about his own standing, and another about the road he is taking. I am speaking about the second, not the first.

paragraphs.original: Let a man get the best evidence for his person that he can, yet to judge that an evil way will end in destruction is his duty; not to do it is atheism. I do not say, that in such a condition a man ought to throw away the evidence of his personal interest in Christ; but I say, he cannot keep them.
paragraphs.modern: Let him obtain the strongest evidence he can that he personally belongs to Christ. Even so, he must judge that an evil course ends in destruction. To deny that is to think as though there were no God. I am not saying that a person in this condition should throw away his evidence of belonging to Christ. I am saying that while he persists in this condition, he cannot securely retain that evidence and its assurance.

paragraphs.original: There is a twofold condemnation of a man’s self:— First, In respect of desert, when the soul concludes that it deserves to be cast out of the presence of God; and this is so far from a business of unbelief that it is an effect of faith. Secondly, With respect to the issue and event, when the soul concludes it shall be damned. I do not say this is the duty of any one, nor do I call them to it; but this I say, that the end of the way [wherein a man is ought by him to be concluded to be death, that he] may be provoked to fly from it. [E1] And this is another consideration that ought to dwell upon such a soul, if it desire to be freed from the entanglement of its lusts.
paragraphs.modern: There are also two ways of condemning yourself. The first concerns what you deserve: you acknowledge that your sin deserves exclusion from God’s presence. That is not unbelief; it is an effect of faith. The second predicts your final fate: you conclude that you will certainly be damned. I do not say that anyone has a duty to make that second judgment, and I am not asking anyone to do so. I am saying that a person should recognize that the path he is following leads to death, so that he will be moved to flee it. [E1] This is another consideration that should remain with anyone who desires freedom from the entanglement of sinful desires.

paragraphs.original: 3. Consider the evils of it; I mean its present evils. Danger respects what is to come; evil, what is present. Some of the many evils that attend an unmortified lust may be mentioned:—
paragraphs.modern: 3. Consider its evils—by which I mean the harm it is doing now. “Danger” concerns what may come; “evil” concerns what is already present. Here are some of the many evils that accompany a sinful desire left alive.

paragraphs.original: (1.) It grieves the holy and blessed Spirit, which is given to believers to dwell in them and abide with them. So the apostle, Eph. iv. 25–29, dehorting them from many lusts and sins, gives this as the great motive of it, verse 30, “Grieve not the Holy Spirit, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.” “Grieve not that Spirit of God,” saith he, “whereby you receive so many and so great benefits;” of which he instances in one signal and comprehensive one,— “sealing to the day of redemption.” He is grieved by it.
paragraphs.modern: (1) It grieves the holy and blessed Spirit, whom believers have received to live in them and remain with them. After warning against various sins in Ephesians 4:25–29, the apostle supplies this great motive in verse 30: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” Do not grieve the Spirit through whom you receive so many great blessings. Paul names one especially important blessing that embraces the others: being sealed for final redemption. Our sin grieves him.

paragraphs.original: As a tender and loving friend is grieved at the unkindness of his friend, of whom he hath well deserved, so is it with this tender and loving Spirit, who hath chosen our hearts for a habitation to dwell in, and there to do for us all that our souls desire. He is grieved by our harbouring his enemies, and those whom he is to destroy, in our hearts with him. “He doth not afflict willingly, nor grieve us,” Lam. iii. 33; and shall we daily grieve him? Thus is he said sometimes to be “vexed,” sometimes “grieved at his heart,” to express the greatest sense of our provocation. Now, if there be any thing of gracious ingenuity left in the soul, if it be not utterly hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, this consideration will certainly affect it. Consider who and what thou art; who the Spirit is that is grieved, what he hath done for thee, what he comes to thy soul about, what he hath already done in thee; and be ashamed.
paragraphs.modern: A tender, loving friend is hurt by the unkindness of someone to whom he has shown nothing but kindness. So it is with this tender, loving Spirit. He has chosen our hearts as his home, where he works to supply everything our souls need. Yet we grieve him by sheltering his enemies—the very sins he has come to destroy—alongside him in our hearts. “He does not willingly afflict or grieve us” (Lamentations 3:33). Shall we then grieve him every day? Scripture sometimes says that he is “vexed” or “grieved at his heart,” expressing how deeply our conduct offends him. If any gracious gratitude remains in us, and sin’s deception has not completely hardened us, this consideration will touch us. Think about who you are and who the Spirit is; what he has done for you, why he has come to you, and what he has already accomplished within you. Let that expose the shame of your ingratitude.

paragraphs.original: Among those who walk with God, there is no greater motive and incentive unto universal holiness, and the preserving of their hearts and spirits in all purity and cleanness, than this, that the blessed Spirit, who hath undertaken to dwell in them, is continually considering what they give entertainment in their hearts unto, and rejoiceth when his temple is kept undefiled.
paragraphs.modern: For those who walk with God, no motive more strongly encourages holiness in every part of life, or purity of heart and spirit, than this: the blessed Spirit who has undertaken to live in them continually observes what they welcome into their hearts. He rejoices when his temple is kept undefiled.

paragraphs.original: That was a high aggravation of the sin of Zimri, that he brought his adulteress into the congregation in the sight of Moses and the rest, who were weeping for the sins of the people, Numb. xxv. 6. And is it not a high aggravation of the countenancing of a lust, or suffering it to abide in the heart, when it is (as it must be, if we are believers) entertained under the peculiar eye and view of the Holy Ghost, taking care to preserve his tabernacle pure and holy?
paragraphs.modern: Zimri’s sin was especially outrageous because he brought his adulterous partner into the congregation in full view of Moses and the others, who were weeping over the people’s sins (Numbers 25:6). Isn’t it likewise a serious aggravation of our sin when we approve a sinful desire or let it remain in our hearts while the Holy Spirit watches? If we are believers, that is necessarily what happens: we shelter it under the very eye of the Spirit who is working to keep his dwelling pure and holy.

paragraphs.original: (2.) The Lord Jesus Christ is wounded afresh by it; his new creature in the heart is wounded; his love is foiled; his adversary gratified. As a total relinquishment of him, by the deceitfulness of sin, is the “crucifying him afresh, and the putting of him to open shame;” so every harbouring of sin that he came to destroy wounds and grieves him.
paragraphs.modern: (2) It wounds the Lord Jesus Christ afresh. It wounds the new life he has created in the heart, resists his love, and pleases his enemy. Completely abandoning Christ through sin’s deception is described as crucifying him again and exposing him to public shame. In the same way, every act of harboring the sin he came to destroy wounds and grieves him.

paragraphs.original: (3.) It will take away a man’s usefulness in his generation. His works, his endeavours, his labours, seldom receive blessing from God. If he be a preacher, God commonly blows upon his ministry, that he shall labour in the fire, and not be honoured with any success or doing any work for God; and the like may be spoken of other conditions. The world is at this day full of poor withering professors. How few are there that walk in any beauty or glory! how barren, how useless are they, for the most part! Amongst the many reasons that may be assigned of this sad estate, it may justly be feared that this is none of the least effectual, — many men harbour spirit-devouring lusts in their bosoms, that lie as worms at the root of their obedience, and corrode and weaken it day by day. All graces, all the ways and means whereby any graces may be exercised and improved, are prejudiced by this means; and as to any success, God blasts such men’s undertakings.
paragraphs.modern: (3) It diminishes a person’s usefulness in his own time. His work, efforts, and labors seldom receive God’s blessing. If he is a preacher, God commonly withholds fruit from his ministry: his labor seems to burn up, and he is not honored with success in God’s work. The same applies in other callings. The world today is full of professing Christians who are spiritually withering. How few display beauty and vitality in their lives! How barren and unhelpful so many are! There are many causes of this sad condition, but we have good reason to fear that one major cause is cherished, soul-consuming sin. These desires act like worms at the roots of obedience, eating away at it and weakening it day after day. They damage every grace and every means by which grace might be exercised and strengthened. As for success, God frustrates such people’s undertakings.

paragraphs.original: This, then, is my second direction, and it regards the opposition that is to be made to lust in respect of its habitual residence in the soul:— Keep alive upon thy heart these or the like considerations of its guilt, danger, and evil; be much in the meditation of these things; cause thy heart to dwell and abide upon them; engage thy thoughts into these considerations; let them not go off nor wander from them until they begin to have a powerful influence upon thy soul, — until they make it to tremble.
paragraphs.modern: This, then, is my second direction for opposing a sinful desire that has made its settled home in the soul: Keep these or similar considerations of its guilt, danger, and evil alive in your heart. Meditate on them often. Make your heart stay with them, and deliberately direct your thoughts toward them. Do not let your thoughts wander away before these truths begin to affect you powerfully—before their seriousness makes you tremble.

chapters.title: Chapter XI: Third–seventh directions: practical resistance

paragraphs.original: The third direction proposed: Load thy conscience with the guilt of the perplexing distemper — The ways and means whereby that may be done — The fourth direction: Vehement desire for deliverance — The fifth: Some distempers rooted deeply in men’s natural tempers — Considerations of such distempers; ways of dealing with them — The sixth direction: Occasions and advantages of sin to be prevented — The seventh direction: The first actings of sin vigorously to be opposed.
paragraphs.modern: The third direction: Make your conscience feel the guilt of the sinful inclination troubling you; how to do this. The fourth: Develop an intense desire for deliverance. The fifth: Recognize that some sinful inclinations are deeply rooted in a person’s natural temperament; how to understand and address them. The sixth: Guard against circumstances that give sin an opportunity. The seventh: Resist sin vigorously at its first movement.

paragraphs.original: This is my third direction, — Load thy conscience with the guilt of it. Not only consider that it hath a guilt, but load thy conscience with the guilt of its actual eruptions and disturbances. For the right improvement of this rule I shall give some particular directions:—
paragraphs.modern: My third direction is this: Make your conscience bear the weight of your sin’s guilt. Do not merely acknowledge in general that it is guilty. Bring home to your conscience the guilt of its actual outbreaks and the disorder it produces. Here are specific directions for applying this rule properly.

paragraphs.original: 1. Take God’s method in it, and begin with generals, and so descend to particulars:— (1.) Charge thy conscience with that guilt which appears in it from the rectitude and holiness of the law. Bring the holy law of God into thy conscience, lay thy corruption to it, pray that thou mayst be affected with it. Consider the holiness, spirituality, fiery severity, inwardness, absoluteness of the law, and see how thou canst stand before it. Be much, I say, in affecting thy conscience with the terror of the Lord in the law, and how righteous it is that every one of thy transgressions should receive a recompense of reward. Perhaps thy conscience will invent shifts and evasions to keep off the power of this consideration; — as, that the condemning power of the law doth not belong to thee, thou art set free from it, and the like; and so, though thou be not conformable to it, yet thou needest not to be so much troubled at it. But, —
paragraphs.modern: 1. Follow God’s method: begin with general truths, then apply them to your particular experience. (1) Confront your conscience with the guilt exposed by the righteousness and holiness of God’s law. Bring that holy law before your conscience, measure your corruption against it, and pray to feel the force of what it reveals. Consider the law’s holiness, its concern with spiritual and inward things, its fiery severity, and its absolute demands. How can you stand before it? Let your conscience feel the fear of the Lord that the law awakens, and acknowledge the justice of punishment for every transgression. Your conscience may invent evasions: “The law no longer has power to condemn me; I am free from it. Even though I fail to obey it, I need not be so troubled.” Answer such evasions as follows.

paragraphs.original: [1.] Tell thy conscience that it cannot manage any evidence to the purpose that thou art free from the condemning power of sin, whilst thy unmortified lust lies in thy heart; so that, perhaps, the law may make good its plea against thee for a full dominion, and then thou art a lost creature. Wherefore it is best to ponder to the utmost what it hath to say. Assuredly, he that pleads in the most secret reserve of his heart that he is freed from the condemning power of the law, thereby secretly to countenance himself in giving the least allowance unto any sin or lust, is not able, on gospel grounds, to manage any evidence, unto any tolerable spiritual security, that indeed he is in a due manner freed from what he so pretends himself to be delivered.
paragraphs.modern: [1] Tell your conscience that while you shelter an unmortified sinful desire, you cannot confidently establish that you are free from sin’s condemning power. The law may still have a valid claim to full authority over you; in that case, you are lost. You should therefore listen carefully to everything it says. Anyone who secretly uses supposed freedom from the law’s condemnation as permission to tolerate even a little sin cannot, on gospel grounds, establish any reliable spiritual assurance that he really has the freedom he claims.

paragraphs.original: [2.] Whatever be the issue, yet the law hath commission from God to seize upon transgressors wherever it find them, and so bring them before his throne, where they are to plead for themselves. This is thy present case; the law hath found thee out, and before God it will bring thee. If thou canst plead a pardon, well and good; if not, the law will do its work.
paragraphs.modern: [2] Whatever your actual standing may be, God has authorized his law to seize transgressors wherever it finds them and bring them before his throne to answer for themselves. That is your present situation: the law has exposed you and will bring you before God. If you can appeal to his pardon, well and good. If not, the law will carry out its sentence.

paragraphs.original: [3.] However, this is the proper work of the law, to discover sin in the guilt of it, to awake and humble the soul for it, to be a glass to represent sin in its colours; and if thou deniest to deal with it on this account, it is not through faith, but through the hardness of thy heart and the deceitfulness of sin. This is a door that too many professors have gone out at unto open apostasy. Such a deliverance from the law they have pretended, as that they would consult its guidance and direction no more; they would measure their sin by it no more. By little and little this principle hath insensibly, from the notion of it, proceeded to influence their practical understandings, and, having taken possession there, hath turned the will and affections loose to all manner of abominations.
paragraphs.modern: [3] In any case, the law’s proper work is to reveal sin’s guilt, awaken and humble the soul, and show sin in its true colors, as in a mirror. Refusing to engage with the law for this purpose is not an act of faith. It comes from a hard heart and sin’s deception. Too many professing Christians have passed through this doorway into open abandonment of the faith. They claimed a freedom from the law that meant they no longer needed its guidance or had to measure their sin against it. Gradually, almost unnoticed, this idea shaped their practical judgment. Once it took control there, it released their wills and desires into all kinds of evil.

paragraphs.original: By such ways, I say, then, as these, persuade thy conscience to hearken diligently to what the law speaks, in the name of the Lord, unto thee about thy lust and corruption. Oh! if thy ears be open, it will speak with a voice that shall make thee tremble, that shall cast thee to the ground, and fill thee with astonishment. If ever thou wilt mortify thy corruptions, thou must tie up thy conscience to the law, shut it from all shifts and exceptions, until it owns its guilt with a clear and thorough apprehension; so that thence, as David speaks, thy “iniquity may ever be before thee.”
paragraphs.modern: Use considerations like these to persuade your conscience to listen carefully to what the law, speaking in the Lord’s name, says about your sinful desire and corruption. If your ears are open, its voice will make you tremble, bring you low, and fill you with astonishment. To put your corruptions to death, you must hold your conscience before the law, closing off every excuse and evasion until you clearly and thoroughly acknowledge your guilt. Then, as David says, your sin will remain before you rather than being pushed out of sight.

paragraphs.original: (2.) Bring thy lust to the gospel, — not for relief, but for farther conviction of its guilt; look on Him whom thou hast pierced, and be in bitterness. Say to thy soul, “What have I done? What love, what mercy, what blood, what grace have I despised and trampled on! Is this the return I make to the Father for his love, to the Son for his blood, to the Holy Ghost for his grace? Do I thus requite the Lord? Have I defiled the heart that Christ died to wash, that the blessed Spirit hath chosen to dwell in? And can I keep myself out of the dust? What can I say to the dear Lord Jesus? How shall I hold up my head with any boldness before him? Do I account communion with him of so little value, that for this vile lust’s sake I have scarce left him any room in my heart? How shall I escape if I neglect so great salvation? In the meantime, what shall I say to the Lord? Love, mercy, grace, goodness, peace, joy, consolation, — I have despised them all, and esteemed them as a thing of nought, that I might harbour a lust in my heart.
paragraphs.modern: (2) Bring your sinful desire before the gospel—not at this point to quiet your conscience, but to see its guilt more deeply. Look at the one you have pierced, and grieve. Say to yourself: “What have I done? What love, mercy, blood, and grace have I treated with contempt and trampled underfoot! Is this how I repay the Father’s love, the Son’s blood, and the Holy Spirit’s grace? Is this my response to the Lord? Have I defiled the heart Christ died to cleanse and the blessed Spirit chose as his home? How can I refuse to humble myself in the dust? What can I say to my dear Lord Jesus? How can I lift my head confidently before him? Do I value fellowship with him so little that I have scarcely left him room in my heart because I wanted this wretched sin? How shall I escape if I neglect so great a salvation? What can I say to the Lord now? I have treated love, mercy, grace, goodness, peace, joy, and comfort as worthless, all so that I could shelter a sinful desire in my heart.

paragraphs.original: Have I obtained a view of God’s fatherly countenance, that I might behold his face and provoke him to his face? Was my soul washed, that room might be made for new defilements? Shall I endeavour to disappoint the end of the death of Christ? Shall I daily grieve that Spirit whereby I am sealed to the day of redemption?” Entertain thy conscience daily with this treaty. See if it can stand before this aggravation of its guilt. If this make it not sink in some measure and melt, I fear thy case is dangerous.
paragraphs.modern: “Was I allowed to see God’s fatherly face so that I could offend him to his face? Was my soul washed merely to make room for new filth? Shall I work against the very purpose of Christ’s death? Shall I daily grieve the Spirit by whom I am sealed for the day of redemption?” Speak to your conscience this way every day. See whether it can remain unmoved when the seriousness of its guilt is brought home like this. If these considerations do not humble and soften it at least somewhat, I fear your condition is dangerous.

paragraphs.original: 2. Descend to particulars. As under the general head of the gospel all the benefits of it are to be considered, as redemption, justification, and the like; so, in particular, consider the management of the love of them towards thine own soul, for the aggravation of the guilt of thy corruption. As, — (1.) Consider the infinite patience and forbearance of God towards thee in particular.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Now apply these truths to your own experience. Under the general heading of the gospel, consider all its blessings—redemption, justification, and the rest. Then consider how God has personally brought those blessings to you in love. That will show more clearly how serious your sin is. For example: (1) Consider God’s immense patience and forbearance toward you personally.

paragraphs.original: Consider what advantages he might have taken against thee, to have made thee a shame and a reproach in this world, and an object of wrath for ever; how thou hast dealt treacherously and falsely with him from time to time, flattered him with thy lips, but broken all promises and engagements, and that by the means of that sin thou art now in pursuit of; and yet he hath spared thee from time to time, although thou seemest boldly to have put it to the trial how long he could hold out. And wilt thou yet sin against him? wilt thou yet weary him, and make him to serve with thy corruptions?
paragraphs.modern: Think how many grounds God has had for exposing you to shame and disgrace in this world and to his wrath forever. How often you have dealt falsely and treacherously with him, flattered him with your lips, and then broken your promises and commitments—through this very sin you are now trying to destroy. Yet he has repeatedly spared you, even when you seemed determined to test how long his patience would last. Will you still sin against him? Will you still burden and weary him with your corruptions?

paragraphs.original: Hast thou not often been ready to conclude thyself, that it was utterly impossible that he should bear any longer with thee; that he would cast thee off, and be gracious no more; that all his forbearance was exhausted, and hell and wrath was even ready prepared for thee? and yet, above all thy expectation, he hath returned with visitations of love. And wilt thou yet abide in the provocation of the eyes of his glory?
paragraphs.modern: Haven’t you often thought that he could not possibly bear with you any longer—that he would cast you off and show you no more grace, that his patience had run out, and that hell and wrath were ready for you? Yet, beyond anything you expected, he came to you again in love. Will you still persist in conduct that offends him in the very sight of his glory?

paragraphs.original: (2.) How often hast thou been at the door of being hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, and by the infinite rich grace of God hast been recovered to communion with him again? Hast thou not found grace decaying; delight in duties, ordinances, prayer and meditation, vanishing; inclinations to loose careless walking, thriving; and they who before were entangled, almost beyond recovery? Hast thou not found thyself engaged in such ways, societies, companies, and that with delight, as God abhors? And wilt thou venture any more to the brink of hardness?
paragraphs.modern: (2) How often have you come close to being hardened by sin’s deception, only for God’s immensely rich grace to restore you to fellowship with him? Haven’t you found your spiritual life declining, your delight in duties, worship, prayer, and meditation disappearing, and your tendency toward careless living growing? Haven’t you seen those already entangled almost pass beyond recovery? Haven’t you found yourself enjoying conduct and company that God hates? Will you venture again to the edge of such hardness?

paragraphs.original: (3.) All God’s gracious dealings with thee, in providential dispensations, deliverances, afflictions, mercies, enjoyments, all ought here to take place. By these, I say, and the like means, load thy conscience; and leave it not until it be thoroughly affected with the guilt of thy indwelling corruption, until it is sensible of its wound, and lie in the dust before the Lord. Unless this be done to the purpose, all other endeavours are to no purpose. Whilst the conscience hath any means to alleviate the guilt of sin, the soul will never vigorously attempt its mortification.
paragraphs.modern: (3) Bring in all God’s gracious dealings with you: his ordering of your circumstances, his deliverances, afflictions, mercies, and the good things he has allowed you to enjoy. Use these and similar considerations to impress your guilt upon your conscience. Stay with them until you thoroughly feel the guilt of your indwelling corruption, recognize the wound, and humble yourself before the Lord. Unless this is done seriously, other efforts will accomplish nothing. As long as the conscience can find a way to make sin’s guilt feel lighter, the soul will never fight vigorously to put that sin to death.

paragraphs.original: Fourthly. Being thus affected with thy sin, in the next place get a constant longing, breathing after deliverance from the power of it. Suffer not thy heart one moment to be contented with thy present frame and condition. Longing desires after any thing, in things natural and civil, are of no value or consideration, any farther but as they incite and stir up the person in whom they are to a diligent use of means for the bringing about the thing aimed at. In spiritual things it is otherwise.
paragraphs.modern: Fourth: Once you have taken your sin to heart in this way, cultivate an unceasing longing to be delivered from its power. Do not let your heart settle contentedly into its present condition, even for a moment. In ordinary, earthly affairs, longing has value only insofar as it moves us to use the means needed to obtain what we desire. In spiritual matters, however, there is more to it.

paragraphs.original: Longing, breathing, and panting after deliverance is a grace in itself, that hath a mighty power to conform the soul into the likeness of the thing longed after. Hence the apostle, describing the repentance and godly sorrow of the Corinthians, reckons this as one eminent grace that was then set on work, “Vehement desire,” 2 Cor. vii. 11. And in this case of indwelling sin and the power of it, what frame doth he express himself to be in? Rom. vii. 24. His heart breaks out with longings into a most passionate expression of desire of deliverance. Now, if this be the frame of saints upon the general consideration of indwelling sin, how is it to be heightened and increased when thereunto is added the perplexing rage and power of any particular lust and corruption! Assure thyself, unless thou longest for deliverance thou shalt not have it.
paragraphs.modern: An earnest, almost breathless longing for deliverance is itself a work of grace. It powerfully shapes the soul toward the holiness it desires. That is why, when Paul describes the Corinthians’ repentance and godly sorrow, he includes “intense longing” among the outstanding graces it produced (2 Corinthians 7:11). And how does he describe his own response to indwelling sin in Romans 7:24? His heart bursts into a passionate cry for deliverance. If believers respond this way to indwelling sin generally, how much stronger should their longing become when a particular sinful desire is also raging with troubling power? Be sure of this: without longing for deliverance, you will not obtain it.

paragraphs.original: This will make the heart watchful for all opportunities of advantage against its enemy, and ready to close with any assistances that are afforded for its destruction. Strong desires are the very life of that “praying always” which is enjoined us in all conditions, and in none is more necessary than in this; they set faith and hope on work, and are the soul’s moving after the Lord. Get thy heart, then, into a panting and breathing frame; long, sigh, cry out. You know the example of David; I shall not need to insist on it.
paragraphs.modern: This longing makes the heart alert to every opportunity to gain ground against its enemy and ready to accept any help toward destroying it. Strong desires give life to the continual prayer we are commanded to practice in every situation—and never more urgently than here. They put faith and hope into action; they are the soul reaching after the Lord. So cultivate this eager longing. Long, sigh, and cry out. You know David’s example; I need not expand on it.

paragraphs.original: The fifth direction is, — Consider whether the distemper with which thou art perplexed be not rooted in thy nature, and cherished, fomented, and heightened from thy constitution. A proneness to some sins may doubtless lie in the natural temper and disposition of men. In this case consider, —
paragraphs.modern: The fifth direction: Consider whether the sinful inclination troubling you is rooted in your natural temperament and is being nourished, stirred up, or intensified by your constitution. People’s natural dispositions can certainly make them especially prone to particular sins. In that case, remember the following.

paragraphs.original: 1. This is not in the least an extenuation of the guilt of thy sin. Some, with an open profaneness, will ascribe gross enormities to their temper and disposition; and whether others may not relieve themselves from the pressing guilt of their distempers by the same consideration, I know not. It is from the fall, from the original depravation of our natures, that the fomes and nourishment of any sin abides in our natural temper. David reckons his being shapen in iniquity and conception in sin [15] as an aggravation of his following sin, not a lessening or extenuation of it. That thou art peculiarly inclined unto any sinful distemper is but a peculiar breaking out of original lust in thy nature, which should peculiarly abase and humble thee.
paragraphs.modern: 1. This does not reduce your guilt at all. Some people openly and irreverently blame terrible behavior on their temperament. Others may more quietly use the same explanation to relieve their sense of guilt. The fuel for sin found in our natural dispositions comes from the fall and the original corruption of human nature. David regards his being formed in iniquity and conceived in sin [15] as deepening the seriousness of his later sin, not excusing it. Your particular inclination toward a certain sin is a particular expression of that original corruption. It should therefore lead you to particular humility, not self-excuse.

paragraphs.original: 2. That thou hast to fix upon on this account, in reference to thy walking with God, is, that so great an advantage is given to sin, as also to Satan, by this thy temper and disposition, that without extraordinary watchfulness, care, and diligence, they will assuredly prevail against thy soul. Thousands have been on this account hurried headlong to hell, who otherwise, at least, might have gone at a more gentle, less provoking, less mischievous rate.
paragraphs.modern: 2. As you seek to walk with God, recognize how great an advantage this temperament gives both sin and Satan. Without exceptional watchfulness, care, and diligence, they will certainly gain ground against your soul. Such natural inclinations have driven thousands headlong toward hell who might otherwise at least have traveled that road less violently, less offensively, and with less harm to others.

paragraphs.original: 3. For the mortification of any distemper so rooted in the nature of a man, unto all other ways and means already named or farther to be insisted on, there is one expedient peculiarly suited; this is that of the apostle, 1 Cor. ix. 27, “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection.” The bringing of the very body into subjection is an ordinance of God tending to the mortification of sin. This gives check unto the natural root of the distemper, and withers it by taking away its fatness of soil.
paragraphs.modern: 3. Alongside all the other means already mentioned or still to come, one practice is especially appropriate for a sinful inclination rooted in a person’s constitution. Paul describes it in 1 Corinthians 9:27: “I discipline my body and bring it under control.” Bringing the body itself under discipline is a practice God has appointed to help put sin to death. It restrains the natural root of the sinful inclination, depriving it of the fertile soil in which it thrives.

paragraphs.original: Perhaps, because the Papists, men ignorant of the righteousness of Christ, the work of his Spirit, and whole business in hand, have laid the whole weight and stress of mortification in voluntary services and penances, leading to the subjection of the body, knowing indeed the true nature neither of sin nor mortification, it may, on the other side, be a temptation to some to neglect some means of humiliation which by God himself are owned and appointed.
