The bringing of the body into subjection in the case insisted on, by cutting short the natural appetite, by fasting, watching, and the like, is doubtless acceptable to God, so it be done with the ensuing limitations:—
paragraphs.modern: The Roman Catholics I am criticizing, ignorant of Christ’s righteousness, his Spirit’s work, and the true nature of this task, have put the whole weight of mortification on self-chosen religious exercises and penances that subdue the body. They have not understood either sin or its mortification. But their error may tempt others into the opposite error: neglecting practices of self-humbling that God himself has appointed. In the case we are considering, restraining bodily appetites through fasting, watchfulness, and similar disciplines is certainly acceptable to God, provided the following limits are observed.

paragraphs.original: (1.) That the outward weakening and impairing of the body be not looked upon as a thing good in itself, or that any mortification doth consist therein, — which were again to bring us under carnal ordinances; but only as a means for the end proposed, — the weakening of any distemper in its natural root and seat. A man may have leanness of body and soul together.
paragraphs.modern: (1) Do not regard bodily weakness or physical depletion as good in itself, or imagine that making the body weak is what it means to put sin to death. That would return us to a religion of merely external regulations. Bodily restraint is only a means toward the intended end: weakening the sinful inclination at its natural root. A thin body can coexist with a spiritually starved soul.

paragraphs.original: (2.) That the means whereby this is done, — namely, by fasting and watching, and the like, — be not looked on as things that in themselves, and by virtue of their own power, can produce true mortification of any sin; for if they would, sin might be mortified without any help of the Spirit in any unregenerate person in the world. They are to be looked on only as ways whereby the Spirit may, and sometimes doth, put forth strength for the accomplishing of his own work, especially in the case mentioned. Want of a right understanding and due improvement of these and the like considerations, hath raised a mortification among the Papists that may be better applied to horses and other beasts of the field than to believers.
paragraphs.modern: (2) Do not think that fasting, watchfulness, or similar practices possess a power of their own to produce genuine mortification. If they did, any unregenerate person could put sin to death without the Spirit’s help. Regard them only as means through which the Spirit may—and sometimes does—exercise his power to accomplish his work, especially in the situation just described. Failure to understand and apply these distinctions has produced among Roman Catholics a kind of “mortification” more suitable for training horses and other animals than for transforming believers.

paragraphs.original: This is the sum of what hath been spoken: When the distemper complained of seems to be rooted in the natural temper and constitution, in applying our souls to a participation of the blood and Spirit of Christ, an endeavour is to be used to give check in the way of God to the natural root of that distemper.
paragraphs.modern: Here is the point: When a troublesome sinful inclination seems rooted in your natural temperament or constitution, seek the benefits of Christ’s blood and Spirit, and at the same time use God’s appointed means to restrain that inclination at its natural root.

paragraphs.original: The sixth direction is, — Consider what occasions, what advantages thy distemper hath taken to exert and put forth itself, and watch against them all.
paragraphs.modern: The sixth direction: Identify the circumstances and opportunities your sinful inclination has used to express itself, and guard against all of them.

paragraphs.original: This is one part of that duty which our blessed Saviour recommends to his disciples under the name of watching: Mark xiii. 37, “I say unto you all, Watch;” which, in Luke xxi. 34, is, “Take heed lest your hearts be overcharged.” Watch against all eruptions of thy corruptions. I mean that duty which David professed himself to be exercised unto. “I have,” saith he, “kept myself from mine iniquity.” He watched all the ways and workings of his iniquity, to prevent them, to rise up against them. This is that which we are called unto under the name of “considering our ways.” Consider what ways, what companies, what opportunities, what studies, what businesses, what conditions, have at any time given, or do usually give, advantages to thy distempers, and set thyself heedfully against them all. Men will do this with respect unto their bodily infirmities and distempers. The seasons, the diet, the air that have proved offensive shall be avoided.
paragraphs.modern: This is part of the watchfulness our blessed Savior commands his disciples: “I say to you all, Watch” (Mark 13:37), and, “Take care that your hearts are not weighed down” (Luke 21:34). Guard against every outbreak of your corruptions. David describes this practice when he says, “I have kept myself from my iniquity.” He watched the different ways his sin worked so that he could prevent and oppose it. This is part of “considering our ways.” Examine the activities, company, opportunities, studies, occupations, and circumstances that have sometimes—or regularly—given your sinful inclination an advantage. Deliberately guard against them. People already do this for physical illnesses: they avoid the weather, food, or air that has proved harmful to them.

paragraphs.original: Are the things of the soul of less importance? Know that he that dares to dally with occasions of sin will dare to sin. He that will venture upon temptations unto wickedness will venture upon wickedness. Hazael thought he should not be so wicked as the prophet told him he would be. To convince him, the prophet tells him no more but, “Thou shalt be king of Syria.” If he will venture on temptations unto cruelty, he will be cruel. Tell a man he shall commit such and such sins, he will startle at it. If you can convince him that he will venture on such occasions and temptations of them, he will have little ground left for his confidence. Particular directions belonging to this head are many, not now to be insisted on. But because this head is of no less importance than the whole doctrine here handled, I have at large in another treatise, about entering into temptations, treated of it.
paragraphs.modern: Are matters of the soul less important? Understand this: someone willing to play with occasions for sin will also become willing to commit the sin. Someone willing to expose himself recklessly to temptation will venture into the evil itself. Hazael could not imagine becoming as wicked as the prophet said he would. To explain, the prophet needed only to say, “You will be king of Syria.” Exposed to those opportunities for cruelty, he would become cruel. Tell someone he will commit a particular sin and he may recoil. Show him that he is willing to enter the circumstances and temptations that lead to it, and he has little basis left for confidence. Many specific directions belong here, but I will not pursue them now. Since this subject is as important as the whole matter before us, I have treated it at length in another work, on entering into temptation.

paragraphs.original: The seventh direction is, — Rise mightily against the first actings of thy distemper, its first conceptions; suffer it not to get the least ground. Do not say, “Thus far it shall go, and no farther.” If it have allowance for one step, it will take another. It is impossible to fix bounds to sin. It is like water in a channel, — if it once break out, it will have its course. Its not acting is easier to be compassed than its bounding. Therefore doth James give that gradation and process of lust, chap. i. 14, 15, that we may stop at the entrance. Dost thou find thy corruption to begin to entangle thy thoughts? rise up with all thy strength against it, with no less indignation than if it had fully accomplished what it aims at. Consider what an unclean thought would have; it would have thee roll thyself in folly and filth. Ask envy what it would have; — murder and destruction is at the end of it. Set thyself against it with no less vigour than if it had utterly debased thee to wickedness.
paragraphs.modern: The seventh direction: Resist your sinful inclination forcefully at its first movement, while the thought is only beginning to form. Do not yield even a little ground. Do not say, “I will let it go this far, but no farther.” Once allowed one step, it will take another. You cannot set secure boundaries for sin. It is like water escaping a channel: once it breaks out, it follows its own course. Preventing it from starting is easier than stopping it after it has begun. James describes the stages by which desire produces sin and death so that we will stop it at the entrance (James 1:14–15). Is your corruption beginning to entangle your thoughts? Rise against it with all your strength, as firmly as if it had already achieved its full purpose. What does an impure thought ultimately want? To draw you fully into foolishness and filth. What does envy want? Its destination is murder and destruction. Oppose these first movements as vigorously as you would oppose their full, degrading outcome.

paragraphs.original: Without this course thou wilt not prevail. As sin gets ground in the affections to delight in, it gets also upon the understanding to slight it.
paragraphs.modern: Without this approach, you will not overcome. As sin gains room in your desires to be enjoyed, it also gains room in your judgment to be treated as insignificant.

chapters.title: Chapter XII: Eighth direction: meditate on God’s greatness

paragraphs.original: The eighth direction: Thoughtfulness of the excellency of the majesty of God — Our unacquaintedness with him proposed and considered.
paragraphs.modern: The eighth direction: Meditate on the excellence of God’s majesty and consider how little we actually know of him.

paragraphs.original: Eighthly, Use and exercise thyself to such meditations as may serve to fill thee at all times with self-abasement and thoughts of thine own vileness; as, —
paragraphs.modern: Eighth: Practice meditations that will keep you humble and conscious of your own sinfulness. For example, consider the following.

paragraphs.original: 1. Be much in thoughtfulness of the excellency of the majesty of God and thine infinite, inconceivable distance from him. Many thoughts of it cannot but fill thee with a sense of thine own vileness, which strikes deep at the root of any indwelling sin. When Job comes to a clear discovery of the greatness and the excellency of God, he is filled with self-abhorrence and is pressed to humiliation, Job xlii. 5, 6. And in what state doth the prophet Habakkuk affirm himself to be cast, upon the apprehension of the majesty of God? chap. iii. 16. “With God,” says Job, “is terrible majesty.” [16] Hence were the thoughts of them of old, that when they had seen God they should die. The Scripture abounds in this self-abasing consideration, comparing the men of the earth to “grasshoppers,” to “vanity,” the “dust of the balance,” in respect of God. [17] Be much in thoughts of this nature, to abase the pride of thy heart, and to keep thy soul humble within thee. There is nothing will render thee a greater indisposition to be imposed on by the deceits of sin than such a frame of heart. Think greatly of the greatness of God.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Think often about the excellence of God’s majesty and the immeasurable, unimaginable distance between him and you. Such thoughts cannot help exposing your sinfulness, and that strikes deeply at the root of indwelling sin. When Job clearly sees God’s greatness and excellence, he abhors his own sinfulness and humbles himself (Job 42:5–6). Consider also how Habakkuk describes his response to God’s majesty in Habakkuk 3:16. “With God is awesome majesty,” says the book of Job. [16] That is why people in earlier times thought they would die after seeing God. Scripture repeatedly humbles us by comparing human beings with grasshoppers, emptiness, and dust on a scale beside God. [17] Dwell on such thoughts to bring down your pride and keep your soul humble. Nothing makes the heart less receptive to sin’s deceptions than this disposition. Let your thoughts of God’s greatness be truly great.

paragraphs.original: 2. Think much of thine unacquaintedness with him. Though thou knowest enough to keep thee low and humble, yet how little a portion is it that thou knowest of him! The contemplation hereof cast that wise man into that apprehension of himself which he expresses, Prov. xxx. 2–4, “Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man. I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy. Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his Son’s name, if thou canst tell?” Labour with this also to take down the pride of thy heart. What dost thou know of God? How little a portion is it! How immense is he in his nature! Canst thou look without terror into the abyss of eternity? Thou canst not bear the rays of his glorious being.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Think often about how little you know him. You know enough to be humbled, yet how small a portion of him you know! Reflection on this led the wise man to say: “I am more uncomprehending than anyone; I lack human understanding. I have not learned wisdom or attained knowledge of the Holy One. Who has gone up to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists, wrapped the waters in a garment, or established the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his Son’s name, if you know?” (Proverbs 30:2–4). Use this thought too to bring down your pride. What do you actually know of God? How little it is! How immeasurable is his being! Can you look into the depths of eternity without trembling? You cannot bear the radiance of his glorious being.

paragraphs.original: Because I look on this consideration of great use in our walking with God, so far as it may have a consistency with that filial boldness which is given us in Jesus Christ to draw nigh to the throne of grace, I shall farther insist upon it, to give an abiding impression of it to the souls of them who desire to walk humbly with God.
paragraphs.modern: I consider this reflection extremely useful for our walk with God—provided it is held together with the confidence Christ gives us as God’s children to approach the throne of grace. I will therefore explore it further, so that it may leave a lasting impression on those who desire to walk humbly with God.

paragraphs.original: Consider, then, I say, to keep thy heart in continual awe of the majesty of God, that persons of the most high and eminent attainment, of the nearest and most familiar communion with God, do yet in this life know but a very little of him and his glory. God reveals his name to Moses, — the most glorious attributes that he hath manifested in the covenant of grace, Exod. xxxiv. 5, 6; yet all are but the “back parts” of God. All that he knows by it is but little, low, compared to the perfections of his glory. Hence it is with peculiar reference to Moses that it is said, “No man hath seen God at any time,” John i. 18; of him in comparison with Christ doth he speak, verse 17; and of him it is here said, “No man,” no, not Moses, the most eminent among them, “hath seen God at any time.” We speak much of God, can talk of him, his ways, his works, his counsels, all the day long; the truth is, we know very little of him. Our thoughts, our meditations, our expressions of him are low, many of them unworthy of his glory, none of them reaching his perfections.
paragraphs.modern: To keep your heart in continual awe of God’s majesty, remember that even the most mature believers, who enjoy the closest fellowship with him, know very little of him and his glory in this life. God revealed his name to Moses, including the glorious attributes displayed in the covenant of grace (Exodus 34:5–6). Yet this was still only a sight of God’s “back”—a very limited glimpse compared with the perfection of his glory. John’s statement that “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18) refers especially to Moses, whom the preceding verse contrasts with Christ. No one—not even Moses, the most eminent of them—has seen God in this full sense. We speak much about God and can discuss his ways, works, and purposes all day. The truth is that we know very little of him. Our thoughts, meditations, and descriptions fall short; many are unworthy of his glory, and none reaches the fullness of his perfections.

paragraphs.original: You will say that Moses was under the law when God wrapped up himself in darkness, and his mind in types and clouds and dark institutions; — under the glorious shining of the gospel, which hath brought life and immortality to light, God being revealed from his own bosom, we now know him much more clearly, and as he is; we see his face now, and not his back parts only, as Moses did.
paragraphs.modern: You may object: “Moses lived under the law, when God’s revelation was veiled in darkness, symbols, and shadowy institutions. Now the gospel shines gloriously and has brought life and immortality to light. God has been made known by the one closest to his own heart. Surely we now know him far more clearly, as he really is. We see his face, not merely his back as Moses did.”

paragraphs.original: Ans. 1. I acknowledge a vast and almost inconceivable difference between the acquaintance we now have with God, after his speaking to us by his own Son, [18] and that which the generality of the saints had under the law; for although their eyes were as good, sharp, and clear as ours, their faith and spiritual understanding not behind ours, the object as glorious unto them as unto us, yet our day is more clear than theirs was, the clouds are blown away and scattered, [19] the shadows of the night are gone and fled away, the sun is risen, and the means of sight is made more eminent and clear than formerly. Yet, —
paragraphs.modern: Answer 1. I acknowledge an immense, almost inconceivable difference between the knowledge of God available to us now that he has spoken through his own Son [18] and the knowledge generally available to believers under the law. Their eyes were as sharp and clear as ours—their faith and spiritual understanding were not inferior, and the God they saw was just as glorious. But the daylight available to us is clearer. The clouds have scattered, [19] the night’s shadows have fled, and the sun has risen. The light by which we see is clearer than before. Nevertheless, consider two further points.

paragraphs.original: 2. That peculiar sight which Moses had of God, Exod. xxxiv., was a gospel-sight, a sight of God as “gracious,” etc., and yet it is called but his “back parts;” that is, but low and mean, in comparison of his excellencies and perfections.
paragraphs.modern: 2. The particular vision Moses received in Exodus 34 was itself a gospel revelation: he saw God as gracious and merciful. Yet it is still described as seeing only God’s “back”—a limited glimpse beside the fullness of his excellence and perfection.

paragraphs.original: 3. The apostle, exalting to the utmost this glory of light above that of the law, manifesting that now the “vail” causing darkness is taken away, so that with “open” or uncovered “face” [20] we behold the glory of the Lord, tells us how: “As in a glass,” 2 Cor. iii. 18. “In a glass,” how is that? Clearly, perfectly? Alas, no! He tells you how that is, 1 Cor. xiii. 12, “We see through a glass, darkly,” saith he. It is not a telescope that helps us to see things afar off, concerning which the apostle speaks; and yet what poor helps are they! how short do we come of the truth of things notwithstanding their assistance! It is a looking-glass whereunto he alludes (where are only obscure species and images of things, and not the things themselves), and a sight therein that he compares our knowledge to.
paragraphs.modern: 3. Paul gives the fullest possible praise to the gospel’s light compared with the law. He says the darkening veil has been removed, so that with an “unveiled face” [20] we behold the Lord’s glory. But how do we behold it? “As in a mirror” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Does that mean clearly and perfectly? No. He explains elsewhere: “Now we see in a mirror, obscurely” (1 Corinthians 13:12). He is not referring to a telescope that brings distant objects nearer—even telescopes leave our knowledge very incomplete. He means a mirror, which gives us reflected images rather than the things themselves. That reflected sight is his comparison for our present knowledge.

paragraphs.original: He tells you also that all that we do see, δι’ ἐσύπτρου, “by” or “through this glass,” is in αἰνίγματι — in “a riddle,” in darkness and obscurity. And speaking of himself, who surely was much more clear-sighted than any now living, he tells us that he saw but ἐκ μέρους, — “in part.” He saw but the back parts of heavenly things, verse 12, and compares all the knowledge he had attained of God to that he had of things when he was a child, verse 11. It is a μέρος, short of the τὸ τέλειον· yea, such as καταργηθήσεται, — “it shall be destroyed,” or done away. We know what weak, feeble, uncertain notions and apprehensions children have of things of any abstruse consideration; how when they grow up with any improvements of parts and abilities, those conceptions vanish, and they are ashamed of them. It is the commendation of a child to love, honour, believe, and obey his father; but for his science and notions, his father knows his childishness and folly.
paragraphs.modern: Paul also says that what we see “through a mirror” is en ainigmati—“in a riddle,” obscurely rather than directly. Speaking of himself, whose spiritual sight was surely clearer than that of anyone now living, he says that he knew ek merous, “in part.” He saw only a limited glimpse of heavenly things (verse 12), and compares his present knowledge of God with childhood understanding (verse 11). It is merely a meros, a part, not to teleion, the complete or perfect. Indeed, it katargēthēsetai—it will be set aside. We know how weak and uncertain a child’s understanding of difficult things can be. As children mature, those early ideas disappear, and they may become embarrassed by them. A child does well to love, honor, trust, and obey his father. But the father knows how childish and mistaken many of the child’s ideas still are.

paragraphs.original: Notwithstanding all our confidence of high attainments, all our notions of God are but childish in respect of his infinite perfections. We lisp and babble, and say we know not what, for the most part, in our most accurate, as we think, conceptions and notions of God. We may love, honour, believe, and obey our Father; and therewith he accepts our childish thoughts, for they are but childish. We see but his back parts; we know but little of him.
paragraphs.modern: However advanced we think we are, our ideas of God remain childlike beside his infinite perfections. Even in what we consider our most precise thoughts about him, we largely lisp and babble, barely understanding what we say. Yet we can love, honor, trust, and obey our Father. He accepts our childlike thoughts along with that love and obedience, while knowing that they are only childlike. We see only a partial glimpse; we know very little of him.

paragraphs.original: Hence is that promise wherewith we are so often supported and comforted in our distress, “We shall see him as he is;” we shall see him “face to face;” “know as we are known; comprehend that for which we are comprehended,” 1 Cor. xiii. 12, 1 John iii. 2; and positively, “Now we see him not;” — all concluding that here we see but his back parts; not as he is, but in a dark, obscure representation; not in the perfection of his glory.
paragraphs.modern: This explains the promises that so often sustain and comfort us in distress: “We shall see him as he is”; we shall see “face to face,” “know as we are known,” and grasp that for which we have been grasped (1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2). We are also explicitly told that we do not see him now. All these statements imply that our present sight is only partial. We do not yet see him as he is, in the fullness of his glory, but through an indirect and dim representation.

paragraphs.original: The queen of Sheba had heard much of Solomon, and framed many great thoughts of his magnificence in her mind thereupon; but when she came and saw his glory, she was forced to confess that the one half of the truth had not been told her. We may suppose that we have here attained great knowledge, clear and high thoughts of God; but, alas! when he shall bring us into his presence we shall cry out, “We never knew him as he is; the thousandth part of his glory, and perfection, and blessedness, never entered into our hearts.”
paragraphs.modern: The queen of Sheba had heard much about Solomon and had formed an impressive picture of his magnificence. But when she came and saw it, she had to admit that she had not been told even half the truth. We too may imagine that we have gained great knowledge of God and formed clear, exalted thoughts about him. But when he brings us into his presence, we will cry, “We never knew him as he truly is! Not a thousandth part of his glory, perfection, and blessedness ever entered our minds.”

paragraphs.original: The apostle tells us, 1 John iii. 2, that we know not what we ourselves shall be, — what we shall find ourselves in the issue; much less will it enter into our hearts to conceive what God is, and what we shall find him to be. Consider either him who is to be known, or the way whereby we know him, and this will farther appear:—
paragraphs.modern: The apostle tells us that we do not yet know what we ourselves will be in our final condition (1 John 3:2). How much less can we now conceive what God is and what we will discover him to be! This becomes clearer when we consider both the one we seek to know and the way we presently know him.

paragraphs.original: (1.) We know so little of God, because it is God who is thus to be known, — that is, he who hath described himself to us very much by this, that we cannot know him. What else doth he intend where he calls himself invisible, incomprehensible, and the like? — that is, he whom we do not, cannot, know as he is. And our farther progress consists more in knowing what he is not, than what he is. Thus is he described to be immortal, infinite, — that is, he is not, as we are, mortal, finite, and limited.
paragraphs.modern: (1) We know so little because the one to be known is God. Much of his own description of himself emphasizes that we cannot fully comprehend him. What else is meant by calling him invisible and incomprehensible? We do not—and cannot—know him fully as he is. Often our progress consists more in understanding what he is not than in comprehending what he is. We call him immortal and infinite: unlike us, he is not mortal, finite, or limited.

paragraphs.original: Hence is that glorious description of him, 1 Tim. vi. 16, “Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see.” His light is such as no creature can approach unto. He is not seen, not because he cannot be seen, but because we cannot bear the sight of him. The light of God, in whom is no darkness, forbids all access to him by any creature whatever. We who cannot behold the sun in its glory are too weak to bear the beams of infinite brightness. On this consideration, as was said, the wise man professeth himself “a very beast, and not to have the understanding of a man,” Prov. xxx. 2; — that is, he knew nothing in comparison of God; so that he seemed to have lost all his understanding when once he came to the consideration of him, his work, and his ways.
paragraphs.modern: That is the force of the glorious description in 1 Timothy 6:16: “He alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see.” No creature can approach that light by its own capacity. The problem is not a lack of glory to be seen, but our inability to bear the sight. God’s light, entirely without darkness, exceeds every creature’s capacity to approach it. We cannot even look directly at the sun in its brilliance; how could we bear infinite brightness? That is why the wise man calls himself like an uncomprehending animal, lacking human understanding (Proverbs 30:2). Compared with God, he knew so little that when he considered God’s being, works, and ways, his understanding seemed to disappear.

paragraphs.original: In this consideration let our souls descend to some particulars:— [1.] For the being of God; we are so far from a knowledge of it, so as to be able to instruct one another therein by words and expressions of it, as that to frame any conceptions in our mind, with such species and impressions of things as we receive the knowledge of all other things by, is to make an idol to ourselves, and so to worship a god of our own making, and not the God that made us. We may as well and as lawfully hew him out of wood or stone as form him a being in our minds, suited to our apprehensions. The utmost of the best of our thoughts of the being of God is, that we can have no thoughts of it. Our knowledge of a being is but low when it mounts no higher but only to know that we know it not.
paragraphs.modern: Let us consider some particulars. [1] We are far from comprehending God’s essential being well enough to describe it fully to one another. If we construct a mental picture of him from the images and impressions through which we know created things, we make an idol. We then worship a god we have made rather than the God who made us. Shaping God in our minds to fit our own capacities is no more legitimate than carving him from wood or stone. Our best thinking about God’s essential being brings us to the recognition that we cannot form an adequate conception of it. Knowledge is certainly limited when its highest achievement is recognizing that it does not comprehend its object.

paragraphs.original: [2.] There be some things of God which he himself hath taught us to speak of, and to regulate our expressions of them; but when we have so done, we see not the things themselves; we know them not. To believe and admire is all that we attain to. We profess, as we are taught, that God is infinite, omnipotent, eternal; and we know what disputes and notions there are about omnipresence, immensity, infiniteness, and eternity. We have, I say, words and notions about these things; but as to the things themselves what do we know? what do we comprehend of them? Can the mind of man do any more but swallow itself up in an infinite abyss, which is as nothing; give itself up to what it cannot conceive, much less express? Is not our understanding “brutish” in the contemplation of such things, and is as if it were not? Yea, the perfection of our understanding is, not to understand, and to rest there.
paragraphs.modern: [2] God has taught us to speak about certain truths concerning him, and has guided the language we should use. Yet using those words does not give us direct sight or full comprehension of the realities themselves. We can believe and wonder. We confess, as he has taught us, that God is infinite, almighty, and eternal. We are familiar with discussions about his presence everywhere, his immeasurable being, infinity, and eternity. But having words and concepts is not the same as comprehending the realities. What do we actually grasp of them? The human mind seems lost in an infinite depth, surrendering before what it cannot conceive, much less express. Doesn’t our understanding appear almost uncomprehending, as though it were nothing, before such realities? Here its highest wisdom is to recognize its inability to comprehend and to rest in that acknowledgment.

paragraphs.original: They are but the back parts of eternity and infiniteness that we have a glimpse of. What shall I say of the Trinity, or the subsistence of distinct persons in the same individual essence, — a mystery by many denied, because by none understood, — a mystery, whose every letter is mysterious? Who can declare the generation of the Son, the procession of the Spirit, or the difference of the one from the other? But I shall not farther instance in particulars. That infinite and inconceivable distance that is between him and us keeps us in the dark as to any sight of his face or clear apprehension of his perfections. We know him rather by what he does than by what he is, — by his doing us good than by his essential goodness; and how little a portion of him, as Job speaks, is hereby discovered!
paragraphs.modern: We glimpse only the edges of eternity and infinity. And what can I say about the Trinity—the distinct persons existing in the one undivided divine being? Many deny this mystery because no one can fully comprehend it, though every part of it is mysterious. Who can explain the Son’s eternal generation, the Spirit’s procession, or precisely how the two differ? I will not multiply examples. The immeasurable, unimaginable distance between God and us prevents a direct vision of his face or a complete understanding of his perfections. We know him more through what he does than through comprehending what he is—through his goodness to us rather than by grasping goodness as it exists in his own being. As Job says, how small a portion of him this reveals!

paragraphs.original: (2.) We know little of God, because it is faith alone whereby here we know him. I shall not now discourse about the remaining impressions on the hearts of all men by nature that there is a God, nor what they may rationally be taught concerning that God from the works of his creation and providence, which they see and behold. It is confessedly, and that upon the woful experience of all ages, so weak, low, dark, confused, that none ever on that account glorified God as they ought, but, notwithstanding all their knowledge of God, were indeed “without God in the world.”
paragraphs.modern: (2) We know little of God because our knowledge of him in this life comes through faith. I will not discuss here the natural awareness of God that remains in every human heart, or what people can reason about him from the creation and providence they observe. The sad experience of every age shows how weak, limited, dark, and confused that knowledge is. No one, on that basis alone, has glorified God as he ought. Despite their knowledge, people have remained “without God in the world.”

paragraphs.original: The chief, and, upon the matter, almost only acquaintance we have with God, and his dispensations of himself, is by faith. “He that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him,” Heb. xi. 6. Our knowledge of him and his rewarding (the bottom of our obedience or coming to him), is believing. “We walk by faith, and not by sight,” 2 Cor. v. 7; — Διὰ πίστεως οὐ διὰ εἴδους· by faith, and so by faith as not to have any express idea, image, or species of that which we believe. Faith is all the argument we have of “things not seen,” Heb. xi. 1. I might here insist upon the nature of it; and from all its concomitants and concernments manifest that we know but the back parts of what we know by faith only.
paragraphs.modern: Our principal—and for this purpose virtually our only—acquaintance with God and his self-disclosure is through faith. “Whoever comes to God must believe that he exists and rewards those who earnestly seek him” (Hebrews 11:6). Believing is how we know him and his promised reward, the foundation of approaching and obeying him. “We walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). The Greek, dia pisteōs ou dia eidous, contrasts faith with visible appearance: we believe without possessing a direct image or sight of the reality believed. Faith is our assurance concerning “things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). I could examine faith’s nature and related features at length to show that knowledge gained by faith is still only a partial glimpse of its object.

paragraphs.original: As to its rise, it is built purely upon the testimony of Him whom we have not seen: as the apostle speaks, “How can ye love him whom ye have not seen?” — that is, whom you know not but by faith that he is. Faith receives all upon his testimony, whom it receives to be only on his own testimony. As to its nature, it is an assent upon testimony, not an evidence upon demonstration; and the object of it is, as was said before, above us. Hence our faith, as was formerly observed, is called a “seeing darkly, as in a glass.” All that we know this way (and all that we know of God we know this way) is but low, and dark, and obscure.
paragraphs.modern: Faith begins with the testimony of the one we have not seen. As the apostle’s words about loving the unseen God imply, we know his reality through faith rather than sight. Faith accepts everything on God’s testimony, and accepts God himself on that testimony. By its nature, faith assents to trustworthy testimony; it does not possess direct, demonstrated sight of its object. And that object, as we have seen, is above our comprehension. This is why faith’s knowledge is compared to seeing obscurely in a mirror. Everything we know of God in this way remains limited and indirect.

paragraphs.original: But you will say, “All this is true, but yet it is only so to them that know not God, perhaps, as he is revealed in Jesus Christ; with them who do so it is otherwise. It is true, ‘No man hath seen God at any time,’ but ‘the only-begotten Son, he hath revealed him,’ John i. 18; and ‘the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true,’ 1 John v. 20. The illumination of ‘the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God,’ shineth upon believers, 2 Cor. iv. 4; yea, and ‘God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, shines into their hearts, to give them the knowledge of his glory in the face of his Son,’ verse 6. So that ‘though we were darkness,’ yet we are now ‘light in the Lord,’ Eph. v. 8. And the apostle says, ‘We all with open face behold the glory of the Lord,’ 2 Cor. iii. 18; and we are now so far from being in such darkness, or at such a distance from God, that ‘our communion and fellowship is with the Father and with his Son,’ 1 John i. 3. The light of the gospel whereby now God is revealed is glorious; not a star, but the sun in his beauty is risen upon us, and the vail is taken from our faces. So that though unbelievers, yea, and perhaps some weak believers, may be in some darkness, yet those of any growth or considerable attainments have a clear sight and view of the face of God in Jesus Christ.”
paragraphs.modern: But you may object: “Perhaps all this applies only to people who do not know God as he is revealed in Jesus Christ. Those who do know him through Christ are different. Certainly ‘no one has ever seen God,’ but ‘the only-begotten Son has made him known’ (John 1:18). ‘The Son of God has come and given us understanding so that we may know the one who is true’ (1 John 5:20). Believers receive the light of ‘the glorious gospel of Christ, who is God’s image’ (2 Corinthians 4:4). The God who commanded light to shine out of darkness shines in their hearts to give them knowledge of his glory in his Son’s face (verse 6). Once we were darkness, but now we are ‘light in the Lord’ (Ephesians 5:8). ‘With unveiled faces we all behold the Lord’s glory’ (2 Corinthians 3:18). Far from remaining distant from God in darkness, ‘our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son’ (1 John 1:3). The gospel’s light is glorious. Not merely a star but the beautiful sun itself has risen upon us, and the veil has been removed. Unbelievers, and perhaps weak believers, may remain somewhat in darkness; but mature believers surely see God’s face clearly in Jesus Christ.”

paragraphs.original: To which I answer, — [1.] The truth is, we all of us know enough of him to love him more than we do, to delight in him and serve him, believe him, obey him, put our trust in him, above all that we have hitherto attained. Our darkness and weakness is no plea for our negligence and disobedience. Who is it that hath walked up to the knowledge that he hath had of the perfections, excellencies, and will of God? God’s end in giving us any knowledge of himself here is that we may “glorify him as God;” that is, love him, serve him, believe and obey him, — give him all the honour and glory that is due from poor sinful creatures to a sin-pardoning God and Creator. We must all acknowledge that we were never thoroughly transformed into the image of that knowledge which we have had. And had we used our talents well, we might have been trusted with more.
paragraphs.modern: I answer as follows. [1] We certainly all know enough of God to love, enjoy, serve, believe, obey, and trust him far more than we do. Our limited understanding is no excuse for negligence or disobedience. Who has actually lived up to his knowledge of God’s perfections, excellence, and will? God gives us knowledge of himself so that we will glorify him as God: love, serve, believe, and obey him, giving our sin-forgiving Creator the honor that sinful creatures owe him. We must all admit that our lives have never been fully transformed to match the knowledge we already possess. Had we used what he entrusted to us well, we might have received more.

paragraphs.original: [2.] Comparatively, that knowledge which we have of God by the revelation of Jesus Christ in the gospel is exceeding eminent and glorious. It is so in comparison of any knowledge of God that might otherwise be attained, or was delivered in the law under the Old Testament, which had but the shadow of good things, not the express image of them; this the apostle pursues at large, 2 Cor. iii. Christ hath now in these last days revealed the Father from his own bosom, declared his name, made known his mind, will, and counsel in a far more clear, eminent, distinct manner than he did formerly, whilst he kept his people under the pedagogy of the law; and this is that which, for the most part, is intended in the places before mentioned. The clear, perspicuous delivery and declaration of God and his will in the gospel is expressly exalted in comparison of any other way of revelation of himself.
paragraphs.modern: [2] Comparatively speaking, the gospel’s revelation of God through Jesus Christ is extraordinarily clear and glorious. It surpasses any knowledge otherwise available, including that given under the Old Testament law, which contained shadows of the good things to come rather than their full representation. Paul develops this comparison in 2 Corinthians 3. In these last days Christ has revealed the Father whom he knows intimately, declared his name, and made his mind, will, and purposes known much more clearly and distinctly than when God kept his people under the law’s tutelage. This comparative superiority is chiefly what the passages just quoted mean. They praise the gospel’s clear revelation of God and his will over other forms of revelation.

paragraphs.original: [3.] The difference between believers and unbelievers as to knowledge is not so much in the matter of their knowledge as in the manner of knowing. Unbelievers, some of them, may know more and be able to say more of God, his perfections, and his will, than many believers; but they know nothing as they ought, nothing in a right manner, nothing spiritually and savingly, nothing with a holy, heavenly light. The excellency of a believer is, not that he hath a large apprehension of things, but that what he doth apprehend, which perhaps may be very little, he sees it in the light of the Spirit of God, in a saving, soul-transforming light; and this is that which gives us communion with God, and not prying thoughts or curious-raised notions.
paragraphs.modern: [3] The difference between believers and unbelievers is not chiefly how much they know, but how they know it. Some unbelievers know more facts and can say more about God, his perfections, and his will than many believers can. Yet they do not know these things rightly—spiritually, savingly, or in a holy light. A believer’s advantage is not necessarily extensive knowledge. It is that whatever he understands, however little, he sees through the light of God’s Spirit, a light that saves and transforms the soul. This gives us fellowship with God, not speculative curiosity or elaborate intellectual notions.

paragraphs.original: [4.] Jesus Christ by his word and Spirit reveals to the hearts of all his, God as a Father, as a God in covenant, as a rewarder, every way sufficiently to teach us to obey him here, and to lead us to his bosom, to lie down there in the fruition of him to eternity. But yet now,
paragraphs.modern: [4] Through his word and Spirit, Jesus Christ reveals God to all his people as their Father, their covenant God, and the one who rewards those who seek him. This revelation is fully sufficient to teach us obedience now and to lead us into his embrace, where we will enjoy him forever. Nevertheless, our present knowledge remains limited.

paragraphs.original: [5.] Notwithstanding all this, it is but a little portion we know of him; we see but his back parts. For, — 1st. The intendment of all gospel revelation is, not to unvail God’s essential glory, that we should see him as he is, but merely to declare so much of him as he knows sufficient to be a bottom of our faith, love, obedience, and coming to him, — that is, of the faith which here he expects from us; such services as beseem poor creatures in the midst of temptations. But when he calls us to eternal admiration and contemplation, without interruption, he will make a new manner of discovery of himself, and the whole shape of things, as it now lies before us, will depart as a shadow.
paragraphs.modern: [5] Despite all this, we know only a small portion of him; we see only a partial glimpse. There are two reasons. First, gospel revelation does not aim to unveil God’s essential glory so that we see him directly as he is. It reveals what he knows is sufficient to ground the faith, love, obedience, and approach to him that he expects from us in this life—the service appropriate to frail creatures surrounded by temptations. When he calls us into uninterrupted, eternal contemplation and wonder, he will reveal himself in a new way. The whole form of things as we now experience them will pass away like a shadow.

paragraphs.original: 2dly. We are dull and slow of heart to receive the things that are in the word revealed; God, by our infirmity and weakness, keeping us in continual dependence on him for teachings and revelations of himself out of his word, never in this world bringing any soul to the utmost of what is from the word to be made out and discovered: so that although the way of revelation in the gospel be clear and evident, yet we know little of the things themselves that are revealed.
paragraphs.modern: Second, we are slow and dull in receiving what the word reveals. Through our weakness, God keeps us continually dependent on him to teach us and disclose himself through Scripture. In this world, he never brings anyone to the full extent of everything that could be understood from his word. Therefore, although the gospel is a clear form of revelation, our grasp of the realities it reveals remains small.

paragraphs.original: Let us, then, revive the use and intendment of this consideration: Will not a due apprehension of this inconceivable greatness of God, and that infinite distance wherein we stand from him, fill the soul with a holy and awful fear of him, so as to keep it in a frame unsuited to the thriving or flourishing of any lust whatever? Let the soul be continually wonted to reverential thoughts of God’s greatness and omnipresence, and it will be much upon its watch as to any undue deportments. Consider him with whom you have to do, — even “our God is a consuming fire;” and in your greatest abashments at his presence and eye, know that your very nature is too narrow to bear apprehensions suitable to his essential glory.
paragraphs.modern: Let us return to the practical purpose of this reflection. Won’t a proper sense of God’s inconceivable greatness and our immeasurable distance from him fill us with holy reverence and awe? Won’t it create a disposition in which sinful desires find it difficult to flourish? Accustom your soul to reverent thoughts of God’s greatness and presence everywhere, and you will become much more watchful over your conduct. Consider the one with whom you are dealing: “Our God is a consuming fire.” Even when you feel most humbled before his presence and searching gaze, remember that your finite nature cannot contain a sense of awe fully proportionate to his essential glory.

paragraphs.original: [16] Job xxxvii. 22. [17] Isa. xl. 12–25. [18] Heb. i. 2. [19] Cant. iv. 6. [20] Ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπω.
paragraphs.modern: [16] Job 37:22. [17] Isaiah 40:12–25. [18] Hebrews 1:2. [19] Song of Songs 4:6. [20] Anakekalymmenō prosōpō: “with an unveiled face.” The Greek phrase describes a face from which the covering has been removed.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII: Ninth direction: receive God’s peace, not self-made peace

paragraphs.original: The ninth direction: When the heart is disquieted by sin, speak no peace to it until God speak it — Peace, without detestation of sin, unsound; so is peace measured out unto ourselves — How we may know when we measure our peace unto ourselves — Directions as to that inquiry — The vanity of speaking peace slightly; also of doing it on one singular account, not universally.
paragraphs.modern: The ninth direction: When sin troubles your heart, do not declare yourself at peace before God speaks peace. Peace without hatred of sin is false, as is peace we manufacture for ourselves. How to recognize self-made peace. Why superficial reassurance fails, and why we cannot seek peace about one sin while ignoring others.

paragraphs.original: Ninethly, In case God disquiet the heart about the guilt of its distempers, either in respect of its root and indwelling, or in respect of any eruptions of it, take heed thou speakest not peace to thyself before God speaks it; but hearken what he says to thy soul. This is our next direction, without the observation whereof the heart will be exceedingly exposed to the deceitfulness of sin.
paragraphs.modern: Ninth: When God troubles your heart over the guilt of a sinful inclination—whether its inward presence or its outward outbreaks—be careful not to reassure yourself before God speaks peace. Listen for what he says to your soul. Unless you follow this direction, your heart will remain dangerously exposed to sin’s deception.

paragraphs.original: This is a business of great importance. It is a sad thing for a man to deceive his own soul herein. All the warnings God gives us, in tenderness to our souls, to try and examine ourselves, do tend to the preventing of this great evil of speaking peace groundlessly to ourselves; which is upon the issue to bless ourselves, in an opposition to God. It is not my business to insist upon the danger of it, but to help believers to prevent it, and to let them know when they do so.
paragraphs.modern: This is extremely important. It is tragic to deceive your own soul here. God’s tender warnings to test and examine ourselves are intended to prevent this serious evil: declaring ourselves at peace without good grounds. In the end, that means blessing ourselves in opposition to God. My purpose here is not to dwell on the danger, but to help believers avoid it and recognize when they are doing it.

paragraphs.original: To manage this direction aright observe, — 1. That as it is the great prerogative and sovereignty of God to give grace to whom he pleases (“He hath mercy on whom he will,” Rom. ix. 18; and among all the sons of men, he calls whom he will, and sanctifies whom he will), so among those so called and justified, and whom he will save, he yet reserves this privilege to himself, to speak peace to whom he pleaseth, and in what degree he pleaseth, even amongst them on whom he hath bestowed grace. He is the “God of all consolation,” in an especial manner in his dealing with believers; that is, of the good things that he keeps locked up in his family, and gives out of it to all his children at his pleasure. This the Lord insists on, Isa. lvii. 16–18. It is the case under consideration that is there insisted on. When God says he will heal their breaches and disconsolations, he assumes this privilege to himself in an especial manner: “I create it,” verse 19; — “Even in respect of these poor wounded creatures I create it, and according to my sovereignty make it out as I please.”
paragraphs.modern: To apply this direction rightly, remember two things. 1. God sovereignly gives grace to whom he pleases: “He has mercy on whom he wills” (Romans 9:18). Among humanity he calls and sanctifies whom he chooses. Likewise, among those he has called and justified and will finally save, he reserves the right to give an experience of peace when and in whatever measure he pleases. He is especially “the God of all comfort” in his dealings with believers. Comfort belongs among the good things of his household, which he distributes to his children as he chooses. Isaiah 57:16–18 addresses precisely the situation we are considering. When God promises to heal his people’s wounds and distress, he expressly claims the work as his own: “I create it” (verse 19). In effect: “For these wounded people, I myself create peace and sovereignly give it as I choose.”

paragraphs.original: Hence, as it is with the collation of grace in reference to them that are in the state of nature, — God doth it in great curiosity, and his proceedings therein in taking and leaving, as to outward appearances, quite besides and contrary ofttimes to all probable expectations; so is it in his communications of peace and joy in reference unto them that are in the state of grace, — he gives them out ofttimes quite besides our expectation, as to any appearing grounds of his dispensations.
paragraphs.modern: When God grants grace to people in their natural, unconverted condition, his choices display a wisdom that often runs contrary to every reasonable expectation based on outward appearances. The same is true when he gives peace and joy to those already living in grace. Judging from the circumstances we can see, his gifts often come in ways we would not have expected.

paragraphs.original: 2. As God creates it for whom he pleaseth, so it is the prerogative of Christ to speak it home to the conscience. Speaking to the church of Laodicea, who had healed her wounds falsely, and spoke peace to herself when she ought not, he takes to himself that title, “I am the Amen, the faithful Witness,” Rev. iii. 14. He bears testimony concerning our condition as it is indeed. We may possibly mistake, and trouble ourselves in vain, or flatter ourselves upon false grounds, but he is the “Amen, the faithful Witness;” and what he speaks of our state and condition, that it is indeed. Isa. xi. 3, He is said not to “judge after the sight of his eyes,” — not according to any outward appearance, or any thing that may be subject to a mistake, as we are apt to do; but he shall judge and determine every cause as it is indeed.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Just as God creates peace for whom he chooses, Christ alone has authority to bring that peace home to the conscience. Addressing Laodicea, a church that had falsely healed its own wounds and reassured itself when it should not have, he calls himself “the Amen, the faithful Witness” (Revelation 3:14). He testifies to our actual condition. We may mistakenly trouble ourselves without reason, or flatter ourselves on false grounds. But he is the faithful Witness; what he says about us is true. Isaiah 11:3 says that he does not judge merely by what appears before his eyes. Unlike us, he does not base his judgment on misleading appearances. He judges every matter as it truly is.

paragraphs.original: Take these two previous observations, and I shall give some rules whereby men may know whether God speaks peace to them, or whether they speak peace to themselves only:—
paragraphs.modern: With these two observations in mind, here are some rules for distinguishing peace spoken by God from reassurance we merely give ourselves.

paragraphs.original: 1. Men certainly speak peace to themselves when their so doing is not attended with the greatest detestation imaginable of that sin in reference whereunto they do speak peace to themselves, and abhorrency of themselves for it. When men are wounded by sin, disquieted and perplexed, and knowing that there is no remedy for them but only in the mercies of God, through the blood of Christ, do therefore look to him, and to the promises of the covenant in him, and thereupon quiet their hearts that it shall be well with them, and that God will be exalted, that he may be gracious to them, and yet their souls are not wrought to the greatest detestation of the sin or sins upon the account whereof they are disquieted, — this is to heal themselves, and not to be healed of God. This is but a great and strong wind, that the Lord is nigh unto, but the Lord is not in the wind. When men do truly “look upon Christ whom they have pierced,” without which there is no healing or peace, they will “mourn,” Zech. xii. 10; they will mourn for him, even upon this account, and detest the sin that pierced him. When we go to Christ for healing, faith eyes him peculiarly as one pierced.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Peace is certainly self-made when it does not come with a deep hatred of the sin in question and grief over our own guilt in committing it. People may be wounded, troubled, and confused by sin. Knowing that their only remedy is God’s mercy through Christ’s blood, they may look to him and to his covenant promises, then reassure themselves that all will be well and that God will show them grace. But if this does not produce a deep hatred of the sins that troubled them, they are healing themselves rather than being healed by God. It is like the great wind near which the Lord was present, but in which he was not. Those who truly look upon Christ whom they have pierced will mourn (Zechariah 12:10). They will grieve over him and hate the sin that pierced him. Without that looking to Christ there is no healing or peace, and when faith seeks healing, it looks particularly at him as the one pierced for sin.

paragraphs.original: Faith takes several views of Christ, according to the occasions of address to him and communion with him that it hath. Sometimes it views his holiness, sometimes his power, sometimes his love, [sometimes] his favour with his Father. And when it goes for healing and peace, it looks especially on the blood of the covenant, on his sufferings; for “with his stripes we are healed, and the chastisement of our peace was upon him,” Isa. liii. 5. When we look for healing, his stripes are to be eyed, — not in the outward story of them, which is the course of popish devotionists, but in the love, kindness, mystery, and design of the cross; and when we look for peace, his chastisements must be in our eye. Now this, I say, if it be done according to the mind of God, and in the strength of that Spirit which is poured out on believers, it will beget a detestation of that sin or sins for which healing and peace is sought.
paragraphs.modern: Faith looks at different aspects of Christ according to the reason we approach him and seek fellowship with him. Sometimes it considers his holiness, sometimes his power, his love, or his favor with the Father. When seeking healing and peace, faith looks especially to his covenant blood and sufferings: “By his wounds we are healed, and the punishment that brought us peace was upon him” (Isaiah 53:5). We look at his wounds not merely as an outward story of suffering, as in the Roman Catholic devotion I am opposing, but with attention to the love, kindness, mystery, and purpose of the cross. In seeking peace, we consider the punishment he bore. When this is done according to God’s will and through the Spirit given to believers, it produces hatred of the sins for which we seek healing and peace.

paragraphs.original: So Ezek. xvi. 60, 61, “Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant.” And what then? “Then thou shalt remember thy ways, and be ashamed.” When God comes home to speak peace in a sure covenant of it, it fills the soul with shame for all the ways whereby it hath been alienated from him.
paragraphs.modern: Ezekiel 16:60–61 says, “I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth and establish an everlasting covenant with you.” What follows? “Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed.” When God brings home the peace of his secure covenant, the soul becomes ashamed of the ways it has turned away from him.

paragraphs.original: And one of the things that the apostle mentions as attending that godly sorrow which is accompanied with repentance unto salvation, never to be repented of, is revenge: “Yea, what revenge!” 2 Cor. vii. 11. They reflected on their miscarriages with indignation and revenge, for their folly in them. When Job comes up to a thorough healing, he cries, “Now I abhor myself,” Job xlii. 6; and until he did so, he had no abiding peace. He might perhaps have made up himself with that doctrine of free grace which was so excellently preached by Elihu, chap. xxxiii. from verse 14 unto 30; but he had then but skinned his wounds: he must come to self-abhorrency if he come to healing.
paragraphs.modern: Among the effects of godly sorrow that produces saving repentance without regret, Paul names a determination to see wrong put right: “What readiness to deal with the wrong!” (2 Corinthians 7:11). The Corinthians looked back on their failures with indignation and a resolve to oppose their own foolishness. When Job comes to thorough healing, he says, “Now I abhor myself” (Job 42:6). Until then, he had no lasting peace. He might have quieted himself with the doctrine of free grace that Elihu preached so beautifully in Job 33:14–30. But that would only have covered the surface of his wounds. Real healing required a humbled rejection of his own sinful response.

paragraphs.original: So was it with those in Ps. lxxviii. 33–35, in their great trouble and perplexity, for and upon the account of sin. I doubt not but upon the address they made to God in Christ (for that so they did is evident from the titles they gave him; they call him their Rock and their Redeemer, two words everywhere pointing out the Lord Christ), they spake peace to themselves; but was it sound and abiding? No; it passed away as the early dew. God speaks not one word of peace to their souls. But why had they not peace? Why, because in their address to God, they flattered him. But how doth that appear? Verse 37: “Their heart was not right with him, neither were they steadfast;” they had not a detestation nor relinquishment of that sin in reference whereunto they spake peace to themselves.
paragraphs.modern: The same problem appears in Psalm 78:33–35. The people were deeply troubled because of sin and approached God in Christ—as their names for him, “Rock” and “Redeemer,” indicate, since these titles point to Christ. I have no doubt that they reassured themselves afterward. But was their peace sound and lasting? No; it vanished like morning dew. God had spoken no peace to their souls. Why not? Because their appeal to him was flattery. Verse 37 explains: “Their heart was not right with him, and they were not steadfast.” They had neither hated nor abandoned the sin about which they reassured themselves.

paragraphs.original: Let a man make what application he will for healing and peace, let him do it to the true Physician, let him do it the right way, let him quiet his heart in the promises of the covenant; yet, when peace is spoken, if it be not attended with the detestation and abhorrency of that sin which was the wound and caused the disquietment, this is no peace of God’s creating, but of our own purchasing. It is but a skinning over the wound, whilst the core lies at the bottom, which will putrefy, and corrupt, and corrode, until it break out again with noisomeness, vexation, and danger.
paragraphs.modern: Someone may make every outwardly appropriate appeal for healing and peace, turn to the true Physician, and quiet his heart with covenant promises. Yet if that peace is not accompanied by hatred of the sin that caused the wound and distress, it is peace he has supplied for himself, not peace God has created. It is merely skin growing over a wound while infection remains underneath. The infection will fester and spread until it breaks out again, painfully and dangerously.

paragraphs.original: Let not poor souls that walk in such a path as this, who are more sensible of the trouble of sin than of the pollution of uncleanness that attends it; who address themselves for mercy, yea, to the Lord in Christ they address themselves for mercy, but yet will keep the sweet morsel of their sin under their tongue; — let them, I say, never think to have true and solid peace.
paragraphs.modern: Some troubled people are more aware of sin’s unpleasant consequences than of its defilement. They seek mercy—even from the Lord through Christ—while still savoring the sweetness of their sin. They must not expect genuine, settled peace while continuing on that path.

paragraphs.original: For instance, thou findest thy heart running out after the world, and it disturbs thee in thy communion with God; the Spirit speaks expressly to thee, — “He that loveth the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” [21] This puts thee on dealing with God in Christ for the healing of thy soul, the quieting of thy conscience; but yet, withal, a thorough detestation of the evil itself abides not upon thee; yea, perhaps that is liked well enough, but only in respect of the consequences of it. Perhaps thou mayst be saved, yet as through fire, and God will have some work with thee before he hath done; but thou wilt have little peace in this life, — thou wilt be sick and fainting all thy days, Isa. lvii. 17.
paragraphs.modern: For example, you find your heart pursuing the world, and this interferes with your fellowship with God. The Spirit speaks plainly: “If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him.” [21] You therefore turn to God through Christ to heal your soul and quiet your conscience. Yet no lasting hatred of worldliness develops. Perhaps you still like it well enough, apart from its consequences. You may ultimately be saved, as through fire, but God has more work to do with you. Meanwhile you will have little peace, remaining spiritually sick and faint throughout your days. Consider Isaiah 57:17.

paragraphs.original: This is a deceit that lies at the root of the peace of many professors and wastes it. They deal with all their strength about mercy and pardon, and seem to have great communion with God in their so doing; they lie before him, bewail their sins and follies, that any one would think, yea, they think themselves, that surely they and their sins are now parted; and so receive in mercy that satisfies their hearts for a little season. But when a thorough search comes to be made, there hath been some secret reserve for the folly or follies treated about, — at least, there hath not been that thorough abhorrency of it which is necessary; and their whole peace is quickly discovered to be weak and rotten, scarce abiding any longer than the words of begging it are in their mouths.
paragraphs.modern: This deception underlies and destroys the peace of many professing Christians. They plead earnestly for mercy and pardon, seemingly enjoying deep fellowship with God. They bow before him and lament their sins so intensely that others—and they themselves—assume they have surely parted with them. They experience a sense of mercy that satisfies them briefly. But closer examination reveals a secret attachment to the very sins they confessed, or at least a lack of the thorough hatred of them that is necessary. Their peace soon proves weak and unsound, scarcely lasting longer than the prayer in which they asked for it.

paragraphs.original: 2. When men measure out peace to themselves upon the conclusions that their convictions and rational principles will carry them out unto, this is a false peace, and will not abide. I shall a little explain what I mean hereby. A man hath got a wound by sin; he hath a conviction of some sin upon his conscience; he hath not walked uprightly as becometh the gospel; all is not well and right between God and his soul. He considers now what is to be done. Light he hath, and knows what path he must take, and how his soul hath been formerly healed. Considering that the promises of God are the outward means of application for the healing of his sores and quieting of his heart, he goes to them, searches them out, finds out some one or more of them whose literal expressions are directly suited to his condition. Says he to himself, “God speaks in this promise; here I will take myself a plaster as long and broad as my wound;” and so brings the word of the promise to his condition, and sets him down in peace. This is another appearance upon the mount; the Lord is near, but the Lord is not in it. It hath not been the work of the Spirit, who alone can “convince us of sin, and righteousness, and judgment,” [22] but the mere actings of the intelligent, rational soul.
paragraphs.modern: 2. Peace is also false and temporary when people produce it merely by reasoning from their convictions and principles. Here is what I mean. A person is wounded by sin. His conscience tells him he has failed to live as the gospel requires; things are not right between God and his soul. He considers what to do. He has enough knowledge to recognize the proper path and remembers how he has previously found healing. Knowing that God uses his promises to heal wounds and quiet hearts, he searches for a promise whose wording fits his situation. He tells himself, “God speaks in this promise. Here is a bandage exactly the size of my wound.” He applies the promise to his case and settles into peace. But this is another scene in which the Lord is near without being in the experience itself. It has not been the work of the Spirit, who alone convicts us of sin, righteousness, and judgment. [22] It has been only the reasoning activity of the mind.

paragraphs.original: As there are three sorts of lives, we say, — the vegetative, the sensitive, and the rational or intelligent, — some things have only the vegetative; some the sensitive also, and that includes the former; some have the rational, which takes in and supposes both the other. Now, he that hath the rational doth not only act suitably to that principle, but also to both the others, — he grows and is sensible. It is so with men in the things of God. Some are mere natural and rational men; some have a superadded conviction with illumination; and some are truly regenerate. Now, he that hath the latter hath also both the former; and therefore he acts sometimes upon the principles of the rational, sometimes upon the principles of the enlightened man. His true spiritual life is not the principle of all his motions; he acts not always in the strength thereof, neither are all his fruits from that root. In this case that I speak of, he acts merely upon the principle of conviction and illumination, whereby his first naturals are heightened; but the Spirit breathes not at all upon all these waters.
paragraphs.modern: Consider the traditional distinction between three forms of life: plant life, animal life with sensation, and rational life. A plant grows; an animal both grows and senses; a rational creature has those capacities and also reasons. Yet a rational creature does not act only by reasoning: it also grows and experiences sensation. Something similar applies in spiritual matters. Some people possess only natural reason. Others also have religious illumination and conviction. Others are truly born again. But a regenerate person still possesses the earlier capacities and may sometimes act merely from natural reason or religious enlightenment. Not every movement of his mind comes from spiritual life, and not every result springs from that root. In the case I am describing, he is acting only from conviction and illumination, which sharpen his natural abilities. The Spirit is not actively bringing these considerations home to him.

paragraphs.original: Take an instance: Suppose the wound and disquiet of the soul to be upon the account of relapses, — which, whatever the evil or folly be, though for the matter of it never so small, yet there are no wounds deeper than those that are given the soul on that account, nor disquietments greater; — in the perturbation of his mind, he finds out that promise, Isa. lv. 7, “The Lord will have mercy, and our God will abundantly pardon,” — he will multiply or add to pardon, he will do it again and again; or that in Hos. xiv. 4, “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.” This the man considers, and thereupon concludes peace to himself; whether the Spirit of God make the application or no, whether that gives life and power to the letter or no, that he regards not. He doth not hearken whether God the Lord speak peace. He doth not wait upon God, who perhaps yet hides his face, and sees the poor creature stealing peace and running away with it, knowing that the time will come when he will deal with him again, and call him to a new reckoning; [23] when he shall see that it is in vain to go one step where God doth not take him by the hand.
paragraphs.modern: For example, suppose repeated returns to sin have wounded and troubled someone’s soul. Whatever the sin may be, even if comparatively small, few things cause deeper wounds or greater distress than relapsing into it. In his agitation he finds Isaiah 55:7: “The Lord will have mercy, and our God will abundantly pardon”—he will pardon repeatedly. Or he finds Hosea 14:4: “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” He considers the promise and concludes that he is at peace, without asking whether the Spirit is actually applying it and giving its words life and power in him. He does not listen for the Lord to speak peace. He does not wait for God, who may still be hiding his face and watching him snatch a reassurance and run away with it. God knows that he will have to bring this person to account again, [23] until he discovers that it is useless to take even one step without God leading him by the hand.

paragraphs.original: I see here, indeed, sundry other questions upon this arising and interposing themselves. I cannot apply myself to them all: one I shall a little speak to. It may be said, then, “Seeing that this seems to be the path that the Holy Spirit leads us in for the healing of our wounds and quieting of our hearts, how shall we know when we go alone ourselves, and when the Spirit also doth accompany us?”
paragraphs.modern: Several further questions naturally arise here. I cannot address them all, but I will briefly consider one. You may ask, “Since turning to the promises seems to be precisely the path the Holy Spirit uses to heal and quiet us, how can we tell whether we are doing it on our own or the Spirit is accompanying us?”

paragraphs.original: Ans. (1.) If any of you are out of the way upon this account, God will speedily let you know it; for besides that you have his promise, that the “meek he will guide in judgment and teach them his way,” Ps. xxv. 9, he will not let you always err. He will, I say, not suffer your nakedness to be covered with fig-leaves, but take them away and all the peace you have in them, and will not suffer you to settle on such lees. You shall quickly know your wound is not healed; that is, you shall speedily know whether or no it be thus with you by the event. The peace you thus get and obtain will not abide. Whilst the mind is overpowered by its own convictions, there is no hold for disquietments to fix upon. Stay a little, and all these reasonings will grow cold and vanish before the face of the first temptation that arises. But, —
paragraphs.modern: Answer: (1) If you have gone wrong in this way, God will soon make it known. He has promised to guide the humble in what is right and teach them his way (Psalm 25:9), and he will not let you continue indefinitely in error. He will not leave you covered by fig leaves. He will remove them, along with the false peace they provide, rather than let you settle complacently into that condition. The outcome will soon show that the wound has not healed. Peace gained this way does not last. While your reasoning feels compelling, distress may find no foothold. But give it a little time: those arguments cool and disappear when the first new temptation comes.

paragraphs.original: (2.) This course is commonly taken without waiting; which is the grace, and that peculiar acting of faith which God calls for, to be exercised in such a condition. I know God doth sometimes come in upon the soul instantly, in a moment, as it were, wounding and healing it, — as I am persuaded it was in the case of David, when he cut off the lap of Saul’s garment; but ordinarily, in such a case, God calls for waiting and labouring, [24] attending as the eye of a servant upon his master. Says the prophet Isaiah, chap. viii. 17, “I will wait upon the Lord, who hideth his face from the house of Jacob.” God will have his children lie a while at his door when they have run from his house, and not instantly rush in upon him; unless he take them by the hand and pluck them in, when they are so ashamed that they dare not come to him. Now, self-healers, or men that speak peace to themselves, do commonly make haste; they will not tarry; they do not hearken what God speaks, but on they will go to be healed. [25]
paragraphs.modern: (2) This approach usually avoids waiting, though patient waiting is the particular exercise of faith God calls for in such a condition. I know that God sometimes meets a soul instantly, bringing conviction and healing almost in the same moment. I believe this happened to David after he cut off the edge of Saul’s robe. Ordinarily, however, God calls for patient, active waiting, [24] with the attentiveness of a servant watching his master. “I will wait for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob” (Isaiah 8:17). After his children have run away from home, God may have them remain at his door for a time rather than rush straight in—unless he himself takes them by the hand and draws them in when they are too ashamed to approach. But those who heal themselves usually hurry. They refuse to wait or listen to what God says; they insist on obtaining immediate reassurance. [25]

paragraphs.original: (3.)
