Such a course, though it may quiet the conscience and the mind, the rational concluding part of the soul, yet it doth not sweeten the heart with rest and gracious contentation. The answer it receives is much like that Elisha gave Naaman, “Go in peace;” [26] it quieted his mind, but I much question whether it sweetened his heart, or gave him any joy in believing, other than the natural joy that was then stirred in him upon his healing. “Do not my words do good?” saith the Lord, Micah ii. 7. When God speaks, there is not only truth in his words, that may answer the conviction of our understandings, but also they do good; they bring that which is sweet, and good, and desirable to the will and affections; by them the “soul returns unto its rest,” Ps. cxvi. 7.
paragraphs.modern: (3) This process may quiet the conscience and satisfy the reasoning mind without bringing the heart the sweetness of genuine rest and gracious contentment. Its answer resembles Elisha’s words to Naaman, “Go in peace.” [26] They quieted his mind, but I question whether they gave his heart the joy of faith beyond the natural happiness of being healed. “Do not my words do good?” the Lord asks in Micah 2:7. When God speaks, his words do more than supply true statements that satisfy our reasoning. They do us good. They bring something sweet, good, and desirable to our wills and affections. Through them the soul returns to its rest (Psalm 116:7).

paragraphs.original: (4.) Which is worst of all, it amends not the life, it heals not the evil, it cures not the distemper. When God speaks peace, it guides and keeps the soul that it “turn not again to folly.” [27] When we speak it ourselves, the heart is not taken off the evil; nay, it is the readiest course in the world to bring a soul into a trade of backsliding. If, upon thy plastering thyself, thou findest thyself rather animated to the battle again than utterly weaned from it, it is too palpable that thou hast been at work with thine own soul, but Jesus Christ and his Spirit were not there. Yea, and oftentimes nature having done its work, will, ere a few days are over, come for its reward; and, having been active in the work of healing, will be ready to reason for a new wounding. In God’s speaking peace there comes along so much sweetness, and such a discovery of his love, as is a strong obligation on the soul no more to deal perversely. [28]
paragraphs.modern: (4) Worst of all, it does not reform the life, heal the evil, or cure the sinful inclination. When God speaks peace, that peace guides and guards the soul against returning to folly. [27] When we manufacture peace ourselves, the heart remains attached to the sin. This readily becomes a pattern of repeated backsliding. If your self-applied remedy makes you more willing to resume the old sinful course instead of turning you away from it, the evidence is plain: you have been working on your own soul without Christ and his Spirit doing the work. Often, within a few days, the natural self comes to claim a reward for its efforts. Having supplied its own remedy, it begins arguing that another wound can be risked. But when God speaks peace, the sweetness and revelation of his love powerfully bind the soul not to act perversely again. [28]

paragraphs.original: 3. We speak peace to ourselves when we do it slightly. This the prophet complains of in some teachers: Jer. vi. 14, “They have healed the wound of the daughter of my people slightly.” And it is so with some persons: they make the healing of their wounds a slight work; a look, a glance of faith to the promises does it, and so the matter is ended. The apostle tells us that “the word did not profit” some, because “it was not mixed with faith,” Heb. iv. 2, — μὴ συγκεκραμένος· “it was not well tempered” and mingled with faith. It is not a mere look to the word of mercy in the promise, but it must be mingled with faith until it is incorporated into the very nature of it; and then, indeed, it doth good unto the soul.
paragraphs.modern: 3. We also speak peace to ourselves when we treat healing superficially. Jeremiah criticizes teachers who “healed the wound of my people lightly” (Jeremiah 6:14). Some people do the same to themselves. They give the promises a quick glance and consider the wound healed and the matter closed. Hebrews 4:2 says the word did not benefit some because it was not mixed with faith. The Greek, mē synkekramenos, expresses the absence of a thorough mixing. A mere look at a promise of mercy is not enough. The promise must be deeply received and taken into faith; then it truly benefits the soul.

paragraphs.original: If thou hast had a wound upon thy conscience, which was attended with weakness and disquietness, which now thou art freed of, how camest thou so? “I looked to the promises of pardon and healing, and so found peace.” Yea, but perhaps thou hast made too much haste, thou hast done it overtly, thou hast not fed upon the promise so as to mix it with faith, to have got all the virtue of it diffused into thy soul; only thou hast done it slightly. Thou wilt find thy wound, ere it be long, breaking out again; and thou shalt know that thou art not cured.
paragraphs.modern: Suppose a wound in your conscience caused weakness and distress, but now you feel free of them. How did that happen? “I looked to the promises of pardon and healing and found peace.” Perhaps—but perhaps you were too hasty and superficial. You may not have nourished yourself on the promise and received it through faith so that its power spread through your soul. You may have only skimmed its surface. Before long the wound will break open again, showing that it was not cured.

paragraphs.original: 4. Whoever speaks peace to himself upon any one account, and at the same time hath another evil of no less importance lying upon his spirit, about which he hath had no dealing with God, that man cries “Peace” when there is none. A little to explain my meaning: A man hath neglected a duty again and again, perhaps, when in all righteousness it was due from him; his conscience is perplexed, his soul wounded, he hath no quiet in his bones by reason of his sin; he applies himself for healing, and finds peace. Yet, in the meantime, perhaps, worldliness, or pride, or some other folly, wherewith the Spirit of God is exceedingly grieved, may lie in the bosom of that man, and they neither disturb him nor he them. Let not that man think that any of his peace is from God. Then shall it be well with men, when they have an equal respect to all God’s commandments. God will justify us from our sins, but he will not justify the least sin in us: “He is a God of purer eyes than to behold iniquity.”
paragraphs.modern: 4. Anyone who reassures himself about one sin while another equally serious evil remains unaddressed before God is saying “Peace” when there is no peace. For example, a person repeatedly neglects a duty he clearly owes. His conscience becomes troubled, his soul wounded, and his whole being restless because of his sin. He seeks healing and feels peace. Meanwhile, pride, worldliness, or another sin that deeply grieves the Spirit remains comfortably in his heart. It does not trouble him, and he does not trouble it. He must not imagine that his peace comes from God. It will be well with us when we show sincere regard for all God’s commandments. God justifies us from our sins, but he never justifies even the smallest sin within us. His eyes are too pure to approve evil.

paragraphs.original: 5. When men of themselves speak peace to their consciences, it is seldom that God speaks humiliation to their souls. God’s peace is humbling peace, melting peace, as it was in the case of David; [29] never such deep humiliation as when Nathan brought him the tidings of his pardon.
paragraphs.modern: 5. Self-made peace rarely comes with the humbling that God produces. God’s peace humbles and softens the heart. David illustrates this: [29] he was never more deeply humbled than when Nathan announced his pardon.

paragraphs.original: But you will say, “When may we take the comfort of a promise as our own, in relation to some peculiar wound, for the quieting the heart?” First, In general, when God speaks it, be it when it will, sooner or later. I told you before, he may do it in the very instant of the sin itself, and that with such irresistible power that the soul must needs receive his mind in it; sometimes he will make us wait longer: but when he speaks, be it sooner or later, be it when we are sinning or repenting, be the condition of our souls what they please, if God speak, he must be received. There is not any thing that, in our communion with him, the Lord is more troubled with us for, if I may so say, than our unbelieving fears, that keep us off from receiving that strong consolation which he is so willing to give to us.
paragraphs.modern: You may ask, “Then when may we personally receive the comfort of a promise to quiet our hearts about a particular wound?” First, the general answer is: whenever God speaks it, whether sooner or later. As I said, he may do so at the very moment of the sin, with such power that the soul cannot help recognizing his message. At other times he makes us wait. But whenever he speaks—soon or late, while we are sinning or repenting, whatever our present condition—we must receive what he says. In our fellowship with him, few things, so to speak, grieve the Lord more than the unbelieving fears that keep us from accepting the strong comfort he is so willing to give.

paragraphs.original: But you will say, “We are where we were. When God speaks it, we must receive it, that is true; but how shall we know when he speaks?” (1.) I would we could all practically come up to this, to receive peace when we are convinced that God speaks it, and that it is our duty to receive it. But, —
paragraphs.modern: You may reply, “That leaves us where we started. Of course we must receive peace when God speaks it. But how can we know that he is speaking?” (1) I wish we all consistently did even this much: receive his peace when we are convinced that he is speaking and that we ought to receive it. But there is more to say.

paragraphs.original: (2.) There is, if I may so say, a secret instinct in faith, whereby it knows the voice of Christ when he speaks indeed; as the babe leaped in the womb when the blessed Virgin came to Elisabeth, faith leaps in the heart when Christ indeed draws nigh to it. “My sheep,” says Christ, “know my voice,” John x. 4; — “They know my voice; they are used to the sound of it;” and they know when his lips are opened to them and are full of grace. The spouse was in a sad condition, Cant. v. 2, — asleep in security; but yet as soon as Christ speaks, she cries, “It is the voice of my beloved that speaks!” She knew his voice, and was so acquainted with communion with him, that instantly she discovers him; and so will you also. If you exercise yourselves to acquaintance and communion with him, you will easily discern between his voice and the voice of a stranger.
paragraphs.modern: (2) Faith has, so to speak, an inward instinct that recognizes Christ’s voice when he truly speaks. Just as the child leaped in Elizabeth’s womb when the blessed Virgin came to her, faith leaps within the heart when Christ draws near. “My sheep know my voice,” Christ says (John 10:4). They are familiar with its sound and recognize when he addresses them graciously. The bride in Song of Songs 5:2 was in a sad condition, sleeping in complacency. Yet as soon as the beloved spoke, she recognized him: “It is my beloved’s voice!” Her familiarity with him enabled her to know him immediately. The same will be true of you. As you cultivate acquaintance and fellowship with Christ, you will increasingly distinguish his voice from a stranger’s.

paragraphs.original: And take this κριτήριον with you: When he doth speak, he speaks as never man spake; he speaks with power, and one way or other will make your “hearts burn within you,” as he did to the disciples, Luke xxiv. He doth it by “putting in his hand at the hole of the door,” Cant. v. 4, — his Spirit into your hearts to seize on you. He that hath his senses exercised to discern good or evil, being increased in judgment and experience by a constant observation of the ways of Christ’s intercourse, the manner of the operations of the Spirit, and the effects it usually produceth, is the best judge for himself in this case.
paragraphs.modern: Take this criterion with you: when Christ speaks, he speaks as no mere person speaks. He speaks with power, and in one way or another makes our hearts burn within us, as he did for the disciples in Luke 24. In the image of Song of Songs 5:4, he puts his hand through the opening of the door: he sends his Spirit into our hearts and takes hold of us. The person best equipped to discern this for himself is one whose judgment has been trained to distinguish good from evil. Such discernment grows through experience and attentive observation of Christ’s dealings, the Spirit’s way of working, and the effects the Spirit ordinarily produces.

paragraphs.original: Secondly, If the word of the Lord doth good to your souls, he speaks it; if it humble, if it cleanse, and be useful to those ends for which promises are given, — namely, to endear, to cleanse, to melt and bind to obedience, to self-emptiness, etc. But this is not my business; nor shall I farther divert in the pursuit of this direction. Without the observation of it, sin will have great advantages towards the hardening of the heart.
paragraphs.modern: Second, when the Lord’s word does spiritual good to your soul, that is evidence that he is speaking it. Does it humble and cleanse you? Does it accomplish the purposes for which the promises were given—deepening love, purifying, softening, binding you to obedience, and emptying you of self-reliance? These are its proper effects. But a fuller treatment is beyond my present purpose, so I will not pursue this direction further. Neglect it, however, and sin gains a powerful advantage in hardening the heart.

paragraphs.original: [21] 1 John ii. 15. [22] John xvi. 8. [23] Hos. ix. 9. [24] Ps. cxxx. 6, cxxiii. 2. [25] Isa. xxviii. 16. [26] 2 Kings v. 19. [27] Ps. lxxxv. 8. [28] Luke xxii. 32. [29] Ps. li. 1.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV: The central means: faith in Christ and the Spirit’s work

paragraphs.original: The general use of the foregoing directions — The great direction for the accomplishment of the work aimed at: Act faith on Christ — The several ways whereby this may be done — Consideration of the fulness in Christ for relief proposed — Great expectations from Christ — Grounds of these expectations: his mercifulness, his faithfulness — Event of such expectations; on the part of Christ; on the part of believers — Faith peculiarly to be acted on the death of Christ, Rom. vi. 3–6 — The work of the Spirit in this whole business.
paragraphs.modern: The purpose of the preceding directions. The central direction for actually putting sin to death: exercise faith in Christ. How to do this: consider the fullness of help available in him, and expect him to supply it. The grounds for that expectation are his mercy and faithfulness. How this expectation relates to Christ’s help and the believer’s activity. Focus faith especially on Christ’s death, as explained in Romans 6:3–6. The Spirit’s work throughout the whole process.

paragraphs.original: Now, the considerations which I have hitherto insisted on are rather of things preparatory to the work aimed at than such as will effect it. It is the heart’s due preparation for the work itself, without which it will not be accomplished, that hitherto I have aimed at. Directions for the work itself are very few; I mean that are peculiar to it. And they are these that follow:—
paragraphs.modern: The considerations discussed so far prepare for the work rather than accomplish it. My aim has been to prepare the heart properly; without that preparation, the work will not be done. The directions specifically concerned with accomplishing the work itself are few. They follow here.

paragraphs.original: 1. Set faith at work on Christ for the killing of thy sin. His blood is the great sovereign remedy for sin-sick souls. Live in this, and thou wilt die a conqueror; yea, thou wilt, through the good providence of God, live to see thy lust dead at thy feet.
paragraphs.modern: 1. Exercise faith in Christ to put your sin to death. His blood is the supreme remedy for souls sick with sin. Live by this faith, and you will die a conqueror. Indeed, through God’s good providence, you will live to see the sinful desire that once mastered you defeated at your feet.

paragraphs.original: But thou wilt say, “How shall faith act itself on Christ for this end and purpose?” I say, Sundry ways:— (1.) By faith fill thy soul with a due consideration of that provision which is laid up in Jesus Christ for this end and purpose, that all thy lusts, this very lust wherewith thou art entangled, may be mortified. By faith ponder on this, that though thou art no way able in or by thyself to get the conquest over thy distemper, though thou art even weary of contending, and art utterly ready to faint, yet that there is enough in Jesus Christ to yield thee relief, Phil. iv. 13.
paragraphs.modern: You may ask, “How does faith look to Christ for this purpose?” In several ways. (1) Let faith fill your mind with the provision stored up in Jesus Christ for putting all your sinful desires to death—including the very one that now entangles you. Consider this with faith: although you cannot conquer this sinful inclination by yourself, although you are exhausted from fighting and almost ready to collapse, Jesus Christ has more than enough to help you. See Philippians 4:13.

paragraphs.original: It staid the prodigal, when he was ready to faint, [30] that yet there was bread enough in his father’s house; though he was at a distance from it, yet it relieved him, and staid him, that there it was. In thy greatest distress and anguish, consider that fulness of grace, those riches, those treasures of strength, might, and help, [31] that are laid up in him for our support, John i. 16, Col. i. 19. Let them come into and abide in thy mind. Consider that he is “exalted and made a Prince and a Saviour to give repentance unto Israel,” Acts v. 31; and if to give repentance, to give mortification, without which the other is not, nor can be. Christ tells us that we obtain purging grace by abiding in him, John xv. 3. To act faith upon the fulness that is in Christ for our supply is an eminent way of abiding in Christ, for both our insition and abode is by faith, Rom. xi. 19, 20.
paragraphs.modern: When the prodigal son was close to collapse, [30] the thought that there was plenty of bread in his father’s house sustained him. Though he was still far away, knowing that the provision existed gave him hope. In your deepest distress, consider the fullness of grace and the rich stores of strength, power, and help [31] laid up in Christ for us (John 1:16; Colossians 1:19). Let these truths enter your mind and remain there. He has been exalted as Prince and Savior to give repentance to Israel (Acts 5:31). To give repentance necessarily includes giving mortification; true repentance cannot exist without it. Christ teaches that we receive cleansing grace by remaining in him (John 15:3). Trusting the fullness of his provision is an important way of remaining in him, because both our being grafted into Christ and our continuing in him are through faith (Romans 11:19–20).

paragraphs.original: Let, then, thy soul by faith be exercised with such thoughts and apprehensions as these: “I am a poor, weak creature; unstable as water, I cannot excel. This corruption is too hard for me, and is at the very door of ruining my soul; and what to do I know not. My soul is become as parched ground, and an habitation of dragons. I have made promises and broken them; vows and engagements have been as a thing of nought. Many persuasions have I had that I had got the victory and should be delivered, but I am deceived; so that I plainly see, that without some eminent succour and assistance, I am lost, and shall be prevailed on to an utter relinquishment of God. But yet, though this be my state and condition, let the hands that hang down be lifted up, and the feeble knees be strengthened. Behold, the Lord Christ, [32] that hath all fulness of grace in his heart, all fulness of power in his hand, he is able to slay all these his enemies. There is sufficient provision in him for my relief and assistance. He can take my drooping, dying soul and make me more than a conqueror. [33]
paragraphs.modern: Let faith lead you to thoughts like these: “I am weak and helpless. Unstable as water, I cannot stand firm. This corruption is stronger than I am and is close to ruining my soul. I do not know what to do. My soul has become like scorched ground, a haunt of wild creatures. I have made promises and broken them; my vows and commitments have come to nothing. Many times I thought I had won and would be free, but I was mistaken. I see clearly that without powerful help I am lost and will be driven toward abandoning God altogether. Yet even in this condition, let my drooping hands be lifted and my weak knees strengthened. Look at the Lord Christ: [32] his heart is full of grace, his hand full of power. He can destroy all these enemies of his. He has everything needed to help and sustain me. He can take my failing, dying soul and make me more than a conqueror. [33]

paragraphs.original: ‘Why sayest thou, O my soul, My way is hid from the Lord, and my judgment is passed over from my God? Hast thou not known, hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding. He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: but they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; they shall walk, and not faint,’ Isa. xl. 27–31.
paragraphs.modern: “‘Why do you say, my soul, that the Lord does not see your way and that your God has disregarded your cause? Have you not known or heard? The Lord is the everlasting God, Creator of the ends of the earth. He never grows faint or weary; his understanding cannot be measured. He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the powerless. Even the young become tired and weak, and strong young men stumble and fall. But those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength. They will rise on wings like eagles, run without growing weary, and walk without fainting’ (Isaiah 40:27–31).

paragraphs.original: He can make the ‘dry, parched ground of my soul to become a pool, and my thirsty, barren heart as springs of water;’ yea, he can make this ‘habitation of dragons,’ this heart, so full of abominable lusts and fiery temptations, to be a place for ‘grass’ and fruit to himself,” Isa. xxxv. 7. So God staid Paul, under his temptation, with the consideration of the sufficiency of his grace: “My grace is sufficient for thee,” 2 Cor. xii. 9. Though he were not immediately so far made partaker of it as to be freed from his temptation, yet the sufficiency of it in God, for that end and purpose, was enough to stay his spirit. I say, then, by faith, be much in the consideration of that supply and the fulness of it that is in Jesus Christ, and how he can at any time give thee strength and deliverance.
paragraphs.modern: “He can turn the scorched ground of my soul into a pool and my thirsty, barren heart into springs of water. He can turn this haunt of wild creatures—this heart full of hateful desires and fierce temptations—into a place of living grass and fruit for himself” (Isaiah 35:7). God likewise sustained Paul in his trial by assuring him that his grace was sufficient: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul did not immediately receive deliverance from the trial, but knowing that God’s grace was sufficient sustained him. So spend much time considering, by faith, the abundant provision in Jesus Christ and his ability to give you strength and deliverance whenever he chooses.

paragraphs.original: Now, if hereby thou dost not find success to a conquest, yet thou wilt be staid in the chariot, that thou shalt not fly out of the field until the battle be ended; thou wilt be kept from an utter despondency and a lying down under thy unbelief, or a turning aside to false means and remedies, that in the issue will not relieve thee. The efficacy of this consideration will be found only in the practice.
paragraphs.modern: Even if this does not immediately bring victory, it will keep you in your chariot rather than fleeing the battlefield before the fight is over. It will guard you from complete despair, from surrendering to unbelief, and from turning to false remedies that cannot ultimately help you. You will discover the power of this consideration only by practicing it.

paragraphs.original: (2.) Raise up thy heart by faith to an expectation of relief from Christ. Relief in this case from Christ is like the prophet’s vision, Hab. ii. 3, “It is for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, yet wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.” Though it may seem somewhat long to thee, whilst thou art under thy trouble and perplexity, yet it shall surely come in the appointed time of the Lord Jesus; which is the best season. If, then, thou canst raise up thy heart to a settled expectation of relief from Jesus Christ, — if thine eyes are towards him “as the eyes of a servant to the hand of his master,” [34] when he expects to receive somewhat from him, — thy soul shall be satisfied, he will assuredly deliver thee; he will slay the lust, and thy latter end shall be peace. Only look for it at his hand; expect when and how he will do it. “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.” [35]
paragraphs.modern: (2) By faith, encourage your heart to expect help from Christ. His help resembles the prophet’s vision: “It awaits its appointed time; at the end it will speak and will not prove false. Though it seems delayed, wait for it. It will surely come; it will not be late” (Habakkuk 2:3). While you are troubled, the delay may feel long. Yet help will come at the Lord Jesus’ appointed time, which is the best time. Let your heart settle into an expectation of his help. Look toward him as a servant looks to his master’s hand, [34] expecting to receive from him. He will satisfy your soul and deliver you; he will destroy the sinful desire’s power, and your final outcome will be peace. Look to him for it, waiting for his chosen time and manner. “If you do not believe, you will not stand firm.” [35]

paragraphs.original: But wilt thou say, “What ground have I to build such an expectation upon, so that I may expect not to be deceived?” As thou hast necessity to put thee on this course, thou must be relieved and saved this way or none. To whom wilt thou go? [36] So there are in the Lord Jesus innumerable things to encourage and engage thee to this expectation.
paragraphs.modern: You may ask, “What grounds do I have for this expectation? How can I know it will not disappoint me?” First, necessity drives you to it: you must receive help and salvation through Christ or not at all. To whom else will you go? [36] Beyond that necessity, countless things about the Lord Jesus encourage and call you to expect his help.

paragraphs.original: For the necessity of it, I have in part discovered it before, when I manifested that this is the work of faith and of believers only. “Without me,” says Christ, “ye can do nothing,” John xv. 5; speaking with especial relation to the purging of the heart from sin, verse 2. Mortification of any sin must be by a supply of grace. Of ourselves we cannot do it. Now, “it hath pleased the Father that in Christ should all fulness dwell,” Col. i. 19; that “of his fulness we might receive grace for grace,” John i. 16. He is the head from whence the new man must have influences of life and strength, or it will decay every day. If we are “strengthened with might in the inner man,” [37] it is by “Christ’s dwelling in our hearts by faith,” Eph. iii. 16, 17. That this work is not to be done without the Spirit I have also showed before. Whence, then, do we expect the Spirit? from whom do we look for him? who hath promised him to us, having procured him for us? Ought not all our expectations to this purpose to be on Christ alone? Let this, then, be fixed upon thy heart, that if thou hast not relief from him thou shalt never have any.
paragraphs.modern: I have already partly explained why this is necessary, in showing that mortification is a work of faith and belongs to believers. “Apart from me you can do nothing,” Christ says (John 15:5), with particular reference to cleansing and fruitfulness in verse 2. Putting any sin to death requires a supply of grace; we cannot do it ourselves. The Father was pleased for all fullness to dwell in Christ (Colossians 1:19), so that from his fullness we might receive grace upon grace (John 1:16). He is the head from whom our new life must continually receive vitality and strength; without that supply, it declines daily. Our being strengthened inwardly [37] is connected with Christ dwelling in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:16–17). I have also shown that the work cannot be done without the Spirit. From whom, then, do we expect the Spirit? Who secured his presence for us and promised to give him? Shouldn’t our entire expectation rest on Christ? Fix this firmly in your heart: without help from him, you will never have the help you need.

paragraphs.original: All ways, endeavours, contendings, that are not animated by this expectation of relief from Christ and him only are to no purpose, will do thee no good; yea, if they are any thing but supportments of thy heart in this expectation, or means appointed by himself for the receiving help from him, they are in vain.
paragraphs.modern: Every method, effort, and struggle that is not animated by the expectation of help from Christ alone will fail to accomplish this work. Your practices must either sustain that expectation in your heart or be means Christ himself appointed for receiving his help. Otherwise they are futile.

paragraphs.original: Now, farther to engage thee to this expectation, — (1.) Consider his mercifulness, tenderness, and kindness, as he is our great High Priest at the right hand of God. Assuredly he pities thee in thy distress; saith he, “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you,” Isa. lxvi. 13. He hath the tenderness of a mother to a sucking child. Heb. ii. 17, 18, “Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people. For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.” How is the ability of Christ upon the account of his suffering proposed to us? “In that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able.” Did the sufferings and temptations of Christ add to his ability and power? Not, doubtless, considered absolutely and in it itself. But the ability here mentioned is such as hath readiness, proneness, willingness to put itself forth, accompanying of it; it is an ability of will against all dissuasions. He is able, having suffered and been tempted, to break through all dissuasions to the contrary, to relieve poor tempted souls: Δύναται βοηθῆσαι, — “He is able to help.” It is a metonymy of the effect; for, he can now be moved to help, having been so tempted.
paragraphs.modern: To strengthen this expectation further, (1) consider the mercy, tenderness, and kindness of our great High Priest at God’s right hand. He certainly has compassion on you in your distress. “As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13). His tenderness is like a mother’s toward her nursing child. Hebrews 2:17–18 says that he had to become like his brothers in every respect so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest, making atonement for the people’s sins; because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those being tempted. In what sense did suffering make him “able”? It did not increase his absolute divine power. The ability described here includes readiness and willingness to use that power despite every objection. Having suffered temptation himself, he is ready to overcome every reason for withholding help from troubled, tempted souls. Dynatai boēthēsai means “he is able to help.” The expression names the result while pointing to his compassionate readiness: because he has been tempted, he is moved to help.

paragraphs.original: So chap. iv. 15, 16: “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” The exhortation of verse 16 is the same that I am upon, — namely, that we would entertain expectations of relief from Christ, which the apostle there calls χάριν εἰς εὔκαιρον βοήθειαν, “grace for seasonable help.” “If ever,” says the soul, “help were seasonable, it would be so to me in my present condition. This is that which I long for, — grace for seasonable help. I am ready to die, to perish, to be lost for ever; iniquity will prevail against me, if help come not in.” Says the apostle, “Expect this help, this relief, this grace from Christ.” Yea, but on what account? That which he lays down, verse 15. And we may observe that the word, verse 16, which we have translated to “obtain,” is λαβωμεν. Ἵνα λάβωμεν ἔλεον, “That we may receive it;” suitable and seasonable help will come in.
paragraphs.modern: Hebrews 4:15–16 makes the same point: “We do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. He has been tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore approach the throne of grace confidently, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in our time of need.” Verse 16 urges precisely what I am urging: expect help from Christ. The Greek describes “grace for timely help”—charin eis eukairon boētheian. The troubled soul says, “If help was ever timely, it would be now. This is what I long for. I am close to ruin; sin will overcome me unless help comes.” The apostle answers, “Expect that help and grace from Christ.” On what basis? The compassionate high priest described in verse 15. Notice also that the word translated “obtain” is labōmen: “that we may receive mercy.” We come to receive appropriate help at the needed time.

paragraphs.original: I shall freely say, this one thing of establishing the soul by faith in expectation of relief from Jesus Christ, [38] on the account of his mercifulness as our high priest, will be more available to the ruin of thy lust and distemper, and have a better and speedier issue, than all the rigidest means of self-maceration that ever any of the sons of men engaged themselves unto. Yea, let me add, that never any soul did or shall perish by the power of any lust, sin, or corruption, who could raise his soul by faith to an expectation of relief from Jesus Christ. [39]
paragraphs.modern: I say this plainly: establishing your soul by faith in the expectation of help from Jesus Christ, [38] because he is your merciful high priest, will do more to destroy your sinful inclination—and bring a better and quicker result—than the harshest bodily punishments people have ever inflicted on themselves. More than that: no soul that truly looks by faith to Christ for help has ever been, or ever will be, finally destroyed by the power of a sinful desire or corruption. [39]

paragraphs.original: (2.) Consider His faithfulness who hath promised; which may raise thee up and confirm thee in this waiting in an expectation of relief. He hath promised to relieve in such cases, and he will fulfil his word to the utmost. God tells us that his covenant with us is like the “ordinances” of heaven, the sun, moon, and stars, which have their certain courses, Jer. xxxi. 36. Thence David said that he watched for relief from God “as one watched for the morning,” [40] — a thing that will certainly come in its appointed season. So will be thy relief from Christ. It will come in its season, as the dew and rain upon the parched ground; for faithful is he who hath promised. Particular promises to this purpose are innumerable; with some of them, that seem peculiarly to suit his condition, let the soul be always furnished.
paragraphs.modern: (2) Consider the faithfulness of the one who has promised. This will encourage and steady you as you wait for help. He has promised help in such cases and will fulfill his word completely. God compares his covenant with us to the fixed order of the sun, moon, and stars (Jeremiah 31:36). That is why David waits for God as a watchman waits for morning [40]—something certain to arrive at its appointed time. So will Christ’s help come to you, in its season, like dew and rain on scorched ground. The one who promised is faithful. There are countless particular promises that support this expectation. Keep some that especially fit your condition ready in your heart.

paragraphs.original: Now, there are two eminent advantages which always attend this expectation of succour from Jesus Christ:— [1.] It engages him to a full and speedy assistance. Nothing doth more engage the heart of a man to be useful and helpful to another than his expectation of help from him, if justly raised and countenanced by him who is to give the relief. Our Lord Jesus hath raised our hearts, by his kindness, care, and promises, to this expectation; certainly our rising up unto it must needs be a great engagement upon him to assist us accordingly. This the Psalmist gives us as an approved maxim, “Thou, Lord, never forsakest them that put their trust in thee.” When the heart is once won to rest in God, to repose himself on him, he will assuredly satisfy it. He will never be as water that fails; nor hath he said at any time to the seed of Jacob, “Seek ye my face in vain.” If Christ be chosen for the foundation of our supply, he will not fail us.
paragraphs.modern: Two important benefits accompany this expectation of help from Jesus Christ. [1] It lays hold of his commitment to give full and timely help. Even among human beings, few things more strongly engage someone to help than another person’s expectation—when the helper has himself encouraged that expectation and given grounds for it. The Lord Jesus has awakened our expectation through his kindness, care, and promises. Surely, then, our trusting him draws upon his own commitment to help. The psalmist states the established truth: “Lord, you never forsake those who put their trust in you.” When a heart has been won over to rest in God, he will not disappoint it. He will not be like a stream that dries up. He has never told Jacob’s descendants to seek him in vain. If Christ is the foundation on which we depend for our supply, he will not fail us.

paragraphs.original: [2.] It engages the heart to attend diligently to all the ways and means whereby Christ is wont to communicate himself to the soul; and so takes in the real assistance of all graces and ordinances whatever. He that expects any thing from a man, applies himself to the ways and means whereby it may be obtained. The beggar that expects an alms lies at his door or in his way from whom he doth expect it. The way whereby and the means wherein Christ communicates himself is, and are, his ordinances ordinarily; he that expects any thing from him must attend upon him therein. It is the expectation of faith that sets the heart on work. It is not an idle, groundless hope that I speak of. If now there be any vigour, efficacy, and power in prayer or sacrament to this end of mortifying sin, a man will assuredly be interested in it all by this expectation of relief from Christ. On this account I reduce all particular actings, by prayer, meditation, and the like, to this head; and so shall not farther insist on them, when they are grounded on this bottom and spring from this root. They are of singular use to this purpose, and not else.
paragraphs.modern: [2] This expectation makes the heart diligent in using every means through which Christ ordinarily gives himself to the soul. It therefore brings in the real help of all the graces and practices God has appointed. Someone expecting a gift seeks it where it is likely to be given. A beggar expecting help waits at the giver’s door or along his path. Christ ordinarily meets us through his appointed means; those expecting help from him must attend to him there. Faith’s expectation sets the heart to work. I am not describing idle or groundless hope. Whatever power prayer or the sacraments have in putting sin to death, the person expecting Christ’s help will seek and receive that benefit. This is why I place prayer, meditation, and similar practices under this main direction rather than discussing each separately. When they rest on this foundation and spring from this root, they are especially useful for mortification; apart from it, they are not.

paragraphs.original: Now, on this direction for the mortification of a prevailing distemper you may have a thousand “probatum est’s.” Who have walked with God under this temptation, and have not found the use and success of it? I dare leave the soul under it, without adding any more. Only some particulars relating thereunto may be mentioned:—
paragraphs.modern: This direction for overcoming a dominant sinful inclination has a thousand testimonies of “probatum est”—“tried and proved.” Who has walked with God through such temptation without finding this approach useful and effective? I would be willing to leave the soul with this direction alone. Still, a few related particulars deserve mention.

paragraphs.original: First, Act faith peculiarly upon the death, blood, and cross of Christ; that is, on Christ as crucified and slain. Mortification of sin is peculiarly from the death of Christ. It is one peculiar, yea, eminent end of the death of Christ, which shall assuredly be accomplished by it. He died to destroy the works of the devil. Whatever came upon our natures by his first temptation, whatever receives strength in our persons by his daily suggestions, Christ died to destroy it all. “He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works,” Tit. ii. 14. This was his aim and intendment (wherein he will not fail) in his giving himself for us. That we might be freed from the power of our sins, and purified from all our defiling lusts, was his design.
paragraphs.modern: First, direct faith especially toward Christ’s death, blood, and cross—toward Christ crucified and slain. Putting sin to death flows particularly from his death. It is one of the central purposes for which he died, and his death will certainly accomplish it. He died to destroy the devil’s works: both the corruption introduced into human nature through the first temptation and the sins strengthened by the devil’s daily suggestions. Christ died to destroy it all. “He gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and purify for himself a people of his own, eager to do good works” (Titus 2:14). That was his purpose in giving himself for us, and he will not fail. He intended to free us from sin’s power and cleanse us from every defiling desire.

paragraphs.original: “He gave himself for the church, that he might sanctify and cleanse it; that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy, and without blemish,” Eph. v. 25–27. And this, by virtue of his death, in various and several degrees, shall be accomplished. Hence our washing, purging, and cleansing is everywhere ascribed to his blood, 1 John i. 7; Heb. i. 3; Rev. i. 5. That being sprinkled on us, “purges our consciences from dead works to serve the living God,” Heb. ix. 14. This is that we aim at, this we are in pursuit of, — that our consciences may be purged from dead works, that they may be rooted out, destroyed, and have place in us no more. This shall certainly be brought about by the death of Christ; there will virtue go out from thence to this purpose. Indeed, all supplies of the Spirit, all communications of grace and power, are from hence; as I have elsewhere [41] showed.
paragraphs.modern: “He gave himself for the church to sanctify and cleanse it, and to present it to himself in glory, without spot, wrinkle, or anything of the kind, holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:25–27). Through the power of his death, this will be accomplished progressively. That is why Scripture repeatedly attributes our washing and cleansing to his blood (1 John 1:7; Hebrews 1:3; Revelation 1:5). Applied to us, that blood cleanses our consciences from dead works so that we may serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). This is our aim: that these dead works be uprooted, destroyed, and given no place in us. Christ’s death will certainly accomplish it; power flows from that death for this very purpose. Indeed, every supply of the Spirit and every communication of grace and power comes from it, as I have shown elsewhere. [41]

paragraphs.original: Thus the apostle states it; Rom. vi. 2, is the case proposed that we have in hand: “How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” — “Dead to sin by profession; dead to sin by obligation to be so; dead to sin by participation of virtue and power for the killing of it; dead to sin by union and interest in Christ, in and by whom it is killed: how shall we live therein?” This he presses by sundry considerations, all taken from the death of Christ, in the ensuing verses.
paragraphs.modern: Paul puts the matter before us in Romans 6:2: “How can we who died to sin still live in it?” We are dead to sin by our profession of faith, by our obligation to reject it, by receiving power to put it to death, and by our union with Christ, in whom and through whom it is defeated. How, then, can we continue living in it? In the following verses Paul reinforces this with several arguments, all drawn from Christ’s death.

paragraphs.original: This must not be: verse 3, “Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?” We have in baptism an evidence of our implantation into Christ; we are baptized into him: but what of him are we baptized into an interest in? “His death,” saith he. If indeed we are baptized into Christ, and beyond outward profession, we are baptized into his death.
paragraphs.modern: We must not continue in sin. Verse 3 asks, “Do you not know that all of us baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?” Baptism gives evidence of our being grafted into Christ. But what aspect of Christ do we share in through it? His death. If our baptism into Christ is real and goes beyond an outward profession, we are baptized into his death.

paragraphs.original: The explication of this, of one being baptized into the death of Christ, the apostle gives us, verses 4, 6: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death; that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.” “This is,” saith he, “our being baptized into the death of Christ, namely, our conformity thereunto; to be dead unto sin, to have our corruptions mortified, as he was put to death for sin: so that as he was raised up to glory, we may be raised up to grace and newness of life.” He tells us whence it is that we have this baptism into the death of Christ, verse 6; and this is from the death of Christ itself: “Our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed;” συνεσταυρώθη, “is crucified with him,” not in respect of time, but causality.
paragraphs.modern: Paul explains this in verses 4 and 6: “We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the Father’s glory, we too might walk in newness of life. We know that our old self was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we would no longer serve sin.” Being baptized into Christ’s death means being conformed to it: becoming dead to sin and having our corruptions put to death, as he was put to death for sin. As he rose to glory, we rise into grace and a new life. Verse 6 also explains the source of this participation: Christ’s death itself. “Our old self was crucified with him.” The Greek synestaurōthē means “was crucified with him.” The connection is causal, not a claim that our personal experience occurred at the same moment in history.

paragraphs.original: We are crucified with him meritoriously, in that he procured the Spirit for us to mortify sin; efficiently, in that from his death virtue comes forth for our crucifying; in the way of a representation and exemplar we shall assuredly be crucified unto sin, as he was for our sin. This is that the apostle intends: Christ by his death destroying the works of the devil, procuring the Spirit for us, hath so killed sin, as to its reign in believers, that it shall not obtain its end and dominion.
paragraphs.modern: We are crucified with Christ on the basis of his merit: he secured the Spirit for us to put sin to death. We are also crucified with him through his effective power: the power that puts our old self to death flows from his death. And his death provides the pattern to which we will be conformed: we will be crucified to sin as he was crucified for our sin. Paul’s point is that Christ, by dying to destroy the devil’s works and securing the Spirit for us, has decisively broken sin’s claim to rule believers. Sin will not achieve its ultimate purpose or dominion over them.

paragraphs.original: Secondly, Then act faith on the death of Christ, and that under these two notions, — first, In expectation of power; secondly, In endeavours for conformity. [42] For the first, the direction given in general may suffice; as to the latter, that of the apostle may give us some light into our direction, Gal. iii. 1. Let faith look on Christ in the gospel as he is set forth dying and crucified for us. Look on him under the weight of our sins, [43] praying, bleeding, dying; bring him in that condition into thy heart by faith; apply his blood so shed to thy corruptions: do this daily. I might draw out this consideration to a great length, in sundry particulars, but I must come to a close.
paragraphs.modern: Second, exercise faith in Christ’s death in two ways: expect power from it, and seek to be conformed to it. [42] What I have already said should be enough about expecting power. For conformity, Galatians 3:1 helps direct us: look by faith at Christ as the gospel sets him before us, dying and crucified for us. Consider him bearing the weight of our sins, [43] praying, bleeding, and dying. Bring this crucified Christ before your heart through faith, and look to his shed blood as the remedy for your corruptions. Do this daily. I could develop these considerations at much greater length, but I must conclude.

paragraphs.original: 2. I have only, then, to add the heads of the work of the Spirit in this business of mortification, which is so peculiarly ascribed to him. In one word: This whole work, which I have described as our duty, is effected, carried on, and accomplished by the power of the Spirit, in all the parts and degrees of it; as, —
paragraphs.modern: 2. It remains only to outline the Spirit’s work in mortification, which Scripture so particularly attributes to him. In brief: the entire work I have described as our duty is brought about, sustained, and completed by the Spirit’s power, in every part and stage. Consider how.

paragraphs.original: (1.) He alone clearly and fully convinces the heart of the evil and guilt and danger of the corruption, lust, or sin to be mortified. Without this conviction, or whilst it is so faint that the heart can wrestle with it or digest it, there will be no thorough work made. An unbelieving heart (as in part we have all such) will shift with any consideration, until it be overpowered by clear and evident convictions. Now this is the proper work of the Spirit: “He convinces of sin,” John xvi. 8; he alone can do it. If men’s rational considerations, with the preaching of the letter, were able to convince them of sin, we should, it may be, see more convictions than we do.
paragraphs.modern: (1) He alone clearly and thoroughly convinces the heart of the evil, guilt, and danger of the sin to be put to death. Without that conviction—or while it remains weak enough to be argued away or comfortably absorbed—no thorough work will be done. An unbelieving heart, and we all retain some unbelief, will evade any argument until clear conviction overcomes it. This is the Spirit’s distinctive work: he convicts of sin (John 16:8). He alone can accomplish it. If human reasoning combined with the mere hearing of scriptural words could do this, perhaps we would see more genuine conviction than we do.

paragraphs.original: There comes by the preaching of the word an apprehension upon the understandings of men that they are sinners, that such and such things are sins, that themselves are guilty of them; but this light is not powerful, nor doth it lay hold on the practical principles of the soul, so as to conform the mind and will unto them, to produce effects suitable to such an apprehension. And therefore it is that wise and knowing men, destitute of the Spirit, do not think those things to be sins at all wherein the chief movings and actings of lust do consist. It is the Spirit alone that can do, that doth, this work to the purpose.
paragraphs.modern: Preaching can give people an intellectual awareness that they are sinners, that certain actions are sinful, and that they are guilty of them. Yet that awareness may lack the power to reach the motives governing their lives, reshape their minds and wills, and produce an appropriate response. This is also why intelligent, knowledgeable people without the Spirit may fail to recognize as sins the very inward movements in which sinful desire chiefly operates. The Spirit alone can accomplish this work effectively, and he does.

paragraphs.original: And this is the first thing that the Spirit doth in order to the mortification of any lust whatever, — it convinces the soul of all the evil of it, cuts off all its pleas, discovers all its deceits, stops all its evasions, answers its pretences, makes the soul own its abomination, and lie down under the sense of it. Unless this be done all that follows is in vain.
paragraphs.modern: This is the Spirit’s first work in putting any sinful desire to death: he convinces the soul of its evil, cuts off its excuses, exposes its deceptions, closes its escape routes, answers its false defenses, and makes it acknowledge and humble itself over its sin. Unless this happens, everything that follows is futile.

paragraphs.original: (2.) The Spirit alone reveals unto us the fulness of Christ for our relief; which is the consideration that stays the heart from false ways and from despairing despondency, 1 Cor. ii. 8.
paragraphs.modern: (2) The Spirit alone reveals the fullness of Christ’s provision for our help. This is what keeps the heart from false remedies and hopeless despair (1 Corinthians 2:8).

paragraphs.original: (3.) The Spirit alone establishes the heart in expectation of relief from Christ; which is the great sovereign means of mortification, as hath been discovered, 2 Cor. i. 21.
paragraphs.modern: (3) The Spirit alone establishes the heart in the expectation of help from Christ. As we have seen, this is the central and effective means of putting sin to death (2 Corinthians 1:21).

paragraphs.original: (4.) The Spirit alone brings the cross of Christ into our hearts with its sin-killing power; for by the Spirit are we baptized into the death of Christ.
paragraphs.modern: (4) The Spirit alone brings Christ’s cross into our hearts with its power to kill sin. Through the Spirit we are baptized into Christ’s death.

paragraphs.original: (5.) The Spirit is the author and finisher of our sanctification; gives new supplies and influences of grace for holiness and sanctification, when the contrary principle is weakened and abated, Eph. iii. 16–18.
paragraphs.modern: (5) The Spirit begins and completes our sanctification. As the opposing principle of sin is weakened, he supplies fresh grace and power for growth in holiness (Ephesians 3:16–18).

paragraphs.original: (6.) In all the soul’s addresses to God in this condition, it hath supportment from the Spirit. Whence is the power, life, and vigour of prayer? whence its efficacy to prevail with God? Is it not from the Spirit? He is the “Spirit of supplications” promised to them “who look on him whom they have pierced,” Zech. xii. 10, enabling them “to pray with sighs and groans that cannot be uttered,” Rom. viii. 26. This is confessed to be the great medium or way of faith’s prevailing with God. Thus Paul dealt with his temptation, whatever it were: “I besought the Lord that it might depart from me.” [44] What is the work of the Spirit in prayer, whence and how it gives us in assistance and makes us to prevail, what we are to do that we may enjoy his help for that purpose, is not my present intendment to demonstrate.
paragraphs.modern: (6) The Spirit sustains the soul in every approach to God during this struggle. Where do prayer’s power, life, and energy come from? What makes prayer effective before God? The Spirit. He is the promised “Spirit of supplication” given to those who look on the one they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10), enabling prayer with groanings beyond words (Romans 8:26). This is the great means by which faith prevails with God. Paul dealt with his trial, whatever it was, in this way: “I pleaded with the Lord that it might leave me.” [44] A full explanation of the Spirit’s work in prayer—how he helps us, makes our prayers effective, and how we should seek his assistance—lies beyond my present purpose.
